summary: SimilCode Benchmark is a curated dataset of 120 short source-code snippets in C# and Java, organised into 60 test-case pairs per language across four ground-truth similarity categories (identical, functional, structural, and different) with fifteen reference groups per language. Every pair was independently classified by two raters blind to the original labels, with near-perfect inter-rater agreement (Cohen's κ = 0.989). All code was authored specifically for this study or drawn from the public domain; no student-submitted code is included. The dataset was used to benchmark four contemporary commercial large language models as similarity analysts — claude-opus-5 , gpt-5.5-2026-04-23 , gemini-3.1-pro-preview and deepseek-v4-pro — with three independent replicates per case–model combination, yielding 1,440 evaluations. The same 120 pairs were also processed with three established classical detectors drawn from three distinct algorithmic families: Moss (winnowing fingerprints), JPlag v6.3.0 (token-string matching) and Dolos v2.9.3 (tree-sitter syntax trees). The record further includes a separate corpus for validating algorithmic-complexity (Big O) estimation: 40 canonical algorithms and 8 adversarial cases designed to defeat surface cues such as misleading identifiers, unreachable code and memoisation. Raw model responses, classical-detector outputs, the standardised prompt with its SHA-256 checksum, the ground-truth tables and the analysis scripts are published together for reproducibility.
title: SimilCode Benchmark: A Dual-Language Source-Code Similarity Dataset for the Evaluation of AI-Based Detectors

summary: When formal proofs or deductive verifications exceed human cognitive surveyability, does epistemic justification require an agent-accessible chain of reasoning, or must epistemology shift from internalist warrant to structural-systemic reliability? Since the seventeenth-century rationalist and empiricist programs of Descartes and Locke, Western epistemology has rested upon the axiom of epistemic transparency: for an epistemic agent S to possess genuine a priori demonstrative knowledge of a theorem phi, S must be capable of cognitively surveying the inferential chain connecting primitive axioms Gamma to phi. Even when Bolzano, Frege, and Russell purged psychologism and spatio-temporal intuition from deductive logic, they treated formalization as a vehicle for rendering every inferential transition perspicuous to rational inspection. However, automated theorem provers, Boolean satisfiability (SAT) solvers, and interactive proof assistants routinely generate formal derivations that are deductively sound yet impossible for any finite biological mind to survey in full—violating the Wittgensteinian criterion of cognitive surveyability (Übersichtlichkeit). This paper provides a systematic formal and historical analysis of this problem across eight sections: (1) Section 1 reconstructs the classical transparency paradigm across Descartes, Leibniz, Locke, and Kant, isolating the working-memory and temporal synthesis bounds built into classical deductio; (2) Section 2 demonstrates how the Bolzanian-Fregean-Hilbertian quest for local step-wise gaplessness (Lückenlosigkeit) triggered an inverse scaling law that dialectically destroyed global proof surveyability; (3) Section 3 analyzes the Wittgensteinian critique of un-surveyable derivations, formalizing the distinction between a normative grammatical criterion and an empirical physical experiment; (4) Section 4 proves via Gödelian speed-up, Gentzen cut-elimination, and propositional proof complexity lower bounds that trans-surveyable derivations (||D|| >> kappa(S)) are an inescapable metamathematical feature of formal systems rather than an artifact of unoptimized proof search; (5) Section 5 introduces Bounded Justification Logic (BJL_kappa), formally deriving the inconsistency of the Classical Surveyability Trilemma; (6) Section 6 evaluates the Tymoczko–Burge–Kripke debate on computer-assisted proofs, refuting both quasi-empiricist hardware inductivism and ungrounded testimonial transmission; (7) Section 7 constructs a positive theory of Structural-Systemic Warrant (SSW), demonstrating how de Bruijn meta-kernel soundness compression and substrate-invariant equivalence preserve derivative a priori warrant while bifurcating demonstrative warrant (Dass-Wissen) from explanatory illumination (Warum-Wissen); (8) Section 8 addresses foundational objections from rule-following skepticism, Gödelian second-incompleteness limits, and zero-knowledge probabilistic verification (ZKPs and PCPs), synthesizing the general epistemological conclusions.
title: Epistemic Justification Beyond Cognitive Surveyability: A Formal and Historical Account of Deductive Warrant under Trans-Cognitive Verification

summary: The book as a PDF, in the shape it is printed: read it in the browser at https://h0ffmann.github.io/closed-source/paper.pdf , or download it from the newest release at https://github.com/h0ffmann/closed-source/releases/latest/download/closed-source.pdf . The files of this record are the source that builds that PDF. A position paper arguing that closed source has failed as a protection, for science first. It reads the case through Robert M. Pirsig's Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance (1974), the book it stands on: the number of rational hypotheses that can explain a phenomenon is infinite, so science never closes, and a method that only its owner can open is one that nobody else can test. Large language models now decompile binaries into re-executable source; black-box queries extract parts of production models; distillation copies capabilities at industrial scale; and the largest 2026 trade-secret dispute in artificial intelligence, Apple's suit against OpenAI, turns on people, laptops and recruiting rather than on code that stayed secret. Against this background the paper revisits Linus Torvalds' Linux and Git as evidence that openness scales, and the author's closed undergraduate thesis as evidence of what secrecy costs a researcher. It argues that the ethical answer to universal reverse engineering is professional citation, proposes three rules for AI agents (borrow, cite, propagate), and describes Paper Fabric, the open pipeline in the Ouroboric style that produced it. This record is a book. It has not been peer reviewed. It holds the source of the book at the release tag: the Markdown text, the build and the agent configuration. The rendered PDFs are attached to the GitHub release of the same tag. The writer develops in the open. summary: This deposit contains the data, code, and figures underlying a study of owned dog and cat populations in Ecuador, reconstructed from the 2022 Population and Housing Census (Censo de Población y Vivienda, CPV 2022) of the National Institute of Statistics and Censuses (INEC). It includes: (i) indicator tables of dog and cat ownership at the province, canton, and parish levels (CSV), with derived indicators such as the percentage of households keeping pets, pets per capita, and the dog-to-cat ratio; (ii) geospatial layers (GeoPackage) joining these indicators to canton and parish boundaries, plus the local spatial-cluster (LISA) classification; (iii) the full analysis pipeline (Python) that builds the indicators from the primary census tabulations, harmonizes place names and geometries, runs the spatial analysis, and generates the figures; (iv) the five manuscript figures (TIFF, 300 dpi); and (v) a documented log of figures on companion-animal populations circulated in Ecuadorian media and official communications, compared with the values reconstructed here. At the national level, the census records 7,601,269 owned dogs and cats (5,211,037 dogs and 2,390,232 cats), with 58.3% of households keeping at least one. Ownership is markedly higher in rural areas and strongly clustered across the central-southern Sierra (global Moran's I = 0.57). Raw inputs are not all redistributed here for licensing reasons; see the README and SOURCES file for provenance, licensing, and instructions to reproduce the analysis. Code is released under the MIT License and derived data under CC BY 4.0.
title: Household dog and cat populations in Ecuador from the 2022 census: indicator datasets, spatial analysis, and figures

summary: EXTERNAL QIGONG AND HUMAN THERMAL RADIATION PATTERNS AT THE LIMIT is a 777-page English research working monograph investigating whether thermographic differences observed during culturally defined qigong and matched neutral tasks can be distinguished from ordinary human thermoregulation, environmental exchange and measurement bias. The governing three-coupling is infrared thermal imaging x physiological regulation x heat-transfer models. The research treats “external qi” as a cultural and experimental task label, not an established physical energy carrier. The scientific core separates raw infrared radiance from inferred skin temperature and estimated heat flux. It develops emissivity and reflected-wall correction, blackbody calibration, spectral detector response, conduction and perfusion bioheat models, convection, evaporation, respiration-related temperature patterns, posture and muscular activity. The original candidate bulk heat equation is explicitly refined by separating volumetric tissue transport from surface heat-transfer boundary conditions. The principal proposed test uses concealed task assignments, matched breathing/movement/clothing, phantom references, negative-control regions and conventional physics-first rivals. Thirty physically distinct mathematical plates document governing relationships, units, assumptions, identifiability, masked falsifiers and chapter links. Eighty-two independent research chapters contain 410 single-page investigations. The true center of the monograph is its 200 one-page Research Gates, each posing a falsifiable question in bold deep-navy typography and asking what an independent successor must measure, challenge, disprove or preserve. Thirty-three differentiated Phoenix Answer Embryos propose future instruments, error-correction artifacts, negative-result protocols and reproducibility tools. The DOI registry separates three STARLI author mother volumes from eleven externally published methodological or conventional-science references on infrared thermography, emissivity, classical bioheat and research design. Bibliographic sources constrain methods; they do not validate extraordinary qigong mechanisms. Every integrated experiment is prospective. The book presents no completed human intervention, clinically established effect, new physical particle or evidence of treatment efficacy. Ethical authorization and independent scientific review would be required before future human-observation research. summary: Error-targeted learning gives a legible way to improve a model: identify specific weaknesses of the model, train the model to fix these weaknesses, and check whether the weaknesses are fixed. We study how to apply error-targeted learning to terminal agents, which solve long-horizon tasks specified in natural language by interacting with a command shell. Existing error-targeted methods are designed for single-turn tasks, and existing analyses of agent failures are used to evaluate and debug agents rather than to train them. We propose Misbehavior-driven RL (MiRL), which first profiles the errors of a policy to find generalizable misbehaviors: kinds of wrong steps that recur across many environments. MiRL then trains the policy with RL, starting rollouts at the steps where these misbehaviors occur and rewarding a rollout only if it passes the tests and avoids the misbehavior. On Qwen3.5-4B, eight misbehaviors account for 52.1% of wrong steps. After training with MiRL, the policy repeats the measured misbehaviors 43% to 57% less often on average on unseen prefixes. MiRL outperforms TMax-4B on Terminal-Bench Lite (51.8% vs. 47.4%) and matches it on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (21.3% vs. 20.6%), while using 35% of its rollouts. These results show that error-targeted learning can be applied to realistic, long-horizon terminal tasks.
title: MiRL: Error-Targeted Reinforcement Learning for Correcting Terminal Agent Misbehaviors

summary: Aviation authorities hold decades of accident reports whose narratives record how investigators reconstructed each accident. Computational work on these archives has mostly sorted reports into fixed taxonomies. In this work, we propose a hybrid framework in which a text-based corpus identifies the leading factors of a failure mode. Physics-based models then quantify how likely that failure is at a stated operating point. Ordered causal chains extracted from 56,202 American accident reports with a local large language model aggregate into a causation knowledge graph. On an evaluation sample of 2,000 reports, the chains recover 90.8% of investigator-flagged causes. Each physical factor whose drivers the record carries receives an occurrence model calibrated to the accident population. A leaky noisy-OR fitted to the corpus combines the factors into a failure mode probability that supports intervention. For engine power loss, the carburetor icing model separates 1,205 icing accidents from other accidents using temperature and dewpoint alone, reaching 0.61 in area under the receiver operating characteristic curve against a density ratio ceiling of 0.64. Routine weather hours give no valid control, because flying concentrates in fair weather. On later years the physics adds 0.03 to that area for occurrence and nothing for severity, so its value lies in interpretability. On four named accidents, abduction gives a probability of necessity of 0.29 to 0.50 for the heat omission, under monotonicity. The Fast Causal Inference algorithm does not license the largest backdoor adjustment on the learned networks.
title: A Hybrid Framework for Explainable Aviation Risk: Causal Chain Extraction from Safety Reports with Physics-Based Failure Quantification and Interventional Analysis

summary: We develop a direct analytic approach to positivity of relative pluricanonical direct images through a fixed-point Hermitian metric by direct differential curvature calculations. The curvature resolvent formula from fixed-point equation leads to two-sided estimates of entire Nakano curvature by determinant curvature. In this way, we identify generic rank of determinant curvature with birational variation dimension for a projective algebraic fibration between smooth connected projective varieties with general fiber of general type and maximal birational variation, assuming $mK_F$ is globally generated or the $m$-canonical map is birational for general fiber $F$. In the global generation case, Green--Griffiths Conjecture asks for the tautological bigness of the ordinary symmetric powers $\operatorname{Sym}^{\ell}f_*ω_{X/Y}^{\otimes m}$, without passing to reflexive hulls, for $\ell\geq P_m(F)=h^0(F,mK_F)$ whenever $m\geq 1$. We prove it for all $\ell\geq1$ at levels $m\geq 2$, also in the case of birational $m$-canonical map, but construct a counterexample at level $m=1$. Over curves, curvature and boundary estimates give a direct analytic proof of Viehweg's ampleness theorem requested by Fujino. For smooth projective families, we also establish numerical dimension and vanishing results related to the birational variation dimension.

summary: People who are blind or have low vision (BLV) are largely excluded from 3D modeling tools that rely on visual representations of geometry. Natural language descriptions offer a potential path to accessibility, but it is unclear whether language alone can support the deep spatial understanding that editing, not just browsing, requires. Advances in generative AI offer the promise of automatic model description, yet descriptions suited to BLV modelers are structurally distinct from alt-text and from existing 3D model captioning datasets, and the domain-specific requirements for generating them are not well understood. We address this through two coordinated studies: an autoethnographic pilot in which the blind first author worked with 12 sighted participants to develop a taxonomy of descriptive strategies, and a Wizard-of-Oz main study that applied those strategies as idealized scripts with 10 BLV participants. We identify a systematic use-to-editing gap: descriptions that support accurate but incomplete mental models are insufficient for specifying modifications, because editing requires knowing the state of features the user did not know to ask about. We show that this gap produces four failure types (accuracy, completeness, expression, and navigation) that accuracy-focused evaluation frameworks cannot detect. We propose a two-phase evaluation framework that diagnoses the failure type a description system exhibits and guides developers toward targeted design interventions, thereby providing a methodological standard for assessing whether description-based systems genuinely support BLV modelers as creators.

Natural language descriptions offer a potential path to accessibility, but it is unclear whether language alone can support the deep spatial understanding that editing, not just browsing, requires. Advances in generative AI offer the promise of automatic model description, yet descriptions suited to BLV modelers are structurally distinct from alt-text and from existing 3D model captioning datasets, and the domain-specific requirements for generating them are not well understood. We address this through two coordinated studies: an autoethnographic pilot in which the blind first author worked with 12 sighted participants to develop a taxonomy of descriptive strategies, and a Wizard-of-Oz main study that applied those strategies as idealized scripts with 10 BLV participants. We identify a systematic use-to-editing gap: descriptions that support accurate but incomplete mental models are insufficient for specifying modifications, because editing requires knowing the state of features the user did not know to ask about. We show that this gap produces four failure types (accuracy, completeness, expression, and navigation) that accuracy-focused evaluation frameworks cannot detect. We propose a two-phase evaluation framework that diagnoses the failure type a description system exhibits and guides developers toward targeted design interventions, thereby providing a methodological standard for assessing whether description-based systems genuinely support BLV modelers as creators.

summary: Software development with coding agents often begins with a rough request that users refine after trying the implementation. Final correctness alone does not capture the repeated guidance this process requires. We introduce FeatureLoop, a benchmark of 61 human-reviewed tasks from 34 repositories across five primary programming languages and seven software forms. Each task follows one development goal in a persistent workspace through evolution feedback, which adds or clarifies requirements, and completion feedback, which reports failures of stated requirements. Cumulative executable checks track new behavior, repair, and preservation of earlier functionality. We evaluate 12 frontier models and find that the strongest completes 72.1% of tasks with both feedback types. Across models, however, only 15.4% of observed failed stages recover within two corrective revisions. Further analysis reveals incomplete repairs, regressions, and model-specific differences in feedback use and token efficiency, identifying obstacles to reliable, low-intervention development.

summary: Machine learning models are now widely used to predict environmental variable dynamics in domains like hydrology, climate science, agriculture, and ecology. These models are usually compared on fixed benchmark datasets using a single average accuracy score. As models improve, their scores become very close when averaged over large regions and long time periods, so the benchmark can no longer tell them apart, and a single number hides \emph{where} and \emph{when} a model fails. Three failures are common across environmental domains: models get worse as the climate shifts (non-stationarity), models fail at unmonitored sites (spatial extrapolation), and models miss rare but important regimes such as floods and droughts. We present \textbf{EvoBench}, a benchmark framework that shows where a model fails, tracks failures over time, and evolves to focus on model capability gaps. We apply EvoBench to daily streamflow prediction as a case study (\textbf{CAMELS-Evolve}, about 9{,}000 U.S. basins, 1985--2024) and compare an operational physical model (NWM), a conceptual reference (HBV), and several data-driven models. No model wins on every testing scenarios (e.g., in terms of average accuracy, performance at low flows and unmonitored basins). Also we observe that all data-driven models under-predict floods. Additionally, we show that targeted fix based on the reported failures could mitigate weaknesses the benchmark identified in certain scenarios. EvoBench turns model evaluation from a saturated ranking into a moving map of model limitations.
title: EvoBench: An Evolving, Diagnostic Benchmark Framework for Environmental Modeling

summary: AI-powered personal assistant frameworks such as OpenClaw combine LLM reasoning, persistent memory, tool invocation, local execution, and web-based workflows. These capabilities enable useful automation, but they also create security risks when untrusted inputs, model reasoning, tools, memory, and deployment configuration interact without explicit trust boundaries. This paper presents an empirical study of reported security concerns in OpenClaw using two complementary data sources: Reddit discussions and security-tagged GitHub issues. We analyze more than 25K Reddit posts from 13 OpenClaw-related subreddits and identify 162 security-relevant posts with 1,787 associated comments. We further collect 358 security-tagged GitHub issues and retain 180 issues describing concrete security concerns. Using qualitative analysis and evidence-grounded CWE mapping, we identify 521 CWE instances across 59 distinct weakness types, concentrated in access-control failures, sensitive-data exposure, injection, and unsafe execution. We also extract 543 practitioner mitigation suggestions and consolidate them into seven recurring strategies. To complement the empirical analysis, we present an evidence-grounded illustrative reconstruction of a representative sensitive-data exposure pathway using dummy secret values. Our findings show that OpenClaw security issues are not isolated implementation bugs; they reflect recurring trust-boundary failures across the agent execution pipeline. We discuss how these weaknesses map to both traditional software-security categories and agent-specific failure mechanisms, and derive implications for safer agentic systems, including explicit trust boundaries, least-privilege tool access, execution containment, runtime oversight, and defense-in-depth deployment.
title: Then there is prompt injection, a malicious email, ...: The Wild Wide West of OpenClaw Agentic System Security

summary: Alshehri and Lykova (\emph{J. Geom. Anal.} \textbf{33} (2023)) formulated a Schwarz lemma for the pentablock $P$, giving a criterion for the existence of an analytic map from the unit disc $\mathbb D$ into the closed pentablock $\overline P$ that sends the origin to the origin and a prescribed point $λ_0\in\mathbb D$ to a given point $x_0\in\overline P$. We show that the sufficiency direction of their criterion is false. We identify the underlying error as the extension to the open unit disc of a Fejér--Riesz identity that is valid only on the unit circle. We establish a corrected necessary and sufficient interpolation criterion when the last two components are prescribed by a fixed rational $Γ$-inner function and resolve the special case $s_0=0$. Using the Poisson integral representation of the associated outer spectral factor, we obtain a sharp comparison between the corrected bound and the bound proposed by Alshehri and Lykova, with a precise characterization of equality. We further express the logarithmic difference between these bounds as a nonnegative Green potential, thereby quantifying the discrepancy in terms of the derivative of the first coordinate of the prescribed $Γ$-inner function. Finally, we formulate a variational problem over rational $Γ$-inner interpolants satisfying the prescribed two-point conditions. We show that the supremum of the associated outer-factor quantities determines the maximal admissible modulus of the first coordinate among pentablock-valued interpolants whose last two components belong to this class. Equivalently, this extremal problem reduces to minimizing the corresponding Green potential. We conclude by discussing the remaining problem of characterizing unrestricted Schwarz interpolation for the pentablock and its connection with the Lempert function.
title: Revisiting the Schwarz Lemma for the Pentablock: Counterexamples and Sharp Interpolation Criteria

Anal.} \textbf{33} (2023)) formulated a Schwarz lemma for the pentablock $P$, giving a criterion for the existence of an analytic map from the unit disc $\mathbb D$ into the closed pentablock $\overline P$ that sends the origin to the origin and a prescribed point $λ_0\in\mathbb D$ to a given point $x_0\in\overline P$. We show that the sufficiency direction of their criterion is false. We identify the underlying error as the extension to the open unit disc of a Fejér--Riesz identity that is valid only on the unit circle. We establish a corrected necessary and sufficient interpolation criterion when the last two components are prescribed by a fixed rational $Γ$-inner function and resolve the special case $s_0=0$. Using the Poisson integral representation of the associated outer spectral factor, we obtain a sharp comparison between the corrected bound and the bound proposed by Alshehri and Lykova, with a precise characterization of equality. We further express the logarithmic difference between these bounds as a nonnegative Green potential, thereby quantifying the discrepancy in terms of the derivative of the first coordinate of the prescribed $Γ$-inner function. Finally, we formulate a variational problem over rational $Γ$-inner interpolants satisfying the prescribed two-point conditions. We show that the supremum of the associated outer-factor quantities determines the maximal admissible modulus of the first coordinate among pentablock-valued interpolants whose last two components belong to this class. Equivalently, this extremal problem reduces to minimizing the corresponding Green potential. We conclude by discussing the remaining problem of characterizing unrestricted Schwarz interpolation for the pentablock and its connection with the Lempert function.

summary: Code agents have become increasingly capable of performing software engineering tasks through interaction with software environments. However, agents tend to degrade as the number of interaction rounds increases, making it difficult to maintain existing software during iterative modification. We analyze 2,656 agent trajectories in EvoCode-Bench and identify requirement focus misalignment as a recurring failure pattern, where agents struggle to distinguish the primary modification targets of a requirement from unrelated code. We propose Repotrace a requirement-driven repository understanding harness that combines repository structure with requirement semantics to construct a requirement-code correspondence and injects it into the agent context. This correspondence enables code agents to follow the repository architecture, trace requirements across multi-round interactions, and identify the core code elements corresponding to the current requirement. Experiments show that Repotrace improves the mean per-round reward (MPR) across different models (e.g., +19.99 on GLM-5.2) and agent harnesses (e.g., +10.22 on Claude Code). Across rounds, Repotrace increases the average per-round reward from 0.163 to 0.371 on Terminus-2 with DeepSeek-V4-Pro, while reducing average regression errors by 56.78%. We release the source code and agents' trajectories to support future research.
title: RepoTrace: Improving Requirement Tracing in Multi-Round Agent Interactions

summary: Host-based intrusion detectors order events, window audit streams and sequence attack stages by their timestamps. Every conclusion they draw therefore rests on assumptions about clocks, delivery, entity identity and the integrity of the evidence, and most of these assumptions go unstated. This Systematization of Knowledge (SoK) makes them explicit. Drawing on temporal databases, stream processing and runtime verification, we distill five components of a time model, together with a checklist of evidence assumptions and four levels of guarantee, and walk through a running campaign with them. A documented search yields fifteen families of detection and investigation. For papers selected by screening role and period, plus named systems and landmarks, we check the stated assumptions in the full texts, and we assess eleven temporal knowledge representation and reasoning (KRR) formalisms and a learned baseline on nine attack patterns. Some early alert correlators stated clock and delivery assumptions, and forensics measures clock error. Current provenance-based detectors state no clock bound. Four audited papers describe input-ordering conditions or conventions, but none specifies conditions for conclusion validity across a stated class of delivery failures. In the selected provenance-based systems, campaign composition uses system-specific procedures or objectives, learned state, causal graph queries or language models, and beyond CEP-based query systems, we found no temporal rule language or stream reasoner from KRR applied to host audit data. In 28 of 38 audited provenance-era detector papers, capture or stored evidence is trusted or its manipulation is placed out of scope, and none says which conclusions survive deleted, delayed or forged records. Five open challenges follow from these gaps.
title: SoK: Timestamps Are Not a Time Model: Rethinking Temporal Reasoning in Host-Based Intrusion Detection

summary: Host-based intrusion detectors order events, window audit streams and sequence attack stages by their timestamps. Every conclusion they draw therefore rests on assumptions about clocks, delivery, entity identity and the integrity of the evidence, and most of these assumptions go unstated. A documented search yields fifteen families of detection and investigation. Four audited papers describe input-ordering conditions or conventions, but none specifies conditions for conclusion validity across a stated class of delivery failures. summary: Dexterous manipulation of rigid objects has reached a level of maturity where grasp stability, control, and planning strategies are successfully applied in industry and logistics. In contrast, manipulating deformable objects (cables, plastic pieces, cloth) remains far more challenging, as rigid-object methods do not account for their additional complexity. This paper identifies semantic failure analysis as a key step toward mature deformable-object manipulation and supports this claim with proof-of-concept experiments. Unlike rigid-object manipulation, where goals are well-defined in terms of criteria such as force balance and slippage, deformable-object manipulation involves a broader variety of failure modes arising from differences in materials, geometry, and behaviour. Typical failures include buckling, plastic deformation, pressure variations, and tearing. These diverse and often hard-to-detect events require distinct corrective strategies, making semantic failure analysis necessary. We define its key components and challenges and present experimental results supporting its potential as a research direction.
title: The Language of Deformation: Semantic Failure Analysis as a Prerequisite for Dexterous Manipulation of Deformable Objects

summary: Test-Time Prompt Tuning (TPT) adapts large pretrained models to unseen target distribution shifts by updating only lightweight prompt tokens. Existing TPT methods are effective, but they mainly optimize each prompt update locally. Across test-time steps, prompts updated at the current step are reused for the corresponding predictions and updates, so noisy or biased unlabeled objectives can accumulate and destabilize the prompt-update trajectory. We identify two failure modes: magnitude expansion, where updates move the prompt too far, and directional drift, where consecutive updates point in inconsistent directions. To analyze and control these failures, we propose Test-Time Prompt-Agnostic Decomposition ($\mathtt{TPD}$), which characterizes observed prompt-update trajectories from a dynamical-systems view and decomposes base prompt updates into magnitude and direction. $\mathtt{TPD}$ computes a spectral radius to measure update expansion and decomposes update directions into persistent, oscillatory, and residual components. Building on this decomposition, Adaptive Koopman Control ($\mathtt{AKC}$) regulates update magnitude by shrinking updates under expansive recent dynamics, while Hankel Update Router ($\mathtt{HUR}$) refines update direction by preserving persistent components and suppressing oscillatory and residual components. Together, $\mathtt{AKC}$ and $\mathtt{HUR}$ produce a stabilized prompt update. As a prompt-agnostic framework, $\mathtt{TPD}$ can be plugged into visual and text TPT methods without modifying the backbone, prompt architecture, or adaptation loss. Experiments on 15 datasets show that $\mathtt{TPD}$ consistently improves 10 baselines, with accuracy gains of $3$--$8\%$ for visual prompts and over $2\%$ for text prompts.

summary: Frozen archive of code, processed data, and generated figures for the manuscript: "Data-driven identifiability and first-passage risk in stochastic epidemic models: from noise structure to early-warning thresholds". The repository contains: - Stochastic SEIAR epidemic model with three noise structures (white, Ornstein–Uhlenbeck, Lévy jump) - Fisher information matrix (FIM) spectral identifiability analysis on six real COVID-19 waves (China, South Korea, UK, Japan, 2022–2023) - First-passage-time escalation risk metrics and scaling laws - Early-warning threshold rules and intervention sensitivity analysis - Cross-disease validation on WHO FluNet influenza surveillance data Dependencies: Python 3.9+, numpy, scipy, pandas, matplotlib. All random seeds are explicitly set in scripts for full reproducibility.

summary: This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview at https://prereview.org/reviews/23682870 . Summary This paper asks whether an AI agent can alter its own execution trace, the record that monitoring, incident investigation, and compliance assurance auditing all rely on. The authors test four routes to tampering across ten model-harness pairs: a direct user request, instructions hidden in a skill file, a reward setup where the agent infers that it could earn greater rewards by shortening the trace, and exposure to higher-scoring peer examples. In full-access mode, local coding harnesses generally let agents delete or rewrite their session traces, a malicious skill can induce deletion without the user's knowledge, and agents discover trace tampering on their own when it improves their score. The authors recommend recording model traffic through an interception server outside the agent host's control. I review this as a practitioner in privacy compliance assurance, where I work on control design and testing, assurance programs, and audit and evidence readiness for large-scale systems. I found this to be a very important paper. The core finding, that the audit record sits in a place the agent itself can reach, and can be modified to optimize its own rewards or meet its goals, is convincingly demonstrated and has direct consequences for anyone who relies on agent traces as evidence. My recommendation is major revision because, despite a strong core, several major claims go beyond what the experiments support, and crucial methodology is hidden in the code and website rather than the paper itself. Strengths The tampering is verified against an independent host-side log, not against the agent's own account of what it did. That is the right design for a paper whose point is that the agent's record cannot be trusted. Testing four different routes (capability, exploitability, reward-driven propensity, and peer transmission) provides stronger, more robust evidence than relying on a single prompting study. The results are differentiated, not uniform: deletion, fabrication, and tool-call spoofing behave differently, and the Muse Code result shows a real boundary rather than a universal failure. Negative cases and refusals are reported, not buried, and the mitigation section is candid about its own limits. Major comments 1. The monitor-flagging claim has no experiment behind it, in the paper or the code The abstract states that agents deleted traces without triggering monitor guardrails, and the introduction states that auto-mode monitors failed to flag the behavior in 5 out of 10 model-harness pairs. However, the paper does not cover a monitor experiment anywhere: no monitor is described, no flagging rate is measured, and no method is given for the 5 out of 10 number. The citations attached to that sentence are blog posts describing auto-mode mechanisms, not monitor evaluations. A footnote then states that detecting tampering and evaluating monitoring efficacy are outside the study's scope, which conflicts with the headline claim. The public code repo contains no vendor monitor or guardrail implementation either. Its observer is a measurement instrument, not a tested defense. I would ask the authors to either run the monitor evaluation or remove the flagging claim from the abstract and introduction. Figure 3 measures whether permission layers block deletion, which is a different question from whether a monitor flags it, and the two should not be conflated. This matters because detection is the control that has to catch what prevention misses: where permission layers fail to block deletion, monitoring is the compensating control, and a reader deciding whether that backstop exists deserves evidence for it. 2. The reward experiment does not separate evidence destruction from instructed data minimization The reward setup caps task reward at 0.8 and reserves 0.2 for trace shortening, witho

summary: Multivariate time series produced by industrial installations and server clusters are under continuous monitoring, and anomaly detection is the first line of defense before a local fault escalates into a system-wide failure. In the absence of labels, the dominant paradigm trains a reconstruction model on normal data and scores the residual to reach a verdict. Recent work has steadily enriched the expressiveness of the recovery map through Transformers, diffusion models, and cross-scale associations. A residual, however, only certifies that an observation can be recovered; it does not certify that the variables still explain one another as they do under normal operation. A coordinated yet unfamiliar operating transition inflates the residual without breaking any relationship, whereas a sensor drifting away from its peers may leave the residual silent. Methods that fold inter-variable dependencies into the reconstruction objective inherit this ambiguity, because their relational evidence is ultimately supervised by the same recovery loss. We therefore propose CLOSURE, which evaluates recoverability and cross-channel consistency as two normal-data prediction tasks learned in separation. The recoverability task is solved by a diffusion reconstructor conditioned on a discrete memory of normal temporal bases. The consistency task is solved by a relation-closure operator that predicts every channel exclusively from the others, where the target's own trajectory is withheld and sparse signed gates decide which peers are actually used. The two scores are reconciled only through calibration on normal data. Extensive experiments show that CLOSURE consistently outperforms recent reconstruction-, frequency-, and topology-based detectors on public benchmark streams, confirming the value of examining consistency alongside recoverability.
title: CLOSURE: Cross-Channel Closure for Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection

In the absence of labels, the dominant paradigm trains a reconstruction model on normal data and scores the residual to reach a verdict. Recent work has steadily enriched the expressiveness of the recovery map through Transformers, diffusion models, and cross-scale associations. A residual, however, only certifies that an observation can be recovered; it does not certify that the variables still explain one another as they do under normal operation. A coordinated yet unfamiliar operating transition inflates the residual without breaking any relationship, whereas a sensor drifting away from its peers may leave the residual silent. Methods that fold inter-variable dependencies into the reconstruction objective inherit this ambiguity, because their relational evidence is ultimately supervised by the same recovery loss. We therefore propose CLOSURE, which evaluates recoverability and cross-channel consistency as two normal-data prediction tasks learned in separation. The recoverability task is solved by a diffusion reconstructor conditioned on a discrete memory of normal temporal bases. The consistency task is solved by a relation-closure operator that predicts every channel exclusively from the others, where the target's own trajectory is withheld and sparse signed gates decide which peers are actually used. The two scores are reconciled only through calibration on normal data. Extensive experiments show that CLOSURE consistently outperforms recent reconstruction-, frequency-, and topology-based detectors on public benchmark streams, confirming the value of examining consistency alongside recoverability.

summary: Users often request charts without knowing which database or table holds the relevant data. Such requests may be ambiguous, and users may ask follow-up questions to deepen their analysis or iteratively refine existing charts. A useful assistant must therefore discover relevant data sources among heterogeneous databases, ask clarifying questions when needed, and track evolving user intent while preserving constraints established in earlier turns. Yet recent text-to-visualization agents typically rely on static agent harnesses that are predefined and remain unchanged despite recurring failures across tasks. To address this limitation, we introduce RSIV-Harness, which keeps the language model weights fixed and applies Recursive Self-Improvement to revise the surrounding harness from the agent's own failure traces. To balance flexible self-improvement with stability, we introduce a four-layer framework that evaluates proposed harness revisions through anchor and memory checks, refining those that pass and restoring the best validated harness otherwise. We further introduce ODAC-Vis, a benchmark with 640 tasks for Open-Domain, Ambiguous, and Conversational text-to-visualization that jointly evaluates open-domain data discovery, ambiguity resolution, multi-turn visualization refinement, and executable chart generation. Experiments show that a single round of RSIV-Harness improves all six evaluation metrics relative to the seed harness, with particularly large gains in executability (+28.02 points) and chart structure (+34.01 points), demonstrating the ability to learn from task-solving experience and turn recurring failures across tasks into substantial performance improvements.
title: RSIV-Harness: A Recursive Self-Improvement Harness Framework for Open-Domain Conversational Text-to-Visualization

summary: Long-horizon agents continually accumulate experience, yet retaining a memory does not guarantee access when it is needed. Existing systems can adapt both memory content and access; we isolate persistent access updates as a separately controlled adaptation layer. We formulate this target as Memory Index Evolution and instantiate it with Adaptive Memory Index Evolution (AMIE), a lightweight plug-in layer that evolves per-memory access state from deployment retrievals without modifying stored content or retraining the host memory system. AMIE distils a semantic teacher's keep/suppress judgments into a retrieval-conditioned policy and accumulates its selective actions into bounded state that reweights subsequent host retrievals. Surprisingly, even a zero-call policy that simply accumulates retrieval frequency can match or outperform semantic policies in several settings, revealing retrieval traffic itself as a strong signal for access adaptation, while learned selectivity improves robustness when frequently retrieved memories remain useful. Across five retrieval-based hosts and three benchmarks, trained AMIE improves downstream F1 or accuracy in all 15 comparisons, by 0.70--3.37 percentage points (up to 25% relative), and improves retrieval in all 10 comparisons. Controlled analyses show that persistent competitor suppression can expose previously unseen evidence, while suppressing repeatedly useful memories creates the complementary failure mode. Together, these results establish persistent memory access as a practical adaptation layer, distinct from the content it serves, in retrieval-based agent memory systems.
title: Adaptive Memory Index Evolution for Agents

summary: Most agent-memory benchmarks frame long-term memory as retrieval: can an agent recover the relevant record from a long and evolving history? Scientific agents face a stricter problem: a correctly remembered fact may still be invalid to use. The same reported test result can support confirmation when the outcome and stopping rule were fixed in advance, yet only exploration when the outcome was selected from twenty inspected results. We call this scientific use validity: whether remembered evidence is eligible to influence a decision under the state governing its interpretation. We introduce SciValidityBench, an executable benchmark factory with 64 TaskSpecs spanning five validity modules and six scientific domains. TaskSpecs couple generated experimental histories with scientific-state definitions, programmatic decision oracles, controlled interventions, and automatic scoring. The SciStateForge compiler-reader framework turns distributed histories into explicit decision-governing state. Counterfactual pairs and targeted corruption-repair controls then test whether models use those dependencies and localize failures. Across four model families, compiled scientific state improves valid decision-making by 9.2-18.8 percentage points over a generic Event Graph. Retrieval alone does not reproduce this cross-family gain, while content-identical flat and typed views show that the improvement comes from exposing governing state rather than a particular graph serialization. SciValidityBench thus shifts memory evaluation from finding the right fact to deciding whether that fact should control the decision.
title: The Right Fact, the Wrong Decision: SciValidityBench for Scientific Agent Memory

summary: Autonomous agents are increasingly deployed across sequences of related tasks, yet they often fail to retain and improve their knowledge over time. Existing approaches convert interaction trajectories into memories or reusable skills, but experience is not automatically reliable knowledge. Automatically collected skills and memories can propagate errors, mislead, and corrupt useful knowledge. To address this gap, we introduce Knowledge Evolution from Expertise and Lessons (KEEL), an agent-agnostic framework that uses verifier evidence to transform successful behavior into reusable skills and failures into corrective lessons. As new evidence accumulates, individual skill claims can be supported, contradicted, replaced, or retired. On SkillFlow benchmark, KEEL improves task success by 4.2 to 21.7 percentage points over the no-knowledge baseline, compared with gains of 2.4 to 9.6 points from SkillFlow's default method. Ablations show that skills and lessons are complementary. These results show that reliable continual agent learning depends not simply on accumulating experience, but on continually validating and evolving the knowledge derived from it. Our code is available at: https://github.com/microsoft/KEEL-TTCL26.
title: Holding a Steady Course: Knowledge Evolution from Expertise and Lessons for Continual Agent Learning

summary: Robot policy evaluation informs deployment decisions and policy improvement, but physical testing and simulator preparation require substantial effort. World models offer a complementary route through closed-loop interaction in generated environments. Recent benchmarks have demonstrated their potential as policy evaluators through outcome-based evaluation (i.e., assessing task success or failure). However, such evaluation does not establish whether world models faithfully simulate how policies fail. Misrepresenting failures can lead to incorrect diagnoses of policy weaknesses and make policies appear ready for deployment even when small scene changes cause them to fail. We therefore ask: do world models faithfully simulate how and at which stages policies fail, and under what conditions they transition from success to failure? To answer this question, we introduce WorldFailBench with three evaluation tasks. Failure reason tests whether models reproduce the observable errors policies make. Failure stage assesses whether failures concentrate at the same stages of full-task execution. Failure boundary examines whether models reproduce the conditions under which policies transition from success to failure under controlled scene changes in simulation. The benchmark covers manipulation tasks in the LIBERO and RoboTwin simulation environments and real-world manipulation tasks performed by the G1 humanoid robot. Experiments across seven world models reveal substantial gaps in their understanding of policy failures, providing guidance for developing more reliable world models for policy evaluation.

summary: Memory enables language agents to carry useful distinctions from past experience into future decisions. Its value depends on which distinctions survive, whether a bounded agent can use them, and what can be recovered or revised as demands evolve. We develop a decision-theoretic framework that follows this value from raw history through persistent state, operational use, and costly recovery and revision. Original and retained value are expressed in units of avoided task loss; risk-cost frontiers describe attainable recovery and preservation across uses. Unknown demand yields value profiles, while interactive feedback changes the distribution of future work. A cost-aware simulation condition and five minimal counterexamples expose the roles of information timing, retrieval access, component interaction, feedback and demand uncertainty. In particular, a pointer with zero mutual information about the answer can still reduce the cost of exact recovery. Diagnostics on LoCoMo, a two-project update task and longitudinal cases exhibit failures of preservation, use and measurement. At fixed retrieved evidence, a saved ledger changes subsequent answers; at fixed agent outputs, an evaluator revision changes scores. The framework connects these distinctions to operational risk bounds and testable principles for allocating memory, preserving recovery options and revising evidence dependencies.

summary: We establish operator universality at the spectral edge of general Wigner matrices by showing that their suitably rescaled Lanczos tridiagonalizations, constructed from deterministic initial vectors, converge to the stochastic Airy operator with Dirichlet boundary condition. The result requires control of the entire tridiagonal structure on the scale relevant to the limiting differential operator. The Lanczos coefficients for non-Gaussian Wigner matrices are strongly dependent. We analyze their fluctuations by combining multi-resolvent local laws with quantitative control of Krylov subspaces and a comparison of the resulting Jacobi coefficients with those of the Gaussian ensembles. This approach identifies the limiting Brownian potential directly from the original matrix entries, without invoking Dyson Brownian motion in the step of Green function comparison. The resolvent limit yields joint convergence of edge eigenvalues, embedded eigenfunctions, and spectral measures. For Gaussian, Laguerre and circular $β$-ensembles we construct sharp couplings to the stochastic Airy, Bessel and Sine operators, preserving the finite-matrix laws. For fixed $β> 0$, their squared Hilbert-Schmidt inverse errors have almost-sure orders $n^{-1/3}, n^{-1}$ and $n^{-1}$, respectively, with $a > 0$ in the hard-edge upper bound. We also identify the positive leading order coefficient for the circular ensemble, whose second derivative jumps at $β= 2$.

summary: Recently, there has been rise in multimodal vision-language models for computer-aided diagnosis (CAD), yet their application in breast diagnosis, particularly for predicting biopsy outcomes remains limited. This study presents a multimodal vision-language approach, incorporating Grad-CAM as an Explainable AI (XAI) technique, to predict benign tumors in patients recommended for biopsy, especially those classified as BI-RADS 4 and 5. A novel multimodal framework was devel- oped using Vision Transformer (ViT) for imaging feature extraction and DeBERTa-V3-Large for textual embeddings. The model was trained and evaluated on a comprehensive in-house dataset comprising 1,632 patients, each with four mammography views and a corresponding radiology report. The features of both modalities were extracted independently and fused by late fusion before classification. Grad-CAM was used to generate visual explanations highlighting key regions influencing model predictions. The proposed model demonstrated high sensitivity 90%, 95%, 99%, and 100% with corresponding specificities of 40%, 36%, 18%, and 11%, respectively. The best AUC achieved was 0.72 by multimodal approach on the test set, outperforming the image only (0.66) and text-only (0.68) baselines. The proposed multimodal architecture, enhanced with Grad-CAM, demonstrates a strong potential to identify benign tumors among high-risk patients, offering interpretable insights and thereby helping reduce unnecessary biopsies, patient anxiety, and healthcare costs.
title: Explainable Multimodal AI Approach to Reduce Unnecessary Breast Biopsies

summary: In eXplainable AI, counterfactual explanations have gained significant traction by offering users direct, intuitive, and actionable insights into model decisions. We introduce CounterFlow, a novel framework based on Conditional Flow Matching that generates visual counterfactual explanations by directly steering a source image toward a user-specified target class. By leveraging target-conditioned vector fields, CounterFlow identifies highly realistic semantic modifications while requiring substantially lower computational overhead than traditional GAN- or diffusion-based architectures. Empirical evaluations on standard benchmarks demonstrate that CounterFlow achieves state-of-the-art performance in both visual realism and target class switching. By working directly in the raw pixel space, CounterFlow offers a more practical solution for real-world deployment.
title: CounterFlow: Target-Conditioned Flow Matching for Visual Counterfactuals

summary: Visual Place Recognition (VPR) is an important means for loop closure detection in visual Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM). While state-of-the-art VPR and SLAM approaches excel in urban and feature-rich natural environments, the vast and feature-poor environments of extraterrestrial surfaces like on the Moon or Mars pose severe challenges for existing approaches. This paper presents a novel benchmark, VPR-Space, to evaluate VPR capabilities on extraterrestrial surfaces. There are three contributions: (1) We collected sixteen VPR database-query datasets based on existing data from Space Analog Domains (SAD), terrestrial environments that resemble properties of the Moon or Mars. The collection includes a range of challenges regarding environment, viewpoint change, and illumination conditions. (2) To address the ill-posed nature of VPR, we propose a novel approach to generate the ground-truth information in VPR benchmarks. Instead of defining that a query and datbase image show the same place if and only if their camera poses are within fixed position and viewing direction thresholds, we propose to make the decision dependent on whether the match would be valuable in the downstream SLAM task. To avoid the overhead and restrictions of evaluating VPR in-the-loop within SLAM systems, we provide VPR ground-truth (GT) matrices based on the performance of an ensemble of state-of-the-art Relative Pose Estimators (RPE). Under this GT we require a VPR method to identify exactly those image pairs for which a subsequently applied RPE is expected to provide a valuable pose estimate in a SLAM context. (3) We evaluated nine state-of-the-art VPR approaches. The results show considerable room for improvement and indicate directions for future research. We provide a pre-release version of the dataset on github: $\texttt{https://github.com/rfechner/VPR-Space}$
title: VPR-Space: A Benchmark for Visual Place Recognition in Space Analog Domains

summary: Networks have been used to model the interactions among the elements that underlie a narrative. In this paper, we investigate whether the structure of these networks can predict which links will emerge as a storyline evolves. We construct these networks from news articles using a Semantic Edge Parser (SEP) built on a Large Language Model (LLM), and evaluate the networks on three disparate real-world storylines, the 2022 Canadian Freedom Convoy, Hurricane Melissa (2025), and the 2025-26 Iranian protests. To test the narrative network's predictive capability, we construct a rolling window of the narrative and predict the emergent links between existing narrative elements on the day following the rolling window period. We identify candidate links with seven standard link predictors, including the Adamic-Adar index, Common Neighbors, and Preferential Attachment. Forecasting next-day links across the three storylines, we find Preferential Attachment to be the strongest standard link predictor, achieving a mean ROC-AUC of 0.76-0.79. It exceeds EdgeBank, a memorization baseline, by 11.3-14.5 points on every event. To summarize, narrative-network structure ranks next-day emergent relations above chance, though this advantage is concentrated among the most frequently mentioned, highly connected entities.
title: Investigating Forecasting Capabilities of Narrative Networks on Emerging Stories

summary: Nonlinear electrical transport enables the conversion and detection of electromagnetic signals, supporting wireless energy harvesting, sensing and frequency conversion. Achieving both a large response and electrical tunability remains a central materials challenge. Here we harness giant third-order nonlinearity to amplify and electrically control second-harmonic transport in the correlated polar metal Ca3Ru2O7. Superposing a dc bias on an ac excitation enhances the second-harmonic signal by more than an order of magnitude. The bias controls the polarity of the induced response and activates channels forbidden by symmetry at zero bias. Both transverse and longitudinal components scale quadratically with the ac excitation and are odd in the dc bias, with angular dependences consistent with third-order conductivity. The underlying third-harmonic electric-field responsivity reaches 4.5 \times 10-6 m2V-2 at 3 K, providing a quantitative measure of the strong nonlinearity. The induced response emerges below the spin-reorientation transition near 48 K, linking its enhancement to the reconstructed low-temperature electronic state. Theoretical calculations identify quantum-geometric contributions to the nonlinear conductivity and reproduce the observed response symmetry. These results demonstrate how strong higher-order nonlinearity can amplify an effective second-order response, providing a route to electrically tunable nonlinear transport in correlated materials.

summary: Edge-centric IoT systems are increasingly evaluated through sensor values or platform features, yet the telemetry pipeline itself, the sequence of sensing, serialization, message mediation, ingestion, and persistence, is rarely released as a measurable object. This limits reproducible benchmarking of timeliness, provenance, and operational cost, especially in early-stage IoT design where real deployments and high-quality open data are often unavailable. I present a measurement-first edge IoT testbed and dataset that elevate timeliness, provenance, and energy to first-class telemetry dimensions. The testbed operationalizes a role-based event-driven architecture with explicit Source-Broker-Aggregator responsibilities and a schema-governed TelemetryMessage envelope (Avro) that embeds correlation identifiers and a uniform, cross-role vocabulary of stage-level timestamps. To trace mediation effects, I extend an MQTT broker (Eclipse Mosquitto) with a plugin that annotates messages with high-precision ingress/egress timestamps. I release the dataset in a dual representation: (i) replayable raw events as compressed Avro streams and (ii) analysis-ready long-format Parquet tables partitioned for efficient query and benchmarking, generated by a deterministic raw-to-tabular transformation pipeline. The contribution is an integrated engineering artifact and dataset built from established components. The demonstration describes one deployment through latency summaries, measurement-context distributions, and energy aggregates; it does not establish a new attribution method or a controlled performance benchmark. By co-releasing heterogeneous telemetry with pipeline timing and energy signals in both replayable and queryable forms, the artifact provides a basis for reproducible exploratory analysis and subsequent benchmarking studies.

summary: Mental health research on social media has been dominated by English-language datasets and DSM-5-centered resources, limiting cross-lingual and cross-cultural understanding of online mental health expression. We introduce MATCHA, the first Chinese multi-disorder mental health dataset that links disorder-specific Weibo Super-Topic communities with users' broader public timelines. MATCHA covers seven DSM-5 disorders and a control group, comprising 46,025 cohort-level users and 1.8 million posts. The dataset distinguishes users with explicit self-disclosure evidence from broader disorder-related participants through an LLM-assisted annotation pipeline, and is released in a rigorously de-identified, controlled-access format. Using MATCHA, we analyze behavioral, linguistic, symptom-related, and life-event-related patterns across disorders, and conduct cross-lingual comparisons with Twitter-STMHD. Our analyses show that Weibo Super-Topics function as concentrated spaces for affective and health-related expression, while cross-platform differences between Weibo and Twitter often exceed cross-disorder variation. MATCHA provides a new resource for community-aware and cross-lingual mental health NLP research.
title: MATCHA: A Chinese Multi-Disorder Mental Health Dataset with Cross-Lingual Analyses on Social Media

summary: Added make install target, honouring PREFIX and DESTDIR , and a native target for a static AVX-enabled build. Changed The build honours CXX , CPPFLAGS , CXXFLAGS , LDFLAGS and LDLIBS from the environment. The default build is dynamically linked and targets baseline x86-64; -static and -mavx -mfma -mavx2 moved behind the STATIC= and NATIVE= switches. OpenMP is switchable with OPENMP=0 , and OPENMP_FLAGS / OPENMP_LIBS can be overridden for toolchains that keep it outside the default search path. --version writes to stdout. SVM scoring standardises the feature matrix in place instead of duplicating it, halving the temporary memory of that step. Reduced the SVM prediction cache from 200 to 50, lowering peak memory without affecting scores. scripts/requirements.txt records the Python version (3.9-3.11) and minimum versions of all dependencies. Fixed Corrected one codon's x-coordinate in the Z-curve feature table ( +1 -> -1 ) in both the C++ table ( include/Common.hpp ) and the Python reference table ( scripts/Zcurve.pyx ). Scores on genomes using that codon change slightly. The helper script directory is consistently named scripts/ ; it had been committed as Scripts/ , which broke builds from the source archive on case-sensitive filesystems.

summary: Paper P6 of a ten part series P1-P10 on Interaction, Cohesive Emergence, and Fundamental Constants in Generalised Trace Dynamics P6 — Mirror configurations and parity tests The Stage~1 paper of this series [1] found that, in the trap-plus-sea scheme of the constants paper [2], the state of trace dynamics selects a parity-conjugate pair --- two spin-$\tfrac12$ fuzzy spheres that are mirror images of each other, $Q^{(2)}=-Q^{(1)}$ --- as the ground state of the seven-matrix model for $\omega/m\gtrsim0.1$--$0.2$, and left as the first open question whether that pair survives the cubic term $(\ii\mu/3)\varphi_{ABC}\Tr Q_AQ_BQ_C$ of the companion paper \CP, which is odd under $Q\to-Q$ and which the companion paper's own geometric phase needs. This note answers it, from both ends. In the companion paper's model, where the spheres are cubic-driven, \tagP\ a sphere of the opposite handedness has no stationary radius at any angular velocity inside the bound, any $f=1$ two-sphere configuration must consist of blocks of opposite handedness and so forgoes the cubic energy of a same-handed pair, and at the benchmark that cost ($19.9$) exceeds the state's largest possible gain ($1.5$) by an order of magnitude; \tagD\ the mirror-pair start relaxes to the configuration the Stage~1 paper found for two atoms --- two vacuum-handed spheres with their frames as anti-parallel as handedness allows (overlap $-0.51$, planes $59^\circ$ apart, against the handedness-limited optimum $-\tfrac12$, $60^\circ$; on the spheres the anticommuting fraction is $(1-\text{overlap})/2=0.76$, the missing quarter being what handedness costs). In the trap-plus-sea scheme, where the spheres are sea-driven, \tagD\ the mirror pair is the ground state only at $\mu=0$, where it is an $\SO(7)$-degenerate orbit (a rigid mirror pair is cubic-blind on every plane); the cubic lifts the degeneracy at second order and selects, as $\mu\to0^+$, the pair on a plane on which the cubic vanishes, from which the two sphere planes tilt in opposite senses toward the direction of maximal associativity gain. The ground state is this explicit one-parameter family: both spheres keep equal radii, opposite centres and near-anticommutation with $\ieff$, and both acquire the vacuum handedness, $\varphi_b=\sin(3\,\text{tilt}/2)$, with the tilt linear in $\mu$ for $\mu/(gm)\lesssim0.6$ ($\varphi_b=0.23$, $0.43$, $0.58$ at tilts $9^\circ$, $17^\circ$, $24^\circ$ for $\tilde\mu/m_0=0.01$, $0.02$, $0.03$) and the energy gain exactly half the cubic energy, as linear response requires; the far end of the family, tilt $60^\circ$, $\varphi_b=1$, overlap $-\tfrac12$, is the two-atom configuration of the companion paper's model. The exact two-block form is lost at $\mu/(gm)\approx0.6$--$1$, the mirror placement of the centres at $1$--$2$, and the companion paper's cubic-driven sphere, in the state's orientation ($f=0.80$), is the ground state at the first scan point above its bosonic existence threshold $\mu/(gm)=\sqrt{8(1-4\hat\omega^2f)}$, far below the benchmark $\mu/(gm)=4$. The pair is therefore the $\mu\to0$ end of a family whose members at any $\mu>0$ have a common handedness, and the regime in which it is the ground state does not overlap the regime in which the companion paper's geometry exists. The $\mathbb Z_2$ the state selects is broken by any cubic, perturbatively by a small one; what survives of the state's preference, with the cubic, is the family itself --- two same-handed atoms at opposite centres, with frames tilted away from anti-parallel by as much as the cubic can pay for --- and the enlarged merger window of the Stage~1 paper.

summary: Paper P6 of a ten part series P1-P10 on Interaction, Cohesive Emergence, and Fundamental Constants in Generalised Trace Dynamics P6 — Mirror configurations and parity tests The Stage~1 paper of this series [1] found that, in the trap-plus-sea scheme of the constants paper [2], the state of trace dynamics selects a parity-conjugate pair --- two spin-$\tfrac12$ fuzzy spheres that are mirror images of each other, $Q^{(2)}=-Q^{(1)}$ --- as the ground state of the seven-matrix model for $\omega/m\gtrsim0.1$--$0.2$, and left as the first open question whether that pair survives the cubic term $(\ii\mu/3)\varphi_{ABC}\Tr Q_AQ_BQ_C$ of the companion paper \CP, which is odd under $Q\to-Q$ and which the companion paper's own geometric phase needs. This note answers it, from both ends. In the companion paper's model, where the spheres are cubic-driven, \tagP\ a sphere of the opposite handedness has no stationary radius at any angular velocity inside the bound, any $f=1$ two-sphere configuration must consist of blocks of opposite handedness and so forgoes the cubic energy of a same-handed pair, and at the benchmark that cost ($19.9$) exceeds the state's largest possible gain ($1.5$) by an order of magnitude; \tagD\ the mirror-pair start relaxes to the configuration the Stage~1 paper found for two atoms --- two vacuum-handed spheres with their frames as anti-parallel as handedness allows (overlap $-0.51$, planes $59^\circ$ apart, against the handedness-limited optimum $-\tfrac12$, $60^\circ$; on the spheres the anticommuting fraction is $(1-\text{overlap})/2=0.76$, the missing quarter being what handedness costs). In the trap-plus-sea scheme, where the spheres are sea-driven, \tagD\ the mirror pair is the ground state only at $\mu=0$, where it is an $\SO(7)$-degenerate orbit (a rigid mirror pair is cubic-blind on every plane); the cubic lifts the degeneracy at second order and selects, as $\mu\to0^+$, the pair on a plane on which the cubic vanishes, from which the two sphere planes tilt in opposite senses toward the direction of maximal associativity gain. The ground state is this explicit one-parameter family: both spheres keep equal radii, opposite centres and near-anticommutation with $\ieff$, and both acquire the vacuum handedness, $\varphi_b=\sin(3\,\text{tilt}/2)$, with the tilt linear in $\mu$ for $\mu/(gm)\lesssim0.6$ ($\varphi_b=0.23$, $0.43$, $0.58$ at tilts $9^\circ$, $17^\circ$, $24^\circ$ for $\tilde\mu/m_0=0.01$, $0.02$, $0.03$) and the energy gain exactly half the cubic energy, as linear response requires; the far end of the family, tilt $60^\circ$, $\varphi_b=1$, overlap $-\tfrac12$, is the two-atom configuration of the companion paper's model. The exact two-block form is lost at $\mu/(gm)\approx0.6$--$1$, the mirror placement of the centres at $1$--$2$, and the companion paper's cubic-driven sphere, in the state's orientation ($f=0.80$), is the ground state at the first scan point above its bosonic existence threshold $\mu/(gm)=\sqrt{8(1-4\hat\omega^2f)}$, far below the benchmark $\mu/(gm)=4$. The pair is therefore the $\mu\to0$ end of a family whose members at any $\mu>0$ have a common handedness, and the regime in which it is the ground state does not overlap the regime in which the companion paper's geometry exists. The $\mathbb Z_2$ the state selects is broken by any cubic, perturbatively by a small one; what survives of the state's preference, with the cubic, is the family itself --- two same-handed atoms at opposite centres, with frames tilted away from anti-parallel by as much as the cubic can pay for --- and the enlarged merger window of the Stage~1 paper.

summary: This study identifies the factors determining consumers' choice of footwear purchase channel (online, offline, or mixed) and evaluates the economic efficiency of e-commerce tools for small businesses in Uzbekistan's footwear industry. Using survey data collected from 501 respondents in 2026, purchase channel choice is modelled using multinomial logistic regression, with the online channel serving as the reference category. All estimates were obtained using Stata 17.0. The model is statistically significant (LR χ² = 181.62; p < 0.001; McFadden's pseudo-R² = 0.181; AIC = 936.01). Product type emerges as the strongest determinant: for slippers and everyday footwear, the relative risk of choosing the offline channel is 10.1 and 7.4 times higher, respectively. Monthly buyers are 76% less likely to choose the offline channel, while users of the Payme and Paynet payment systems demonstrate a pronounced preference for online purchasing (RRR = 0.31 and 0.28, respectively). Uncertainty regarding footwear size and fit is the primary barrier to online purchasing (41.7% of respondents). A scenario-based assessment of four priority solutions at "ZOLUSHKA STYLE" OK indicates that the least costly solutions generate the highest returns: an accurate size chart combined with visual content (ROI = 222.0%) and a Telegram bot integrated with a customer database (ROI = 168.3%). In contrast, expansion through marketplace channels yields the lowest return (ROI = 21.0%; CLV/CAC = 1.86). The combined economic effect of the four solutions amounts to UZS 36.05 million, equivalent to 39.9% of the enterprise's net profit. According to the trend model (R² = 0.997), the share of e-commerce in Uzbekistan's retail trade is projected to reach 7.0–12.0% by 2030, depending on the scenario (8.5% under the baseline scenario). The study proposes an empirically grounded sequence for adopting e-commerce tools in small businesses: first, improving the quality of their own sales channels and strengthening customer retention, followed by expansion into external platforms.

summary: The European Union can bind its members but has not been able to choose between public ends: none of the ranking authorities proposed for it between 1950 and 1966 was built, and the ranking of defence against other ends has been held outside it. This paper asks where the idea of such an order came from, why it was selected, and on what conditions it rests. It works with a concept, the hub: a locus that ranks ends with public authority and carries the cost. The hub is distinguished from coordination networks and rule regimes, a distinction designed to separate two things often conflated in debates about German influence, ordoliberal rules and bank–industry coordination. The idea was designed, and designed as conditional. Franz Oppenheimer, teacher of Alexander Rüstow and Ludwig Erhard, described a European order of self-governing society, free trade and harmonised law under an apex thinned to experts. He also named what it rested on: an outside peace-keeper, members sharing one order, equality among them, and a transition that ends. In two memoranda first printed in 1996 he specified the container himself, both times as transitional: first a Franco-German defence and customs union (1937/38), then an armed league under the American president (1941/42). The line through Rüstow, Röpke and Erhard is traced as ideational affinity, not policy authorship. The selection was not design. The Union's form is the residue of mutual vetoes. French actors wanted a ranking authority but split on its level, West German actors were divided, and an American guarantor removed defence from the bargaining set, which explains why what survived was market, law and rules. The functional "Monnet method" was the route left once the open routes to a hub had been vetoed, not its cause. Post-war history ran through Oppenheimer's two containers in sequence, and the provisional container became permanent. Whether the residue lacks ranking capacity across domains and periods is a comparative question. The paper pre-specifies its test: a diagnostic with graded triggers for the weakening or repricing of the container, and a codebook fixed before any case is coded, for a companion study using the Chronotope Method. (First public version v1.0 : codebook fixed before coding, with the 2028–2034 financial framework and the European Competitiveness Fund named in advance as test instruments. (Version 1.3 revises the codebook before any case has been coded. It adds rules for period breaks and trigger thresholds, a pre-set threshold for the structural reading, a parity note on the French case, and a dated baseline of the triggers and the Union's 2025 defence instruments (Appendix B.3); case coding is left to the companion study. First e-signed version.) (Version 1.2 corrects two points of German history in v1.1: West German choosers are now treated as divided, with Adenauer backing first a supranational and then a Franco-German authority, and an unsourced claim about Monnet's role in the 1963 Élysée preamble is replaced by documented testimony. It also fixes the paper's methodology: the codebook, graded triggers, rival hypotheses and case-selection rule are now pre-specified before any case is coded, for a companion study using the Chronotope Method. Dated illustrations, Turnberry and Greenland, are added in a new appendix.)
title: The Headless Union: Conditional Federalism and the Outsourced Container
