summary: This repository provides the source code, simulation datasets, computational benchmarks, numerical results, and reproducibility materials supporting Paper I of the Principle of Representation Integration for Stable Models (PRISM-M), prepared for the Journal of Computational Neuroscience . PRISM-M V4 is a minimal recurrent computational framework organized around five functional operations: Extraction, Compression, Integration, Stabilization, and Prediction/Action (ECISP). The implementation uses a single independently evolving recurrent state, with finite-precision quantization and explicitly defined information-processing transformations. The framework is intended to examine the functional organization of information processing, contextual integration, and memory stabilization within established recurrent and state-space dynamics. The repository includes the frozen V4 implementation, mathematical definitions, parameter configurations, experimental protocols, random seeds, simulation trajectories, statistical analyses, and comparative benchmarks involving autoregressive models (ARX), Kalman filtering, and recurrent neural networks. The deposited materials document the original parameter-landscape and stability analyses, targeted perturbation experiments, memory-retention studies (M1–M5), and additional computational experiments (V1–V5) evaluating noise robustness, adaptability, recovery, interference resistance, and information recoverability. Additional validation materials include information-matched representation controls, intrinsic-noise sensitivity analyses, and mathematical verification of contraction and perturbation equivalence. These retrospective analyses are distinguished from the original experimental protocols. The repository also contains the numerical datasets, figure files, supplementary materials, execution instructions, software dependencies, provenance records, and SHA-256 integrity checks associated with Figures 1–6 and Supplementary Figures S1–S4. Computational reproduction and numerical verification have been performed for the principal analyses. Complete automated regeneration of all final publication artwork and independent cross-platform verification remain outside the scope of the completed checks. The purpose of this deposit is to facilitate independent evaluation, computational reproduction, and further investigation of the PRISM-M V4 framework. The model is a theoretical computational implementation and does not constitute direct biological validation or demonstrate a new class of recurrent dynamics.

summary: American states already hold the constitutional authority to check, prosecute, and outlast a captured federal government. The architecture has always been there. Scholarship on federalism and democratic backsliding has accurately described why subnational opposition to authoritarian federal measures tends to fail: states deploy individual tools in isolation, get outmaneuvered, and lose. What that scholarship has not provided is a unified taxonomy of the tools themselves or the recognition that they constitute an architecture that, when assembled deliberately and deployed concurrently, produces something qualitatively different from any single tool applied alone. Each of these postures has existed throughout American constitutional history. What the literature has never provided is the recognition that they constitute discrete categorical tiers within a single deployable architecture. This paper names and maps that taxonomy across five tiers. Tier Zero is cooperative federalism, the assumed ground state requiring no deliberation. Tier One, uncooperative federalism, describes governments withholding cooperation from federal enforcement, a category Bulman-Pozen and Gerken named in 2009. Tier Two, soft secession, describes states building parallel institutional and financial capacity that reduces dependence on federal partnership and builds resilience against federal mismanagement, corruption, and captured law. Tier Three, oppositional federalism, describes governmental actors at any level using sovereign powers offensively to confront and impose direct personal costs on federal officials and institutions, including through criminal prosecution under state law for offenses that are unpardonable by a corrupt federal executive. Tier Four is constitutional non-compliance, the condition at which states actively do the thing the federal government has prohibited, constructing competing legal regimes that directly contradict specific federal law as a matter of explicit state policy, with documented historical precedent across the political spectrum. The architecture is tier-modular, domain-modular, and actor-modular. A mayor, a city council, a state attorney general, a governor, or a state legislature can move from Tier Zero directly to Tier Three in a single session without prerequisites; any tier is independently deployable without activating the others; and any governmental actor can occupy different tiers simultaneously across different policy domains. Full concurrent deployment produces the constitutional infrastructure specifically suited to the failure mode the existing literature identifies but has not prescribed for: authoritarian federal capture by actors engaged in the systematic dismantling of democratic governance and the rule of law. The doctrinal foundation draws on dual sovereignty, the anti-commandeering doctrine, intergovernmental immunity, and the Tenth Amendment's structural reservation of sovereign authority to the states, doctrines consistently applied across two and a half centuries of American constitutional law because they reflect the Constitution's design rather than any particular political moment. Notably, the anti-commandeering doctrine at the architecture's foundation was built by conservative jurisprudence for entirely different purposes. Justice Scalia wrote Printz to protect states from federal gun control mandates. The doctrine he articulated does not ask which political faction is deploying it. They enable every tier of this framework, from refusing federal cooperation to prosecuting federal officials, without federal permission, federal oversight, or presidential interference. The framework does not conflict with the Supremacy Clause, which governs conflicts between state and federal regulatory regimes and has never been understood to immunize federal officials from state criminal liability for conduct that violates state law, to compel states to assist federal enforcement, or to displace the paralle

Scholarship on federalism and democratic backsliding has accurately described why subnational opposition to authoritarian federal measures tends to fail: states deploy individual tools in isolation, get outmaneuvered, and lose. What that scholarship has not provided is a unified taxonomy of the tools themselves or the recognition that they constitute an architecture that, when assembled deliberately and deployed concurrently, produces something qualitatively different from any single tool applied alone. Each of these postures has existed throughout American constitutional history. What the literature has never provided is the recognition that they constitute discrete categorical tiers within a single deployable architecture. This paper names and maps that taxonomy across five tiers. Tier Zero is cooperative federalism, the assumed ground state requiring no deliberation. Tier One, uncooperative federalism, describes governments withholding cooperation from federal enforcement, a category Bulman-Pozen and Gerken named in 2009. Tier Two, soft secession, describes states building parallel institutional and financial capacity that reduces dependence on federal partnership and builds resilience against federal mismanagement, corruption, and captured law. Tier Three, oppositional federalism, describes governmental actors at any level using sovereign powers offensively to confront and impose direct personal costs on federal officials and institutions, including through criminal prosecution under state law for offenses that are unpardonable by a corrupt federal executive. Tier Four is constitutional non-compliance, the condition at which states actively do the thing the federal government has prohibited, constructing competing legal regimes that directly contradict specific federal law as a matter of explicit state policy, with documented historical precedent across the political spectrum. The architecture is tier-modular, domain-modular, and actor-modular. A mayor, a city council, a state attorney general, a governor, or a state legislature can move from Tier Zero directly to Tier Three in a single session without prerequisites; any tier is independently deployable without activating the others; and any governmental actor can occupy different tiers simultaneously across different policy domains. Full concurrent deployment produces the constitutional infrastructure specifically suited to the failure mode the existing literature identifies but has not prescribed for: authoritarian federal capture by actors engaged in the systematic dismantling of democratic governance and the rule of law. The doctrinal foundation draws on dual sovereignty, the anti-commandeering doctrine, intergovernmental immunity, and the Tenth Amendment's structural reservation of sovereign authority to the states, doctrines consistently applied across two and a half centuries of American constitutional law because they reflect the Constitution's design rather than any particular political moment. Notably, the anti-commandeering doctrine at the architecture's foundation was built by conservative jurisprudence for entirely different purposes. Justice Scalia wrote Printz to protect states from federal gun control mandates. The doctrine he articulated does not ask which political faction is deploying it. They enable every tier of this framework, from refusing federal cooperation to prosecuting federal officials, without federal permission, federal oversight, or presidential interference. summary: Memory helps LLM-based multi-agent systems reuse experience, but stored advice can be flawed or applied in the wrong situation. Team-level success or failure alone cannot reliably show whether a memory needs correction or should not have been used. We propose DiscernMem, a training-free framework that improves both memory quality and memory use. To improve quality, Defect-Aware Memory Refinement (DMR) compares team executions with a single memory and with no memory, diagnoses rule defects, and tests repairs on current and earlier tasks to guard against losing previously useful behavior. To guide appropriate use, Boundary-Learning Meta-Memory (BLM) records each memory's past uses and effects, learning when its owner role should apply or avoid it based on task context and incoming messages. Together, these components help teams correct flawed experience while retaining useful rules that were applied incorrectly. Experiments with Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 on four benchmarks show that DiscernMem achieves the highest average score on AutoGen, CAMEL, and MacNet, exceeding the strongest reported baselines by 0.51-4.32 points. It leads on code generation and symbolic planning across all three systems, including a PDDL score of 37.71 versus 28.48 on CAMEL.
title: Remembering Is Not Enough: Refining Memories and Learning When to Use Them in Multi-Agent Systems

summary: Coding agents are beginning to develop the production-grade AI infrastructure that trains and serves large models, yet existing benchmarks cover only single kernels or single-GPU tasks, and grade with tests and prompts that misjudge both correct and incorrect patches. We introduce InfraDev, a benchmark of 36 tasks built from real-world pull requests to Megatron-LM, vLLM, and verl, covering infrastructure development for training, inference, and reinforcement learning. Each task asks an agent to reimplement a real change that spans many files and must run correctly across many GPUs. To grade such changes, we jointly synthesize hidden probes, which enforce the requirements the original tests leave unchecked, and a prompt that states every interface the probes call without revealing the solution. We also design a shared execution environment that reuses dependencies and artifacts across tasks, cutting storage by 52-57% and build time by 13-14% on Megatron-LM and vLLM. Across six frontier models, the best resolves only 38.9% of the tasks; the probes reject 32% of the submissions that pass every official test, and with the original pull request descriptions as prompts, no model resolves a single task. Failure analysis shows that structural and state errors dominate and that agents' own tests rarely check memory, time, or traffic. Turning these findings into an agent skill raises the resolved rate of a frontier model on the Megatron-LM tasks by 10.5%.
title: InfraDev: Can Coding Agents Develop AI Infrastructure, and How Can We Tell?

We introduce InfraDev, a benchmark of 36 tasks built from real-world pull requests to Megatron-LM, vLLM, and verl, covering infrastructure development for training, inference, and reinforcement learning. Each task asks an agent to reimplement a real change that spans many files and must run correctly across many GPUs. To grade such changes, we jointly synthesize hidden probes, which enforce the requirements the original tests leave unchecked, and a prompt that states every interface the probes call without revealing the solution. We also design a shared execution environment that reuses dependencies and artifacts across tasks, cutting storage by 52-57% and build time by 13-14% on Megatron-LM and vLLM. Across six frontier models, the best resolves only 38.9% of the tasks; the probes reject 32% of the submissions that pass every official test, and with the original pull request descriptions as prompts, no model resolves a single task. Failure analysis shows that structural and state errors dominate and that agents' own tests rarely check memory, time, or traffic. Turning these findings into an agent skill raises the resolved rate of a frontier model on the Megatron-LM tasks by 10.5%.

summary: Memory-agent benchmarks often collapse retrieval and answer generation into one score, making it hard to tell whether a failure comes from missing an update or from not using an update that was already retrieved. We examine this distinction on the single-hop FactConsolidation task of MemoryAgentBench. With Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on 6K-history BM25 accuracy drops from 45% to 32% when the retrieved evidence budget grows from 64 to 512 tokens, even though a gold-assisted post-hoc audit finds the newest statement in every retrieved set. Most of the errors occur on questions that also contain an obsolete statement version. Under a frozen prompt and equal four-statement evidence size, replacing one unrelated statement with the obsolete competing statement reduces accuracy from 100% to 44.6% for Qwen2.5 and from 100% to 87.8% for Qwen3-14B, with all 50 harmful paired flips classified as stale. A 32K-history replication likewise favors BM25-64 over BM25-512 (69% versus 58%). These results suggest that retrieving the correct fact is not enough. An obsolete competing statement can be more harmful than an unrelated piece of evidence of the same size.
title: When Retrieval Is Not Enough: Obsolete Facts in Agent Memory

summary: Deploying LLM agents in specialized domains often require fine-grained task-specific procedures and knowledge a general model lacks, yet parameter training is costly and non-interpretable, and hand-engineered agent systems shift the cost to expert labor. Episodic memory updates at context level, but single agent adaptation struggles to alleviate cross-task interference, especially with complex tasks such as multi-application navigation or data pool analysis. Although multi-agent evolution alleviates this problem, existing methods lack clear definitions on update rules and rely on the backbone model to decide where and how much the system changes. This ill-scoped evolution makes learning follow the backbone's structural preferences rather than the observed failures: one backbone accumulates skills while another spawns agents. We present EMMA (structured Episodic Memory for Multi-Agent workflow synthesis), which treats the configuration of a multi-agent system (controller routing memory, specialists inheriting a generalist prompt, and per-step procedural skills) as episodic memory. EMMA makes the ownership and admissibility of updates explicit: a reflector assigns each diagnosed failure to the scope owning its correction and proposes one edit within it, and backbone-independent guards keep every accepted edit scoped, incremental and bounded. Across KramaBench, AppWorld and BBEH with five backbones and four baselines (ACE, GEPA, EvoMAS and ADAS), EMMA attains the best overall performance on every benchmark, up to 32.5% over the strongest baseline, maintains consistent improvements across backbones, and uses 17-38% fewer training executions than the most efficient baseline.
title: EMMA: Structured Episodic Memory for Multi-Agent Workflow Synthesis

summary: Log messages are employed to identify anomalies in IoT systems and have been widely used across many applications. To enable collaboration among infrastructures belonging to different organizations, federated log anomaly detection has been thoroughly investigated for this purpose, often assuming the availability of ground truth log templates. However, this is typically not the case, as it is still necessary to depend on log parsers to extract log templates at inference time, while the design and deployment of such parsers in distributed environments remains largely an open problem. To this end, we report on an empirical investigation of distributed parsing and its key challenges, providing insights and lessons learned towards closing the gap between research and application. To further refine and contextualize the resulting benchmarks, we examine and introduce new metrics that provide a more comprehensive view for evaluating distributed parsers and how they behave in distributed environments. We propose a set of lessons learned and recommendations to support the design, deployment, and evaluation of distributed parsers. In particular, we evaluate the performance of five distinct parsing algorithms in combination with aggregation techniques that allow a unified agreement of event-template mappings across all participating clients, a prerequisite for federated log anomaly detection. In total, 6,720 distinct distributed configurations were tested for this purpose.
title: Too many clients spoil the logs: distributed parsing, aggregation techniques and metrics

summary: Machine learning recommendations are often evaluated one model at a time, despite deployment across interconnected decision makers. For continuous NPK fertilizer prescriptions, correlated errors can aggregate across farms and generate systemic costs. A model of shared and farm-specific recommendation errors links expected social loss to model adoption shares; the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index characterizes concentration effects when common model errors are independent and predictive risks are equal. A covariance-generalized formulation captures the dependence between model families. A two-model threshold characterizes when privately optimal monoculture is socially dominated, and a convex portfolio rule limits average private predictive regret. Nine model families across five Moroccan cereal systems provide a benchmark-based calibration. Under illustrative parameters and a 10% regret cap, accuracy-constrained diversification lowers modeled social loss in all five systems by 10.89-41.53% (mean 19.41%). Uniform allocation reduces modeled loss in this setting, but breaches the regret cap in every crop. Correlation sensitivity shows that highly dependent model errors attenuate the benefits of diversification. These counterfactual outcomes are not estimates of agronomic or monetary welfare; the framework identifies adoption architecture and error dependence as ecosystem-level evaluation variables.
title: Algorithmic Monoculture in Machine Learning-based Site-Specific Fertilizer Recommendation

summary: Generative recommendation (GR) represents items as semantic identifiers (SIDs) and autoregressively generates the next item's SID from interaction history. However, most methods assign the same SID length to all items despite highly unequal interaction frequencies. This uniform design repeatedly incurs the cost of fine-grained codes for popular items, while shortening codes to reduce this cost also compresses the semantic representations of long-tail items. Inspired by the compact forms of frequent expressions in natural language, we propose JevRec to encode items as variable-length words and generate the next item from interaction context. Linguistic encoding retains frequency-dependent semantic prefixes from shared codebooks, producing shorter SIDs for popular items and richer descriptions for long-tail items. Yet predicting a sequence-level length and generating token-level content impose different optimization requirements that may conflict under a shared output head. Our Jev-like decision modeling component therefore predicts a length distribution with a dedicated head and generates content conditioned on length through a separate head while sharing the interaction-history representation. Experiments on three public datasets show that JevRec outperforms all compared baselines across the evaluated recommendation metrics. Further analyses show lower training and inference time than TIGER and reduced gradient conflict between length and content prediction.
title: JevRec: Linguistic Encoding with Jev-like Decision Modeling for LLM-based Generative Recommendation

summary: Optimizing discrete allocation weights across competing segments of a shared budget is a fundamental challenge in resource-constrained, sequential decision-making environments. In practice, this optimization is often hindered by delayed, noisy, and aggregate feedback, alongside strict operational constraints on how frequently weights can be adjusted. Because of the resulting combinatorial action space and extreme data sparsity, classical multi-armed bandit algorithms that evaluate arms independently are rendered highly inefficient. To overcome these limitations, we propose a segmentation-agnostic approach utilizing Gaussian Process Upper Confidence Bound (GP-UCB) algorithms. By placing a Gaussian Process prior on the reward function, our method effectively shares information across neighboring configurations, drastically reducing the necessary exploration horizon. In this paper, we bridge the gap between theoretical bandit research and production-scale deployment. We first introduce a high-fidelity synthetic simulator to evaluate various kernel configurations under stationary, drifting, and reactive environments, identifying a composite Matérn + Linear kernel as the most robust choice for overcoming local noise and global shifts. Finally, we validate our findings through a large-scale Randomized Controlled Trial (RCT) in a live production environment. Our empirical results demonstrate that the GP-UCB approach delivers a statistically significant efficiency lift compared to a standard $\varepsilon$-greedy baseline, offering a highly practical solution for real-world black-box lever optimization.
title: Gaussian Process Bandits for Constraint Black Box Lever Optimization

summary: Multimodal transformer models have driven unprecedented performance breakthroughs in modern document understanding. However, the inherent black-box nature of these models remains a major obstacle to their safe deployment in high-stakes sectors. Despite significant progress in explainability for vision and language tasks, explainable AI (XAI) research tailored to multimodal document understanding has received little attention. To address this gap, we present \ourframework{}, the first comprehensive explainability framework that adapts existing XAI methods and evaluation metrics to the multimodal (text, layout, and image) document understanding context, while introducing efficient multi-target adaptations of both methods and metrics for domain-specific tasks such as semantic entity recognition. Using \ourframework{}, we systematically evaluate 13 XAI methods across 3 document understanding tasks, 8 datasets, 4 models, and 17 evaluation metrics, and find that only a few methods perform consistently across all evaluation criteria, with Occlusion emerging as the most faithful and interpretable method overall. Through a dedicated meta-evaluation, we observe moderate to strong agreement among several faithfulness and complexity metrics while identifying certain ones that produce unreliable results. Finally, through multiple dataset-wide diagnostic analyses, we uncover key insights into model behavior, including the contribution of individual modalities across tasks and labels, spatial attribution patterns around target entities, and potential dataset biases. Overall, this work serves as both a benchmark and a practical guide for future XAI research in multimodal document understanding. To support reproducibility, we publicly release our code at https://github.com/saifullah3396/docxeval/.

summary: This work investigates how site-specific digital twins (DTs) can support wireless localization using simplified distributed infrastructure. We propose PRISM (Probabilistic Refinement using Inverse learning and a Site-specific Model), a DT-guided probabilistic localization scheme with single-antenna access points (APs). Localization is formulated as a probabilistic inverse problem in which a conditional proposal distribution over UE locations is learned from multi-node channel impulse responses (CIRs). The proposal generates candidate locations, with its spread regularized during training and DT consistency used to reweight candidates and refine the estimate at inference. The DT serves as an approximate forward-consistency model, avoiding assumptions of exact channel fidelity or differentiability with respect to user position. Numerical experiments demonstrate gains over data-driven and classical fingerprinting benchmarks, while achieving a median error of approximately $0.7$ m using 10 single-antenna APs. Without retraining, PRISM remains effective under degraded inference-time DT features. PRISM also yields uncertainty estimates from its proposal covariance, with empirical $χ^2$ calibration approaching ideal behavior as APs increase.

Localization is formulated as a probabilistic inverse problem in which a conditional proposal distribution over UE locations is learned from multi-node channel impulse responses (CIRs). The proposal generates candidate locations, with its spread regularized during training and DT consistency used to reweight candidates and refine the estimate at inference. The DT serves as an approximate forward-consistency model, avoiding assumptions of exact channel fidelity or differentiability with respect to user position. Numerical experiments demonstrate gains over data-driven and classical fingerprinting benchmarks, while achieving a median error of approximately $0.7$ m using 10 single-antenna APs. Without retraining, PRISM remains effective under degraded inference-time DT features. PRISM also yields uncertainty estimates from its proposal covariance, with empirical $χ^2$ calibration approaching ideal behavior as APs increase.
title: Digital Twin-Guided Wireless Localization via Probabilistic Inverse Learning

summary: We propose HiLo-RD (High-to-Low Budget Representation Distillation) to improve masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) under a limited generation budget. Unlike autoregressive models, MDLMs choose both what to generate and where to commit it. This creates two coupled challenges: predicting useful content before reasoning is complete, and deciding when to fix answer tokens that shape later predictions. We identify budget-induced premature commitment: even when a correct solution fits, the model can fix answer fragments near the window boundary before resolving intermediate steps. These fragments become context for later predictions and redirect subsequent reasoning. Existing post-training methods do not directly transfer the stronger trajectories that the same model follows with a larger window. HiLo-RD addresses this gap by (1) pairing large-window teacher states with cropped small-window views and (2) matching their hidden representations at committed positions. This supervision guides both token prediction and commitment order without an external teacher. Across mathematics benchmarks, HiLo-RD improves low-budget accuracy and shortens responses; these gains extend to code generation without code-domain training. On GSM8K, accuracy rises by 9.4 percentage points as mean readable length falls by about 25%. Attention diagnostics and fixed-budget order interventions support the proposed mechanism. Together, these results show that large-window reasoning can improve small-window decoding.
title: HiLo-RD: Cross-Budget Self-Distillation for Masked Diffusion Language Models

summary: Generative planners are often evaluated by the trajectories they can generate, although closed-loop driving ultimately depends on the single candidate committed to control. We identify this mismatch as the sample-to-execution gap and show that improving proposal quality alone can worsen the executed decision. Here, we introduce ExecDiffuser, a recurrent proposal-to-execution framework that couples candidate generation, trajectory selection, and subsequent replanning through shared execution semantics. Intent-Guided Diffusion Proposal (IGD) assigns hypothesis responsibility and shapes trajectories with execution-conditioned supervision. Execution-Grounded Selection (EGS) learns a candidate-conditioned publication utility, commits one trajectory to control, and returns it as context for the next planning cycle. Across nuPlan, InterPlan, and NAVSIM, ExecDiffuser achieves leading closed-loop performance against strong state-of-the-art baselines. Under a unified five-seed protocol, it obtains an average score of 85.62, improving over Diffusion Planner and FlowDrive by 4.02 and 1.31 points, respectively. On NAVSIM, it achieves 92.6 PDMS under the official evaluation pipeline. Matched counterfactual analysis further shows that ExecDiffuser more reliably converts strong candidates into committed decisions, while prefix interventions confirm that this advantage persists after physical execution and subsequent replanning.
title: ExecDiffuser: Closing the Sample-to-Execution Gap in Diffusion Planning

summary: In this paper, we propose a model-based boosting approach for fitting structured additive distributional copula regression models with bivariate responses, focusing particularly on the joint modeling of claim frequency and claim severity. The proposed approach is based on generalized additive models for location, scale, and shape (GAMLSS), which extend the general idea of GAMs by allowing multiple parameters of a response distribution, rather than only its conditional mean, to depend on covariates. The model is therefore intrinsically interpretable at the level of its additive predictors, providing greater transparency and auditability than black-box alternatives. We evaluate the proposed framework using synthetic and real-world data. We demonstrate its ability to recover the underlying covariate effects and dependence structure, identify informative variables, and achieve competitive predictive performance relative to benchmark models. We also illustrate how the fitted model can be interpreted.
title: Joint Distributional Copula Regression for Insurance Claim Frequency and Severity via Boosting

summary: System One (decision) models return small structured answers, but can retain host dispatch, GPU launch overhead and full-vocabulary projection. We present DFIP (Decision-Focused Inference Path), an empirical systems study of established inference techniques in PPLX-Decider, Liquid d1-3B, Clef-Flash and GLiNER2.5-Decide. Selective CUDA graph replay, candidate-token projection and schema-compatible length-aware batching are applied at compatible model boundaries. We compare resident requests with stronger native baselines, audit exposed answers and measure changing arrivals. With optional native Qwen kernels installed, short Boolean resident speedups over strengthened native are 2.47x for Decider across five containers and 1.45x for Clef across four of five planned containers; Clef's fifth fails in native preflight. Liquid is effectively tied with released compilation; replay supplies most of its eager-baseline gain, while projection alone adds little full-request benefit. In a one-worker GLiNER follow-up, length-aware batching is 1.40x faster than compiled native FIFO batching on a diverse resident trace, but has worse arrival p95. Decider and Clef audits cover 3,024 decisions per model and preserve all 1,112 returned choices, while Clef changes scores, probabilities and serving confidence thresholds. Diverse external arrivals reverse fixed-shape replay gains and expose overload losses and a replay-path CUDA error. The results identify workload-specific acceleration and its limits, rather than a universal optimizer or production readiness.
title: DFIP: Decision-Focused Inference Path for System One Models

summary: Gradient-based data attribution has become an important tool for high-quality data selection in the instruction fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs), as it estimates the contribution of training examples through their influence on model optimization. However, we find that existing global gradient attribution methods suffer from surface-form bias: minor changes to semantically irrelevant details, such as wording or formatting, can produce highly inconsistent attribution scores even when the underlying content remains unchanged. To address this issue, we propose Content-Invariant Gradient Attribution (CIGA), a robust framework for instruction data selection. CIGA first identifies layers whose gradients are both influential for attribution and stable under semantics-preserving surface-form perturbations, thereby reducing formatting noise in gradient features. It then dynamically fuses these attribution signals with semantic representations of the input, combining optimization-level influence with content-level information. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks show that CIGA produces more stable rankings under surface-form perturbations while preserving downstream capabilities and improving average performance. CIGA also reduces attribution cost, offering a robust and efficient approach to data selection for LLM instruction tuning.

summary: Enterprise email security protects employees behind a corporate mail gateway. The people most exposed to employment and support-impersonation scams - students and early-career job seekers - are contacted inside consumer platforms, where no gateway sees the message. We present a dependency-free, explainable detector that works at the level of the individual message and its sender, and a public benchmark for comparing such detectors under cheap adversarial transformation. The detector has four layers: (1) deterministic lookalike checks built on Unicode UTS #39 confusable skeletons, mixed-script detection, bounded edit distance, and brand-agnostic detection of a domain hidden inside a link host; (2) a logistic-regression sender scorer over 23 named features trained on a synthetic generator spanning eight brands (holdout F1 0.987); (3) a message-intent classifier, with a rule baseline and a prompt-injection-hardened LLM wrapper, that receives structured sender facts from the first two layers and whose impersonation verdicts are discounted deterministically only when the sender is verified or unremarkable, nothing sensitive is asked, links stay under the sender's control, and the body does not claim the platform's authority; and (4) a 76-message, brand-parametric benchmark with ten label-preserving adversarial variants and three model-paraphrased corpora, scored on per-layer recall, false-positive rate, injection hijack rate, and latency. On a paraphrased corpus frozen before a single evaluation, all three Layer 3 backends reach recall 1.00 in the fused pipeline, at FPR 0.03 for the rule baseline and Gemma 3 27B and 0.10 for Llama 3.1 8B, against 0.83/0.03, 1.00/0.07 and 1.00/0.47 for the same backends unfused: the sender layers are worth 17 points of recall to the rules and 37 points of FPR to the small model. The 8B model obeyed an appended injection on 6 of 46 attacks, each caught only by a deterministic overrule; the 27B model obeyed none. Three findings fall out: UTS #39 skeletons do not fold Cyrillic U+0442 or Greek U+03BA to ASCII, so skeleton equality alone misses a mixed-script brand lookalike; regex intent cues lose 33 points of recall to a single confusable glyph unless text is confusable-folded first; and negation must be handled at clause level with an exception for conditionals. Code, weights, corpora, and per-message verdict dumps are released under the MIT license.
title: Message-Level Detection of Support-Team and Recruiter Impersonation on Consumer Platforms: A Layered Detector and Adversarial Benchmark

summary: Open-Set Test-Time Adaptation (OSTTA) operates on non-stationary target streams where covariate and semantic shifts coexist. Existing TTA methods often obtain adaptation signals by updating model parameters or maintaining mutable memories, which can be costly and vulnerable to unknown samples. We present TALOR, a lightweight, backward-free rectification module that uses the source linear head as a geometric anchor. The head-induced basis decomposes each normalized feature into high-gain principal coordinates and low-gain tail coordinates. TALOR estimates a soft-routed affine correction in the principal subspace, combining a regime-level principal bias with a tail-conditioned slope that captures sample-level tail-to-principal coupling. Using weighted ridge regression, it subtracts this drift estimate from the principal coordinates, reconstructs the feature and feeds it into the source head. On the ImageNet-C benchmark with six csOOD datasets, TALOR outperforms the next-best UniEnt by 2.2% H-score while running 2.5x faster and using only 12% of its GPU memory; as a post-correction plug-in, it further boosts COME to 68.4% H-score with only 2% additional memory overhead.
title: Tail Cues, Principal Corrections: Plug-and-Play Rectification for Open-Set Test-Time Adaptation

title: Tail Cues, Principal Corrections: Plug-and-Play Rectification for Open-Set Test-Time Adaptation

summary: Autonomous agents increasingly depend on harnesses that govern interaction, memory, tools, and execution around large language models (LLMs). While recent work has begun to evolve these harnesses from execution experience, the supervision used to guide evolution often remains relatively static, making it difficult to track changing behavioral weaknesses across rounds and potentially limiting generalization to unseen tasks. To address this issue, we propose RuHarness, a rubric--harness co-evolution framework for continual agent self-improvement. RuHarness continually discovers and reassesses behavioral criteria from execution trajectories, prioritizes the most relevant unresolved weaknesses, and uses them to guide targeted harness updates while keeping the task objective fixed. Extensive experiments across diverse agent tasks and backbone models show that RuHarness outperforms strong harness-evolution baselines, particularly on unseen held-out tasks. Further analyses show that adaptive rubric prioritization tracks shifting weaknesses and supports more sustained improvement and stable generalization across evolution rounds.
title: When the Critic Falls Behind: Co-Evolving Rubrics and Harnesses for Continual Agent Self-Improvement

summary: Test-time training (TTT) enables a deployed language model to internalize incoming context on-the-fly into a small set of fast-weight parameters, rather than merely treating it as transient context for attention. In-Place TTT recently made this idea practical for large language models by repurposing the down-projection of standard MLP blocks as fast weights. However, we find that its benefit largely disappears on realistic web long-context question answering. We attribute this to In-Place TTT's uniform write schedule: every chunk is written with equal strength, so irrelevant content dilutes query-relevant information in fast-weight memory. Building on this insight, we propose Select-TTT, a model-agnostic, query-conditioned rule for In-Place TTT that scales each chunk's write strength by its relevance to the user query. This relevance signal requires no supervision and no new parameters: it is read directly from the model's frozen output head, as the probability mass that a chunk's hidden states assign to the query tokens. A temperature-scaled softmax turns these scores into learning-rate multipliers, leaving the chunk-wise, context-parallel computation of In-Place TTT intact. Select-TTT consistently improves long-context question answering on two benchmarks and two backbones. These findings highlight the value of query-conditioned fast weight writes for practical test-time training on long-context question answering, which is also potentially promising for long-horizon agent tasks involving multiple user queries over evolving contexts.
title: Select-TTT: Query-Conditioned Selective Fast Weight Updates for In-Place Test-Time Training

summary: Personalized spoken agents must identify speakers before accessing user-specific memory, yet memory benchmarks typically assume correctly attributed histories. We argue that voiceprints are observations of identity, not identities themselves, and formulate online speaker-memory construction to maintain persistent user entities as acoustic evidence evolves. We introduce EvoSpeakerMem, a training-free layer for causal speaker routing, selective acoustic-state updates, and identity-partitioned memory writes and retrieval through a replaceable text-memory backend. We also construct LoCoMo-ID, a spoken-memory benchmark with hidden speaker identities, speaker-sensitive queries, simulated recording-condition shifts, and four-speaker identity-confusion tests. On longitudinal SMIIP-TV, genuine-probe rejection under a frozen near-enrollment threshold rises from 29.8% to 55.6% over approximately one year. On LoCoMo-ID speaker-sensitive queries, gated updating improves identity-gated QA over fixed representations by 3.86 and 11.62 percentage points under clean and shifted conditions, respectively, with no wrong-user authorizations. The advantage persists in the four-speaker test. Yet reducing fragmentation and improving QA can coexist with incorrect cross-user links, revealing a fragmentation--contamination trade-off that QA alone cannot capture.
title: From Voiceprints to User Entities: Online Speaker-Memory Construction for Multi-User Spoken Agents

summary: Mamba-2 compresses all context into a fixed-size recurrent state that dominates decoding memory and bandwidth. Existing compressors quantize state values or prune state coordinates, scoring each channel independently in the native basis. We examine trained Mamba-2 states and find that energy is almost rank-one, but the output does not read the energetic directions: energy concentrates in a bias-like direction accumulated by the recurrence, while the content the output reads lives in a low-dimensional subspace that is not aligned with the state's coordinates. Even output-aware scores are computed coordinate by coordinate, so they miss the directions that determine the input--output map. Compression should therefore target the write--read subspace rather than individual coordinates. We propose \method{}, a post-training transform that instantiates balanced truncation with full controllability and observability Gramians and applies the rotation exactly via Mamba-2's scalar-identity transition. Because the useful rank varies widely across layers, we further introduce HARP, which allocates ranks per layer from the Hankel spectrum and protects retrieval-sensitive layers, improving both perplexity and retrieval over uniform budgets. Calibration takes a single forward pass, an order of magnitude faster than GHOST's released protocol, with lower peak memory. With HARP, \method{} halves the state dimension at an average WikiText-2 perplexity increase of $0.3$ points ($1.8\%$) across 130M--2.7B, versus $1.6$ ($9.3\%$) for GHOST, and the gap widens at 25\% retention.
title: Balanced State Subspaces for Mamba-2 State Compression

summary: Stationary tail computation for high-dimensional reflected Brownian motions (RBMs) remains computationally challenging. Building on NN4MGF's shared-coordinate basic-adjoint-relationship (BAR) framework, we develop Holomorphic Cauchy Networks (HCNs). Native complex-valued rational Cauchy subnetworks enforce holomorphicity on pole-free domains, removing sampled Cauchy-Riemann penalties and their input-derivative graphs. Exact origin anchoring and boundary-coordinate exclusion enforce structural identities, while anchored interactions represent dependent transforms. Under holomorphic-log assumptions, we establish simultaneous value and first-derivative approximation for the constrained architectures and a mixed-derivative lower bound for coordinate-only representations under nonzero cross-covariance. Closed-form real-axis derivatives and sequential backpropagation further control memory. On the same NVIDIA H100 NVL, the tested 30D HCN configuration uses approximately tenfold less peak allocated memory and has 9.7-fold lower mean update time than NN4MGF; extrapolation to the respective scheduled update counts gives a projected full-schedule update-time ratio of 58.2. With 64 million sampled base inputs per high-dimensional run, HCN reaches 50 dimensions on a laptop GPU with 6.367% mean relative error over thresholds 1 through 8. Degree-matched comparisons yield lower reported mean relative errors over the primary evaluation ranges, including 1.422% versus 6.684% on the 2D Harrison non-product benchmark. An exploratory 10D correlated example illustrates the interaction extension.

summary: Modeling multi-scale dynamics in urban road networks is essential for intelligent transportation systems but is often hindered by the computational cost of long-range historical context and the challenge of fusing heterogeneous modalities. Existing spatio-temporal frameworks face a trade-off between sequence length and memory overhead, while frequently neglecting the transient effects of exogenous factors such as road incidents and weather. To address these limitations, we propose SpecLST, a frequency-enhanced long-short-term spatio-temporal multimodal framework. SpecLST leverages a fast Fourier transform-based frequency-domain representation module to efficiently encode multi-week historical dependencies, bypassing the memory bottlenecks of standard attention mechanisms over raw long sequences. Heterogeneous context is integrated through attention-based fusion, followed by a sparse Mixture-of-Experts backbone with graph augmentation for spatio-temporal representation learning. Additionally, a frequency-enhanced residual head isolates high-frequency transients, improving sensitivity to abrupt traffic anomalies. At the 60-minute horizon, SpecLST achieves mean relative error reductions of 14.10% in MAE, 10.35% in RMSE, and 15.78% in MAPE across eight neural forecasting baselines and four datasets, with the dataset- and metric-specific average reductions ranging from 5.63% to 22.21%.

summary: Large-scale linear programs with millions of variables and constraints strain time and memory budgets. First-order methods such as the primal-dual hybrid gradient scale to this regime because they avoid matrix factorizations, but they require many iterations. Learned accelerators can reduce these iterations, yet fewer iterations do not guarantee a shorter solve. Learning inference also takes time, and running the accelerator longer trades solver time for inference time. Existing unrolled accelerators handle this trade-off poorly: each layer processes every variable and constraint, the predicted iterates still need solver refinement, and every instance runs the same layers. We therefore ask: What neural accelerator design achieves end-to-end speedups on large-scale linear programs across sizes and target accuracies? We introduce AHEAD, an accelerator that predicts step sizes for first-order linear programming solvers while keeping their update rules. Its weight-shared predictor reads compact solver statistics and rescales the primal and dual step sizes, so each warm-start iteration stays inexpensive and a short warm-start phase hands the solver a warm start. A learned handoff policy sets the number of warm-start iterations for each instance and target accuracy, after which the solver finishes under its own termination criterion. On packing linear programs with up to $10^7$ variables, AHEAD achieves $6.5$--$11.6\times$ end-to-end speedups over Gurobi's first-order solver from a cold start, including on instances of unseen sizes and distributions. The gains extend to PageRank linear programs and hold across difficulty levels and target accuracies.

summary: A retrieval-augmented language model answers from two sources, the retrieved context and its own knowledge, and the two disagree whenever the context is incomplete or wrong. Existing methods settle the disagreement with a rule fixed at design time: follow the context, amplify it in proportion to how far it moves the model, or trust the model's memory. Each rule is confidently wrong in some deployment. In a decision-theoretic model of two sources, the score of any fixed rule is linear in the share of reliable contexts while the best attainable score is convex, so every fixed rule is beaten wherever it is not exactly optimal; and a symmetric divergence between the two sources, the signal adaptive decoding uses, carries no information about which one is right. Resolving a conflict therefore needs two inputs that no existing method keeps: evidence about each source separately, and a prior on how often the context is right. We test these claims on GRACE, a benchmark that intervenes on the knowledge-graph context of a fixed question, so that what the model knows, what the context says and what is true are measured separately. There, every baseline from four families is strong on right contexts or on wrong ones, never on both. We then build the two inputs: the model states its knowledge as notes, a small policy voices each note with a calibrated confidence, a reader answers in two voices, and a selector commits or abstains under a prior $π$ applied as an exact prior shift. With $π$ set to the true share of right contexts, the system is above the best baseline at every mixture of GRACE contexts, by up to 26 points. Its overall score is 45.3 and 35.0 (Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, Llama-3.1-8B), against 29.4 and 27.5 for the best baseline. On preregistered ClashEval it beats same-backbone CK-PLUG and TCR by 12 and 26 points. Where the model lacks the knowledge, the gains vanish, as the theory predicts.
title: Don't Pick a Winner: Knowledge Conflicts Need a Prior, Not a Rule

summary: This study presents an inverse analysis to determine the stiffness parameters of a bimodulus constitutive model formulated within a granular micromechanics framework. Full-field normal strain measurements are obtained by Digital Image Correlation (DIC) during three-point bending tests and are used as experimental input to a hybrid numerical optimization procedure. The experimental campaign is designed to ensure that the measured strain fields remain within the elastic regime. Since the identification is formulated as a nonlinear regression problem, a physically informed initial parameter set is constructed to guide the optimization toward mechanically meaningful values. An initial estimate of the compressive stiffness is first obtained from the available manufacturer data. The tension-compression stiffness asymmetry is then estimated from the experimentally measured neutral-axis shift, which provides a macroscopic signature of bimodulus material behavior in bending. These estimates define the initial parameter set, which is subsequently refined through a hybrid optimization procedure based on the full-field comparison of the experimental and numerical normal strain distributions. The identified parameter set enables the numerical model to reproduce more closely both the through-depth profile and the spatial distribution of the normal strain component over the selected surface region. These results demonstrate that full-field normal strain measurements provide an effective basis for identifying the stiffness parameters of bimodulus granular micromechanics models. The largest differences between the numerical and experimental strain fields are observed near the load-application region, where localized strain variations are induced by the concentrated load.
title: Stiffness coefficients in granular micromechanics determined with three-point bending experiments and digital image correlation for a bimodulus material

summary: This paper is concerned with the simultaneous recovery of the trajectory and intensity of an unknown moving point source in an inhomogeneous acoustic medium. We prove that the whole-boundary measurements over a finite time interval uniquely determine the moving source. Furthermore, under suitable propagation and rank assumptions, Lipschitz stability of determining both the trajectory and intensity is derived using waveforms measured at four fixed receivers outside the source region. A novel Volterra--Euler reconstruction scheme is developed for solving the inverse problem, and the error estimate is derived for the proposed scheme. Numerical experiments are presented to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed numerical method.

summary: By treating black-hole states as topological defects in thermodynamic parameter space, we investigate a static, asymptotically flat magnetic black holes in Einstein gravity coupled to causal nonlinear electrodynamics. Using the generalized off-shell free energy and Duan's $φ$-mapping topological current theory, we analyze the physical single-horizon sector in the canonical ensemble. We identify four representative defect-curve profiles, including realizations of the conjectured $W^{0+\leftrightarrow1-}$ class and $\overline{W}^{1-}$ subclass, as well as a new thermodynamic topological subclass, $\overline{W}^{0+\leftrightarrow1-}$. This new subclass features paired generation and annihilation points, with unstable innermost and outermost branches. As the auxiliary inverse temperature increases, the system evolves from two equilibrium states to three and then back to one, with an unstable small-black-hole defect entering through the physical lower boundary and changing the global topological number from $W=0$ to $W=-1$. This boundary-induced change signals a thermodynamic topological phase transition. These results show that the same inverse-temperature endpoint behavior and winding-number sequence from small to large black holes can accompany different defect evolution, highlighting the role of the physical horizon boundary in thermodynamic topological classification. More broadly, this causal nonlinear-electrodynamics black-hole family provides a setting for discovering further defect structures and thermodynamic topological phase transitions.
title: Novel topological subclasses of a magnetic black hole in causal nonlinear electrodynamics

summary: We have discovered an inverse relationship between the earthquake source deactivation coefficient and the magnitude of the main shock. Recently, this pattern was confirmed through an analysis of earthquakes in the Central Himalayas (Poudel et al., 2026). On the one hand, independent confirmation of a previously unknown pattern strengthens our confidence in the relevance of the phenomenological theory of aftershocks, upon which we have based our method for processing and analyzing aftershocks. On the other hand, Poudel et al. (2026) presented our method in a distorted manner. Poudel et al. mistakenly believe that our method is based on a modified Omori law. Both circumstances provide an occasion and a basis for a simple and clear explanation of the essence of our approach to the study of aftershocks. First and foremost, our approach to the problem is diametrically opposed to Omori approach. Omori law and its modification, proposed by Hirano and Utsu, describe the decay of aftershocks. In contrast, we formulated and solved the inverse problem. The essence of the inverse problem lies in the need to calculate the source deactivation coefficient based on aftershock observation data, without making any prior assumptions regarding the law governing the decay of aftershocks. A crucial concept in our theory is the rather complex notion of the proper time of a source. Proper time differs radically from astronomical time. The paper describes the continuous and discrete representations of proper time. This paper is methodological in nature and may prove useful to researchers studying the dynamics of an earthquake source following the formation of a main rupture within the rock mass. Keywords: earthquake source, main shock, relaxation, deactivation coefficient, proper time, inverse problem.

summary: Spectral-temporal unmixing of MODIS time series is essential for applications such as abundance mapping and spectral library construction, yet it remains challenging due to (i) spectral-temporal information coupling in MODIS data, (ii) intra-class endmember spectral variability and inter-class signature ambiguity, and (iii) the instability of naively fusing multiple expert representations. This paper presents the Multi- task Disentangling Fusion Mamba (MDF-Mamba) to address these limitations. To resolve spectral-temporal coupling, we design a disentangling architecture that pairs per-channel spectral experts with a dedicated bidirectional state-space (Mamba) temporal branch. Convolutional modules each process a single spectral channel, while the Mamba branch encodes the cross-channel seasonal trajectory, forming a multi-branch expert ensemble with soft inter-expert reweighting based on squeeze-and-excitation. For the integration of these spectral and temporal expert outputs, we introduce mHCFusion, adapting the manifold-constrained hyper-connection framework to merge the outputs in a stable and interpretable manner. Endmember variability is addressed by extending the linear mixing model with pixel-wise learnable spectral variability weights that capture intra-class endmember variation. Finally, we design a multi-task training objective that combines supervised abundance estimation with self-supervised spectral reconstruction and endmember regularization terms on the same training data, yielding a highly efficient framework for spectral-temporal unmixing. Experiments on MODIS time series covering the Alberta and Saskatchewan provinces show that MDF-Mamba achieves the best performance on 12 of 14 evaluation metrics across both datasets (7 of 7 on Alberta; 5 of 7 on Saskatchewan), ranking second on the remaining two.

summary: Open Data Analysis Tool for Science and Engineering (ODAT-SE) is an open-source Python framework for inverse problems that are solved by repeated forward simulations. It succeeds 2DMAT, which was developed for surface-structure analysis with quantum-beam diffraction and has since been applied to other fields. In version 3, the search algorithms were separated from the application-specific solvers, which became independent packages, and the software was renamed; this paper describes the current version 4.0. The framework connects optimization and sampling algorithms to solvers through a common interface for parameter mapping, constraints, and objective evaluation, so that an existing simulation code can be used with any of the algorithms. Relative to the previously published 2DMAT, it provides two-level MPI parallelism, which distributes candidate evaluations over processes and each evaluation over a parallel solver, checkpoint and continuation facilities, random search, global optimizers from SciPy, tensor-train optimization, and a Bayesian workflow that estimates partition-function ratios, model evidence, effective noise levels, and marginal posterior distributions. We validate the Bayesian workflow against closed-form results for a linear regression, benchmark tensor-train optimization on continuous, binary, and mixed-integer problems, and verify the two-level parallelization by the same optimum for all process decompositions. Taking up the positron-diffraction example of the 2DMAT paper, the workflow identifies the correlated structural solutions and an effective noise scale close to the imposed perturbation, while exposing incomplete convergence of symmetry-related mode weights. Solver packages, templates, and a gallery of examples support the use of the framework as a general platform for inverse-problem analysis.

summary: A thermopower that turns a temperature gradient into a perpendicular electric field in every in-plane direction has relied on magnetism. Reciprocity permits it without magnetism, yet under a three-fold or higher axis it vanishes both in reciprocal elastic band transport and in composites of two isotropic phases with ideal interfaces. Here we show that composites of three isotropic phases carry it, and that under such an axis three is the minimum. A third, linearly independent transport matrix escapes the exact two-phase reduction; at weak contrast the first allowed axial term is cubic, proportional to a determinant of the three matrices times material-weighted, handed three-point correlations. Treating the phases as colours identifies the arrangements that allow the response, and crystal nets from reticular chemistry supply printable three-dimensional ones. Certified two-sided bounds give axial Seebeck coefficients of 49.5-50.2 $μ$V K$^{-1}$ in a planar cell and 76-84 $μ$V K$^{-1}$ in a printable woodpile; reflections in planes containing the axis reverse the response, and recolouring 24 nets to restore their parent symmetry switches it off. Around a line heat source the axial driving field has the $1/r$ azimuthal form of the magnetic field of a straight wire and drives circulating currents.

summary: Magnetic energy gaps do not reveal the spatial distribution of magnetic-state-dependent atomic forces. We compare ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic forces at identical nuclear positions in 64-site substitutional Mn-doped Ge using collinear PBE calculations. For nearest-neighbour Mn pairs, the radial force projection reverses sign between magnetic branches. In the second-neighbour geometry, the shared Ge neighbour has the largest force contrast, about 2.2 times that of equally near Ge sites coordinated to one Mn. Bridge-displacement gap slopes agree with direct force derivatives across four numerical settings. Tightening the electronic threshold by 100-fold preserves magnetic ordering and the leading site, while the force-contrast vector changes by 1.08% despite a nearly unchanged energy gap. The results identify coordination-associated localization of magnetic-branch force contrasts within the frozen model, without establishing relaxed distortions, full numerical convergence or a unique exchange mechanism.
title: Spatial localization of magnetic-branch force contrasts in substitutional Mn-doped Ge: A first-principles study

summary: This paper unifies six decades of image modeling, evolving from handcrafted mathematical tractable priors to solve inverse problems in imaging to data-driven deep foundation image models for both image generation and solving inverse problems, under a common Bayesian framework that formulates image modeling as an implicit or explicit probabilistic characterization of a data manifold. Every image restoration or generative task fundamentally seeks to answer the same question: What makes an image look like a real image? In the Bayesian framework, this question is encapsulated by the prior probability density p(x), or its more optimization-friendly counterpart, the log-prior log p(x). While early works in solving inverse problems, such as Tikhonov, Total Variation (TV), and Non-local priors relied on explicit handcrafted definitions of log prior to model local smoothness, modern techniques, such as Plug-and-Play (PnP) priors and Denoising Diffusion models, are rooted in algorithmic uncoupling and implicit manifold learning that apply to both inverse problems and conditional image generation. By grounding imaging inverse problems and conditional image generation under a single mathematical engine: the gradient of the log-prior, or the Stein Score Function, we bridge the gap between signal processing and machine learning communities, turning what seems like parallel developments into a single, evolution of image modeling from handcrafted analytical models to models learned from big data, demonstrating that the pursuit of the denoising score is the common thread connecting variational optimization (in MAP estimation) to posterior sampling (in modern foundation image models).

summary: System identification, namely the inference of mathematical representations of dynamical systems from measured data, is fundamental to engineering diagnostics, prognostics, and decision-making. Bayesian filtering offers a principled framework for probabilistic state estimation but traditionally relies on prescribed transition and observation models. Recent advances in deep Bayesian filtering address this limitation by embedding learnable representations within probabilistic state-space formulations, enabling data-driven identification of unknown dynamics while retaining physical structure and uncertainty-aware inference. This tutorial provides a systematic introduction to deep Bayesian filtering for nonlinear structural system identification, focusing on the interplay between learned dynamics, physical inductive biases, and posterior inference. The Deep Markov Model serves as a data-driven reference, while the Physics-guided Deep Markov Model (PgDMM) and Neural Extended Kalman Filter (Neural EKF) illustrate complementary approaches based on amortized variational inference and differentiable Kalman filtering, respectively. Their capabilities are examined through dynamic state estimation and joint dynamic state and parameter estimation on a three-dimensional shear-frame benchmark with hysteretic Bouc-Wen connections and sparse acceleration measurements. The results highlight important distinctions between measurement-conditioned reconstruction and open-loop forecasting, demonstrate how physical structure can improve latent-state interpretability without necessarily ensuring predictive fidelity, and reveal differences in the robustness of response and parameter estimation. Practical guidelines for model construction, training, evaluation, and deployment are provided, together with an outlook on remaining challenges in uncertainty calibration, identifiability, and real-world validation.

summary: Black-and-Gold Series Paper 1 Quasi-Equivalence Index as the Common Gate of Graded Integrity and Golden Scaling C. J Tully Independent Researcher, Engineer Tamworth, NSW, Australia ORCID: 0009-00075661-7332 28th October 2026 Abstract This paper is the first of the black-and-gold series. It fixes the Quasi-Equivalence Index as the single integrity gate that both the dark graded formalisms and the golden-spectrum arithmetic must respect. /5 The index is derived from the graded square of a five-dimensional Z Z-product whose structure constants encode golden-ratio weights. A hard threshold of 0.12 rejects incoherent states. Golden scaling by the fundamental unit of Q( 5) is proved to be an automorphisms that leaves the index exactly invariant on the coherent locus, so the gate remains inactive under iteration. The inverse recovers the original state. The construction is parameterfree once the threshold is fixed. No claim is made that preservation of the index constitutes cryptographic security beyond the gate itself, nor that algebraic reversibility implies metric boundedness.

summary: Australian Spend-Based Emission Factors (Aus-EFs) for AASB S2, ASRS and GHG Protocol Scope 3 Reporting   Aus-EFs  is the Australian Spend-Based Emission Factor dataset: Scope 1, 2 and upstream Scope 3 emissions in kilotonnes CO 2 -equivalent per million AUD, for every industry in the Australian Bureau of Statistics input-output classification. The factors are purpose-built for AASB S2 climate disclosures and the Australian Sustainability Reporting Standards (ASRS), and are directly usable for ISSB IFRS S2, CDP, PCAF financed-emissions, and GHG Protocol Scope 3 Standard reporting. Multiply a spend line by the relevant factor to estimate upstream emissions without activity data. Any use by for-profit entities or for commercial purposes requires a licence (see below). We are flexible to user needs, and use income to cover costs in updating and improving the database so you can save time on the data and concentrate on reporting and reducing emissions.   Contents Units:  kt CO 2 e per million AUD (equivalently kg CO 2 e per AUD). Scopes:  1 (direct), 2 (electricity), upstream 3 (supply chain, including imports). Sectors: 115 ABS input-output groups (IOPG / IOIG), and a beta version of 914 products provided to licensees and upon request. Bases:  product basis (PxP, for purchases) and industry basis (IxI, for business operations). Years: FY2018-19 to FY2025-26 (Australian financial years, July to June). FY2018-19 to FY2023-24 are measured. FY2024-25 and FY2025-26 are price-extended from the FY2023-24 reference. Method Environmentally-extended multi-regional input-output analysis. Factors are calculated from the Leontief inverse of an environmentally-extended input-output table. Direct emissions come from the Australian National Greenhouse Gas Inventory (NGGI) by economic sector; emissions embodied in imports come from EXIOBASE 3.11.3, coupled to the ABS system through a SNAC-style bridge. Import multipliers are anchored to EXIOBASE's own total for emissions embodied in Australian imports. Global warming potentials are AR6 GWP-100 (IPCC 2021). LCA scope is cradle-to-gate, producer perspective. The Data_quality sheet of each workbook flags groups where a caveat applies. Source data ABS input-output tables (5209.0), and for the detailed beta the ABS detailed supply-use tables (5215.0.55.001) Australian National Greenhouse Gas Inventory (NGGI), by economic sector Clean Energy Regulator Safeguard Mechanism facility reports and the National Pollutant Inventory EXIOBASE 3.11.3 Licence Free non-commercial use for universities, research institutes, NGOs and government bodies under a CC-BY-NC-SA-based licence. Commercial use, republication, and AI/ML training or RAG ingestion require prior written permission. See LICENCE.txt in this record. Consulting Reach out if you need help using the data, require further breakdowns or input-output detail (such as the 914-product beta set, supply-chain tiers or emissions by source), or would like us to do the calculation and reporting for you. We map general ledgers and procurement data to the factors, prepare Scope 3 inventories and climate disclosures under AASB S2 and ASRS, and support assurance. Beyond carbon, we work on water, land, biodiversity and financed emissions with EXIOBASE.  Documentation and tools Full documentation, methodology, FAQ and a free in-browser calculator:  vectorsustainability.com .  This dataset was created by  XIO Sustainability Analytics and Vector Sustainability . summary: Learning from experience is essential for building the next generation of agents that continually expand their capabilities. Pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) already internalize rich world knowledge, yet this knowledge is rarely leveraged to drive policy improvement through online interaction. Realizing this potential efficiently remains challenging, as policy updates shift the agent's interaction distribution, requiring the world model to adapt accordingly, while continually updating large pretrained models is computationally expensive. To address this challenge, we introduce Dwell, a model-based reinforcement learning (RL) framework that reframes a VLM as a recurrent latent transition operator, endowing it with the ability to predict, adjust, and act in latent space. Leveraging the VLM's own representations and its dual role as both world model and policy, the agent continually learns from real interactions to anticipate and evaluate action outcomes, and from latent imagination to improve its behavior. Across five interactive visual environments, Dwell achieves the strongest overall performance among trainable methods while substantially reducing the compute required for imagination, showing that effective world models for VLM agents need not reconstruct the future; they need to predict futures that are useful for action. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/Tom111-lhx/Dwell
title: Vision-Language Agents Can Learn in Their Own Latent Worlds

summary: Sparse expert execution does not remove the stored states needed to adapt a mixture-of-experts language model. We present DuplexTune, a framework for replaying coupled hidden states through pretrained attention and expert modules. Trainable width bridges connect two residual streams to the backbone. Bridge warm-up precedes backbone adaptation, with router weights kept frozen. We analyze the implicit state-recovery equation and identify the convergence and replay conditions needed for reconstruction. On Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B, the single-H800 evaluation reports 38.8 GB peak memory, versus 64.8 GB for supervised fine-tuning with checkpointing, and throughput of 25.1 versus 19.9 samples/s. DuplexTune achieves 67.2% MMLU, 75.6% GSM8K, and 7.69 MT-Bench, with a weaker multilingual score than the checkpointed baseline. The results characterize a configuration-dependent tradeoff among state storage, throughput, and adaptation quality.
title: DuplexTune: Coupled-State Replay for Memory-Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Adaptation

We present DuplexTune, a framework for replaying coupled hidden states through pretrained attention and expert modules. Trainable width bridges connect two residual streams to the backbone. Bridge warm-up precedes backbone adaptation, with router weights kept frozen. We analyze the implicit state-recovery equation and identify the convergence and replay conditions needed for reconstruction. On Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B, the single-H800 evaluation reports 38.8 GB peak memory, versus 64.8 GB for supervised fine-tuning with checkpointing, and throughput of 25.1 versus 19.9 samples/s. DuplexTune achieves 67.2% MMLU, 75.6% GSM8K, and 7.69 MT-Bench, with a weaker multilingual score than the checkpointed baseline. The results characterize a configuration-dependent tradeoff among state storage, throughput, and adaptation quality.

summary: Edge SoCs pack CPUs, GPUs, and NPUs, yet vision--language model (VLM) runtimes keep generation on one engine and leave the others idle. Streaming VLMs expose further parallelism: new frames arrive while earlier queries are still being answered. Engines differ in compute and memory access and contend when they co-run, so no single placement of stages wins across SoCs and workloads. Backend-local KV state keeps other engines from continuing the work. \name coordinates heterogeneous accelerators to execute stateful VLM inference concurrently. It separates a stream's versioned context from each engine's KV state, so any engine can continue the stream by reusing, importing, or reconstructing that state. Stateful Streaming Generation ingests new frames on one engine while another answers, and Concurrent Sequence Generation serves different ready requests in parallel. State-aware dispatch sends each request to the engine expected to finish it first. Each answer reads a fixed, published version of its history and matches its serial reference. \name beats the strongest single-engine baselines on Apple M4 Max, Rockchip RK3588, and Qualcomm QCS6490, even when they reuse context. On two RK3588 video streams, it delivers $19.6\%$ more throughput than the best single engine with context reuse and $27.2\%$ more than parallel engines without shared state. Cross-engine KV import cuts first-token latency by a factor of $4.6$ over prefix recomputation. Stateful Streaming Generation delivers up to $2.48\times$ the throughput of serial execution, and state-aware dispatch cuts query completion time by up to $72.7\%$.
title: Shared Context, Separate Engines: Streaming Vision--Language Inference on Edge SoCs

summary: Low-bit weight--activation quantization reduces the memory and computation needed to deploy large language models, but activation rounding can still degrade accuracy after calibration. Reconstruction from rounded inputs cannot distinguish activations within the same quantization bin. We propose ResCom, a low-rank correction that uses the activation rounding residual to compensate for the resulting layer-output error. An output-aware calibration procedure selects residual directions by their contribution to output reconstruction and computes the correction in closed form, without gradient training or updates to the calibrated weights. On Llama-3-8B with 4-bit weights and activations, rank-32 attention corrections reduce WikiText-2 perplexity from 7.708 to 7.147, improve MMLU by 2.89 percentage points, and raise five-shot GSM8K accuracy from 23.96 to 36.16 percent. Evaluations on models from 1B to 70B parameters and on held-out C4 test the method beyond this setting. The evaluated FP32 implementation adds 2.25 percent to 4K prefill time; a separate compact-storage implementation retains a 27.7 percent peak-memory reduction relative to FP16.
title: ResCom: Activation Residual Compensation for Large Language Model Quantization

summary: A large language model maintains conversational content in an external storage that is outside the model and grows as the dialogue continues. This work assumes an environment where a language model has no external memory and no prior knowledge of the future question or its answer. The motivation is to research whether a dialogue can be stored in the model parameters and later answer a question about it. This work proposes self-keyed in-parameter memorization (SKIM), a closed-form method in which the model generates its own questions about each dialogue turn and writes those questions into its parameters as the keys that later retrieve the turn's content. Generating many varied questions for each turn allows a later user question to match one even when phrased differently, and its answer is recalled from the parameters alone. Evaluated on five language models, SKIM recalls most stored dialogue turns from later user questions, and it answers from the model parameters without any external storage.
title: Self-Keyed In-Parameter Memorization for External Memory-Free Dialogue Recall in Frozen Language Models
