summary: Replication package of the paper "Does Ontology-Guided Rule Selection Generalize to Independent Coding Standards?". It contains the harness, the registered hypotheses and their freeze files, the human-written and LLM-drafted ontologies for three coding standards (Godot C++, .NET runtime C#, Odoo Python), the model pins, the trial records of every run, the benchmark files, and the scripts and outputs of the analyses. The source files of the three repositories are not included; a script rebuilds the corpus from pinned commits and checks every file against its git blob identifier. See README.md for contents and commands, and THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md for the licenses of code excerpts and standard documents.
title: Replication package for "Does Ontology-Guided Rule Selection Generalize to Independent Coding Standards?"

summary: v2: for changes compared to v1 please see Revision Notes in accompanying zip bundle. -------------------------- Generalized trace dynamics (GTD) proposes that quantum theory is the thermodynamic equilibrium of a deterministic matrix dynamics, and that the collapse of the wave function is what controlled departures from that equilibrium produce. In the same framework the Standard Model and gravitation are sought as emergent structures, so that one programme aims at unification and at the measurement problem together. We ask, carefully, what such a programme must deliver to explain \emph{both} state-vector reduction \emph{and} the Born rule---and we argue that the right target is collapse-with-Born statistics, not the specific phenomenological law of continuous spontaneous localization (CSL), which may or may not be the correct law. We first set out the four ingredients any dynamical account of collapse requires, recall the sense in which CSL's stochastic structure is forced by its premises, and locate the premise a foundational theory most naturally questions. We then identify what GTD already supplies---an intrinsically fermionic, anti-self-adjoint reduction channel---and what it does not: a derived noise, a spatial collapse operator, and the Born weights. On the simplest GTD-relevant model we establish several facts. A static distribution over a state-independent drift variable cannot reproduce the Born rule; the randomness must be a state-coupled process. For continuous reduction that completes, the Born rule is the statement that the branch-weight process is a driftless It\^o martingale. Because the collapse noise in GTD is emergent from a \emph{deterministic} substrate (hence smooth), its simplest white-noise limit is \emph{Stratonovich}, which carries a spurious drift; we show this both spoils the martingale at order one (independently of the noise correlation time) and prevents the collapse from completing. This is not a claim that non-white noise generically spoils Born---it does not---but that a \emph{bare} smooth-noise branch-weight equation, lacking a response counterterm, fails. The Born rule is recovered only if a dissipative drift---a candidate being the response part of the \emph{projected} Adler--Millard charge fluctuation---cancels this Stratonovich drift; we present this as a precise, conjectural acceptance test, not a derived identity. We further show that this required cancellation is equivalent to linearity of the noise-averaged dynamics, and hence to no-signalling, so the Born condition acquires three equivalent faces; in generalized trace dynamics, however, no-signalling is itself an emergent, off-equilibrium property rather than a fundamental input, so this sharpens the open problem rather than resolving it. Ordinary fluctuation--dissipation relations are exact at thermal equilibrium; \emph{if} the projected Adler--Millard equilibrium relation induces the specific nonlinear counterterm required, then the Born rule is exact at equipartition and violations are controlled by the mismatch from that balance---a quantity distinct from the overall strength of collapse, and small near equilibrium. Finally we work out, on the model, what a non-zero mismatch $\epsilon$ would look like. The completed-outcome probabilities are given in closed form by a regularized incomplete beta function, $P_+=I_{p_0}(1-\epsilon,1-\epsilon)=p_0+\epsilon\,g(p_0)+O(\epsilon^2)$ with $g(p)=(1-p)\ln(1-p)-p\ln p$: every outcome probability is pushed toward one half. Applied to the two wings of an entangled pair---through a sequential local map, and through a two-qubit stochastic equation with simultaneous collapse---this gives Bell--CHSH correlations $S=2\sqrt2-1.17\,\epsilon$, a \emph{sub}-Tsirelson deviation, with $S=2$ exactly at half cancellation; a supra-quantum value would require an over-cancelling response, for which no mechanism is known. The same mismatch produces statistical signalling (setting dependence of remote marginals,
title: Wave-function collapse and the Born rule in generalized trace dynamics: requirements, a fluctuation--dissipation condition, and a near-equilibrium prediction

summary: Analysis code and result artefacts: data loading for three public datasets (Beltrame et al. 2017; WEEE, Gashi et al. 2022; Ingraham et al. 2019), causal per-participant preprocessing, nested leave-one-participant-out model selection and training of eleven linear, tree and temporal models, baseline-relative, transition-resolved, significance/equivalence and agreement analyses, figure and table generation, per-fold predictions and result tables, and the code of a previous, non-nested version of the analysis. The primary dataset (Beltrame et al. 2017, Scientific Reports 7:45738, CC BY 4.0) is included; the two external datasets are available from their own repositories.
title: Comparative Evaluation of Wearable Oxygen-Uptake Estimators Using Baseline-Relative, Transition, and Equivalence Analyses: analysis code and result artefacts

summary: Replay-based Continual Learning mitigates catastrophic forgetting by keeping a buffer of past samples, making buffer composition critical under a fixed memory budget. Recent coreset-based replay methods improve buffer quality using model-derived gradients, losses, or auxiliary optimization, but incur substantial computational overhead as memory is repeatedly updated. We propose CARES, a continual model-optimization-free approach for buffer construction that instead exploits the geometry of a frozen pretrained feature space using class-aware, density-weighted coverage. We evaluate CARES across balanced, imbalanced, and label-noisy streams under online class- and task-incremental settings. On Tiny-ImageNet, CARES is 2.3 to 8.8 times faster than existing coreset-based selectors. Although CARES achieves this speedup using no training signal from the continual learner, it ranks among the state of the art across balanced, imbalanced, and label-noisy streams under online class- and task-incremental settings, outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 7.58 percentage points under class imbalance while also attaining higher average accuracy on Tiny-ImageNet. Code will be released upon publication
title: CARES: Coverage-Aware Replay Exemplar Selection for Continual Learning

summary: LLM agents need long-term memory that can recover precise and mutually consistent evidence from growing interaction histories, particularly when answers depend on relations among facts rather than isolated semantic matches. Current memory pipelines remain vulnerable at two stages: indexing errors can fragment repeated entities or merge distinct ones, and online retrieval often treats initial similarity scores as final even when the surrounding graph provides evidence for revising them. We introduce ActionRAG, a graph memory architecture that couples cautious indexing with query-time graph retroevaluation. Its indexing pipeline reconciles type labels and applies tiered entity resolution. Given a query, dual-channel entity and triple retrieval forms an initial evidence set and induces a bounded local graph. Query-conditioned receiver-normalized diffusion refines triple scores using local path structure. Seed protection, hub-penalized flux, and triple materialization preserve direct evidence while recovering missed connections. We evaluate ActionRAG on MemoryAgentBench (MAB), which tests accurate retrieval, conflict resolution, long-range understanding, and test-time learning. Across its eight deterministic-scoring columns, ActionRAG achieves 55.1 average accuracy, improving over the strongest retrieval-based memory baseline by 5.4 points. Under MAB's query-time cost accounting, mean synthesis cost stays below \$0.001 per query on the four reported cost columns, and the sum of separately measured retrieval-side p99 components is 440.7 ms on our consumer Apple Silicon setup.
title: ActionRAG: Evidence-Refining Graph Diffusion for Long-Term Memory in LLM Agents

summary: Continual Wi-Fi sensing must balance plasticity, learning new rooms or users, against stability, keeping earlier ones, yet nodes often cannot retain channel state information (CSI) for privacy and storage reasons. We propose WiMoT (Wi-Fi Moment Transport), which stores the per-class feature mean and covariance of every earlier domain instead of samples. When the representation changes, stored statistics become stale. WiMoT restricts the change to an affine map on a frozen feature basis and applies the same map to the statistics, so they stay valid without old samples. Supervised contrastive learning learns the new domain, a closed-form loss on the stored statistics keeps earlier classes separable, and a Gaussian discriminant classifier, refitted from the transported statistics with equal weight per domain, predicts without domain identity. On 3DO, WiMANS, and Widar3.0, WiMoT's average final accuracies are 94.02%, 89.61%, and 95.16% with at most 0.58 percentage points (pp) of forgetting. On 3DO and Widar3.0, it also has the highest balance of new- and earlier-domain accuracy and is 3.77 and 13.11 pp ahead of the strongest of 21 baselines, which uses replay, staying ahead across domain orders and label budgets. On WiMANS, it matches the strongest replay baseline in accuracy (+0.41 pp) while reducing forgetting from 2.78 to 0.00 pp, and has the highest six-order average accuracy. Because full covariances dominate the memory, storing them as rank-32 factors shrinks the moment memory to 6.4%, losing at most 0.49 pp of accuracy, within edge-node storage budgets.
title: WiMoT: Replay-Free Continual Wi-Fi Sensing via Moment Transport

summary: Decision Transformer (DT) has demonstrated strong performance in various offline reinforcement learning (RL) tasks by conditioning action generation on expected future returns and historical trajectories. However, treating expected future returns as the condition provides an incomplete description of the future, as trajectories with different state transitions and behaviors may share similar returns. Moreover, expected future returns inherently depend on task-specific reward functions, which makes policy learning reliant on reward-labeled datasets and restricts its scalability to tasks with similar but unseen rewards. Recently, Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPA) have emerged as a promising paradigm of self-supervised learning-based world models, which learn predictive representations of future dynamics in latent space rather than reconstructing future states in the original space. Inspired by JEPA, we propose DT-JEPA, an offline pretraining and online fine-tuning framework that learns general knowledge from reward-free offline trajectories and achieves excellent adaptation to unseen tasks. Instead of predicting a single deterministic future embedding, we design a novel probabilistic predictor to model the conditional distribution of future representations in the latent space, thereby capturing both predictive information and uncertainty about future dynamics. Theoretically, we show that 1) the JEPA objective seeks to maximize a variational lower bound on the mutual information between historical representations and future trajectories; and 2) predictive future-conditioned policy learning admits a finite-sample performance bound with an O(N-1/4) estimation term. Experiments on D4RL benchmarks demonstrate that DT-JEPA achieves efficient adaptation across varying offline RL tasks, outperforming traditional DT-based and other offline RL methods.
title: DT-JEPA: Learning to Predict Future Representations for Decision-Making

summary: LLM inference is increasingly deployed as a core service for enterprise and interactive applications, but sovereignty, compliance, latency and resource-locality requirements can limit the suitability of centralised cloud deployments. Telco operators offer geographically distributed compute and network infrastructure for addressing these constraints. However, existing LLM serving frameworks are designed for tightly coupled data centres and provide limited support for coordinating geographically distributed and heterogeneous resources. We present InferSlice, a reference architecture for Service-Level Objective (SLO)-driven LLM inference over a telco infrastructure, integrating network slicing, GPU partitioning, elastic serving and observability. Led by BT in collaboration with the University of Bristol and NVIDIA, and realised on the JOINER UK national-scale wide-area network (WAN), InferSlice is evaluated on service differentiation across tiers, elastic scale-out, client-edge bandwidth as a bottleneck, and the reach of tensor, pipeline, data parallelism, and prefill/decode disaggregation over the WAN. Our results show that, on a general-purpose telco network, tiers yield distinct latency-throughput regimes, and weight streaming shortens scale-out time. Replication is placement-insensitive but memory-bound; pipeline parallelism tolerates near- and mid-cross-site hops, while tensor parallelism and disaggregation fail beyond a single subnet hop. We share practical insights from operating SLO-driven inference on a telco network, lessons learned and open questions, and hope to encourage further research on distributed and heterogeneous LLM inference systems.
title: InferSlice: A Reference Architecture for SLO-driven LLM Inference over a Telco Wide-Area Network

summary: Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellite mega-constellations such as Starlink require frequent handovers due to high orbital velocities, resulting in substantial Round-Trip Time (RTT) fluctuations. Accurate RTT prediction can mitigate these fluctuations, yet it fundamentally relies on continuously updated serving- satellite information. Existing serving-satellite identification methods typically complete identification only at the end of each scheduling cycle, creating an identification blind zone that limits real-time prediction. To overcome this limitation, we develop StarRTT, an end-to-end real-time framework that eliminates the blind zone by integrating per-second serving-satellite identification with RTT prediction. Within this framework, we propose Real-Time Long Short-Term Memory (RT-LSTM), an LSTM-based RTT prediction model designed to capture both non-stationary RTT evolution and time-varying geometric relationships among the serving satellite, user terminal, and gateways. Specifically, a historical LSTM encodes historical RTT observations and real-time serving-satellite and gateway-relative features, while a future LSTM processes Two-Line Element (TLE)-propagated future features of the identified serving satellite up to the next scheduling instant. Under strict real-time back-testing, RT-LSTM achieves a Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 1.405 ms averaged over all 15 prediction horizons and 15 reference time-slot indices, reducing the error by 4.3 %, 11.6 %, and 22.1 % compared with the existing baseline models, LSTM, StarNet, and Attention-based Spatiotemporal Model (ASTM), respectively. Notably, the reduction over LSTM reaches 12.5 % at the scheduling instant, highlighting the benefit of real-time serving-satellite information when recent RTT observations are limited.
title: StarRTT: An End-to-End Real-Time Framework for Blind Zone-Free RTT Prediction in Starlink LEO Satellite Networks

summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly support long-horizon tasks by leveraging external memory and past experience. However, existing agents mainly retrieve records or summaries, lacking the ability to form and refine causal understanding of the world. Inspired by human causal cognition, we introduce CauProphet, an agent that develops and updates causal knowledge within its Causal Cognition. For each task, CauProphet combines relevant knowledge in Causal Cognition with current evidence to construct a Causal Belief, a structured belief capturing causal factors and the effects of possible actions. It uses this belief for decision-making and continuously updates both the belief and Causal Cognition as new observations emerge, enabling causal knowledge that persists beyond individual experiences. Evaluations demonstrate that CauProphet progressively acquires causal knowledge and transfers it to future decision-making. In financial research, CauProphet leverages prior discoveries to improve downstream analyses and outperforms all baselines in mean rank correlation with next-day returns, achieving a 25.4% improvement over a baseline agent. It also improves prediction accuracy from 21.3% to 28.6% in dynamic real-world settings. Further experiments validate its ability to perform reliable causal analysis and action selection across scientific and everyday tasks, demonstrating the potential of causal experience learning for next-generation LLM agents.
title: CauProphet: Teaching Agents to Develop Causal Cognition like Humans

summary: Controlling scientific instruments requires parameters to be adjusted progressively in response to feedback from successive operations. When unobserved operating conditions evolve with operational history, responses become nonstationary, and a static mapping from actions to responses becomes inadequate for decisions across shots. Shot-to-shot tuning of neutral beam injection (NBI) ion sources in magnetic confinement fusion devices is representative of this class of problems: the conditions of electrode surfaces and vacuum are difficult to observe directly, discharge outcomes vary between shots, and experiments are costly and carry operational risks. We propose a physically grounded multimodal agent with three independently auditable components. Deterministic algorithms extract symbolic physical quantities and visual evidence from multichannel waveforms; a memory with two layers organizes trajectories from the current task, experience from earlier tasks, and procedural knowledge, from which a multimodal large language model (MLLM) generates candidate actions; and an independent action feasibility check enforces action constraints before execution. In a strictly chronological replay of 455 shots from four EXL-50U platforms, physical symbols alone outperformed waveform images alone by 0.21-0.32 in macro-F1 for quality classification across all four evaluated models. Retrieved context increased the mean agreement with historical action directions by 22.4-42.7 percentage points, whereas the contribution of visual evidence varied across models. Under supervised operation on five ion sources, the system achieved a beam-extraction rate of 86.80% across 409 executed shots. These results demonstrate the engineering feasibility of the framework for supervised sequential tuning on a physical scientific instrument.
title: Adaptive Control of Scientific Instruments with Nonstationary Responses through Multimodal Agents

summary: Humans efficiently process multimodal streams spanning hours to years, building persistent, fine-grained spatiotemporal memories that support reasoning about and predicting long-horizon events. In contrast, existing benchmarks focus on short- and medium-context tasks, and most foundation models struggle to preserve fine-grained information over long horizons. To evaluate and improve long-horizon spatiotemporal reasoning, we introduce the LongVideo dataset and the 4DMemoryBench. LongVideo comprises about 900 hours of video and over 5,000 manually reviewed questions covering visual, textual, and spatiotemporal reasoning across diverse context lengths. We further develop the 4DMemory Harness, which integrates four complementary skills, 22+ specialized tool models, and a model-specific retrieval-augmented generation system. Evaluating 13 leading models, we find that standalone foundation models struggle with long-horizon tasks, while the 4DMemory Harness improves all of them by over 50\%. Compared to previous benchmark, the same models exhibit a performance drop of more than 10\% on 4DMemoryBench. We hope 4DMemory will facilitate the development of spatiotemporal agents capable of addressing complex, long-horizon tasks.
title: 4DMemory: Benchmarking Long-Horizon Spatiotemporal Memory with Harness-Augmented Agents

summary: Lifelong LLM agents must learn from an expanding history of interactions while making each decision within a bounded context window. Memory makes past experience available, but the agent may still need to infer how to solve each new task from the retrieved records. Skills provide reusable procedures, yet may omit the task-specific facts needed to apply them. Because retrieved memory and skills shape the agent's behavior, they also influence the experience available for future learning. We introduce MemCryst, a framework for lifelong context adaptation through bidirectional learning of memory and skills with a frozen language model. Recurring episodes stored in memory support skill creation and revision, and the interactions guided by those skills supply new memory for subsequent learning. Facts retrieved from memory and learned skills jointly form the agent's context, while task outcomes adjust the future retrieval influence of the records actually served without rewriting their content. Across ten settings spanning embodied control, long-document reading, conversation, mathematics, and code, MemCryst leads seven reported comparisons. On ALFWorld, joint serving achieves 63.17% success, compared with 59.83% for memory-only and 50.50% for skill-only serving. Code is available at https://github.com/tianyi0216/Memcryst.git
title: Lifelong Context Adaptation through Bidirectional Memory-Skill Learning

summary: Training large language models (LLMs) in sub-8-bit arithmetic promises substantial gains in memory bandwidth and compute throughput, yet FP4 formats introduce quantization error severe enough to destabilize optimization if left unaddressed. We present ALTO, an open-source training recipe for GPT-OSS-20B, a 20-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts (MoE) model, on the MLPerf Small MoE Training benchmark under the MXFP4 microscaling format. The recipe combines established techniques from Abecassis, Felix et al. [arXiv:2509.25149] (hybrid 1D/2D block quantization, randomized Hadamard transforms, and stochastic rounding) with a simplified weight de-oscillation scheme adapted from TetraJet-v2 [arXiv:2510.27527]. On C4 validation at global batch size 16, MXFP4 + RHT + SR + de-oscillation reaches a validation loss of 3.3350 at 16,128 steps, only 0.007 above the BF16 baseline (3.3283), closing roughly 50% of the gap left by MXFP4 without de-oscillation (3.3418). Measured by steps to reach the MLPerf quality target (validation loss 3.34), de-oscillation cuts the FP4 convergence overhead relative to BF16 from +20.0% to +5.0%. We also report negative end-to-end results from differential gradient estimation, outlier clipping, and macro-block scaling, despite each showing operator-level SNR gains. All experiments use simulated MXFP4 kernels on AMD MI300 hardware and wall-clock speed has not been optimized.
title: Training an MoE LLM in MXFP4: How We Closed the Gap to BF16

summary: Quantum-centric supercomputing (QCSC) approaches, such as sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD), combine quantum processors with high-performance computers (HPC), offering a promising route toward solving challenging electronic structure problems. However, implementation of QCSC approaches to large active space calculations is constrained by the associated number of qubits, deep quantum circuits, sampling cost, and large-scale Hamiltonian diagonalization. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a distributed QCSC framework that decomposes complex molecular problems into parallel sub-problems requiring fewer qubits, shallower circuits, and reduced shot budgets. A physically motivated, two-step aggregation scheme then reconstructs the global solution: first, a computational bit assignment strategy optimizes a cost function to appropriately map local bit indices to global ones, yielding a mapped tensor product state (MTPS); second, an inter-fragment correlation recovery module restores missing cross-fragment interactions. Herein, we employ a multi-layered generative machine learning architecture, starting with utilizing the recently proposed physics-informed generative SQD (PIGen-SQD) as a distributed QCSC solver, followed by a secondary generative module to model configuration distributions and identify dominant sectors of the global Hilbert space. For water and formamide dimers, our method achieves up to $95\%$ reduction in the diagonalization dimension while enhancing energy accuracy by an order of magnitude over conventional SQD. Furthermore, application to the water hexamer ($\mathrm{(H_2O)_6}$) cage successfully decomposes a 120-qubit problem into six 20-qubit monomeric subsystems, and stitches the monomers under a dimeric approximation, demonstrating excellent agreement with the reference classical methods.
title: Distributed Quantum-Centric Supercomputing with Multi-Layered Generative Learning for Intermolecular Interactions

summary: Inferring constitutive laws from transient response data is a central inverse problem in soft condensed-matter physics, particularly when the relevant relaxation spectrum extends beyond the time window of a single experiment. Time-temperature superposition (TTS) constrains this problem for thermorheologically simple materials in the linear viscoelastic regime by allowing temperature to rescale the characteristic relaxation time without changing the underlying shape of the relaxation spectrum. We incorporate this constraint into a physics-informed machine-learning framework for time-resolved mechanical spectroscopy via chirp rheometry. We encode compact fractional viscoelastic models as causal convolutional features derived from the Boltzmann superposition principle, and we jointly fit multi-temperature chirp records using sparse variational Gaussian process regression. The model infers horizontal shift factors, constitutive parameters, and an observational-noise scale directly from time-domain stress-strain signals measured in the linear viscoelastic regime, without first extracting frequency-domain spectra or manually shifting separate curves. For synthetic Fractional Maxwell data, the method recovers the generating constitutive law from a prescribed model library and latent shifts over stress-noise levels from 3% to 25%. Applied to a DGEBA-IPDA epoxy dataset spanning the glass-transition regime, the pooled likelihood distinguishes competing fractional rheology models using the Bayesian information criterion. These results recast TTS master-curve construction as probabilistic inference over latent time rescaling and linear viscoelasticity, while also identifying limitations, such as homoscedastic noise and weakly informative spectral regimes.
title: Time-temperature superposition from multi-temperature chirp rheometry of thermorheologically simple materials via physics-informed Gaussian processes

summary: Large language models are trained to predict tokens from a finite vocabulary, each represented by a vector in a $d$-dimensional embedding space. Therefore, token prediction is a classification problem whose classes have a geometry determined by the embedding. We study how this geometry affects learning in a minimal solvable model: a linear predictor that maps a sequence of $N$ embedded tokens to a $d$-dimensional output through one $d\times d$ matrix per position, trained in the teacher--student setting. We call this the \textit{token perceptron}. We compute its generalization error with the replica method, taking $N\to\infty$ at fixed number of examples per position $α=P/N$ and keeping $d$ and the vocabulary size $D$ finite. As a first reference case, we consider continuous embeddings on the sphere, which isolate the role of the embedding dimension. The natural load is then $α/d$, and for $d>1$ a normalized label fixes the direction of the teacher output, so the problem becomes a noiseless regression: the teacher is recovered exactly above $α_{\rm rec}=d^2/(d-1)$, and spherical cross-entropy reaches this threshold at large inverse temperature. In the same setting the storage capacity of random associations scales as $d^2$ for margins $O(1/\sqrt{d})$. We then turn to vocabulary embeddings, where a label only identifies the Voronoi cell of the teacher output, so that each example imposes inequalities rather than equations, as in the classical perceptron. We compute the Bayes-optimal error for a given embedding matrix through an approximate spectral closure and show that the optimal learner first resolves the directions in which the vocabulary has the largest variance, even when the teacher is isotropic.
title: Generalization properties of the token perceptron: the role of embedding and vocabulary

summary: I analyze decision problems where a planner must choose, based on data from an experiment in a pilot population, how to simultaneously distribute a limited number of treatments that generate network spillovers across individuals in a target population. A global treatment rule maps the target population's observed covariates and network features into a jointly feasible allocation. Under local-response, stability, support, and policy-relevant overlap conditions, I identify the resulting welfare using a transported inverse propensity weighted criterion and construct an empirical welfare maximizer. I derive a finite-sample regret bound under restrictions on the complexity of network spillovers and the complexity of the global rule class, measured by its Natarajan dimension. The upper bound uses independent node-level variation, dyadic network formation without imposing a bounded maximum degree. A minimax lower bound establishes a corresponding rate comparison under additional welfare-relevant richness. Finally, I compare oracle optimal global and local rules (which allocate treatments on an individual-by-individual basis) and bound the welfare gap between them. An empirically calibrated oracle comparison illustrates the magnitude of this welfare gap.
title: Optimal Treatment Assignment Rules on Networked Populations

summary: The regularity of solutions to the two-dimensional radiation transport equation plays a central role in understanding the behavior of scalar flux near geometric corners. In a previous study of Kaper's corner singularity problem, the physical transport kernel was decomposed into its principal inverse-distance singularity and a lower-order remainder, reducing the corner asymptotic analysis to the question of whether the scalar flux possesses sufficient continuity to justify differentiation of the associated singular potential. The required regularity, however, remained unresolved. In this paper, we establish a sharp modulus-of-continuity estimate for the scalar flux generated by the physical transport kernel and prove the estimate $ω_φ(h)=O\!\left(h\log(D/h)\right)$, which implies Dini continuity. This estimate yields absolute convergence of the fluctuation term arising in the differentiated principal potential and permits a rigorous differentiation formula for transport solutions. Using this regularity framework, we derive the fixed-angle asymptotic behavior of the scalar flux and its first derivatives near a rectangular corner. For every fixed interior ray, the gradient exhibits logarithmic growth, while the scalar flux admits an $r\log(1/r)$ correction with an explicitly identified coefficient determined by the corner values of the flux and source. The analysis shows that a rectangular corner does not generate a singularity stronger than the logarithmic first-derivative singularity already present in smooth-boundary transport theory. Numerical calculations on benchmark problems are consistent with the theoretical predictions. These results provide a rigorous resolution of the regularity issue underlying Kaper's corner singularity problem and establish a mathematical framework for corner asymptotics in two-dimensional radiation transport.
title: Corner Regularity and Asymptotics for the Two-Dimensional Radiation Transport Equation

summary: Natural Language Autoencoders (NLAs) express a model's internal activations in the form of readable text. The verbalizer turns an activation into an English explanation; the reconstructor then converts that explanation back into an activation, and the explanation is considered successful if the round trip brings back the original activation. We claim that this criterion evaluates whether the information is sufficient and does not address descriptive faithfulness. A sentence can contain sufficient information to make it possible to identify an activation even if it wrongly explains what the activation does: in the case of reconstruction, the primary aim is to accurately identify the activations and not to describe them. This issue has the same structure as the chain-of-thought faithfulness problem, in which verbal output that has been trained to go with a process is taken as a report on that process, and it parallels the dissociation between an individual's introspective report and the actual governing process as documented in human psychology. Although proposed as interpretability tools for the purpose of alignment, NLAs reintroduce, through unverified explanations, the epistemic problem that they were intended to resolve.
title: Natural Language Autoencoders Identify Without Explaining

summary: Interactions between ultrasound and microbubbles underlie a range of biomedical and industrial applications, yet predicting how the physical parameters of the medium and bubbles govern nonlinear wave propagation remains difficult. This study proposes a parameter estimation framework that combines a Korteweg-de Vries-Burgers (KdVB) equation, describing weakly nonlinear wave propagation in a bubbly liquid, with a physics-informed neural network (PINN). The contributions are threefold. First, the PINN reproduces the reference solution of the governing equation in the forward problem, with a near-zero prediction error at the initial time that confirms the initial condition is enforced exactly as intended. Second, prior to inverse estimation, a sensitivity analysis is introduced that quantifies, at both the coefficient and solution levels, how each of eight physical parameters influences the KdVB equation, allowing the expected difficulty of estimating each parameter to be assessed in advance. Third, based on this assessment, single-parameter inverse estimation is performed for seven of the eight parameters using the PINN. Liquid viscosity, bubble initial radius, liquid density, sound speed, and liquid pressure are estimated with errors of 0.8-2.1%, the polytropic exponent converges only partially, and the surface tension coefficient cannot be estimated at all, consistent with the sensitivity analysis. These results establish a general framework for identifying and estimating the physical parameters governing nonlinear wave propagation in bubbly liquids from observed waveform data.
title: Sensitivity-Guided Parameter Estimation of Bubbly Liquid via a Nonlinear Wave Equation and Physics-InformedNeuralNetworks

summary: We consider the small-time asymptotic expansions for the Dirichlet and Open heat contents of convex planar domains. We prove that the small-time asymptotic expansion for the Open heat content can determine a triangle among triangles, a parallelogram among parallelograms, and an acute trapezium among acute trapezia of the same height. In addition, for a sequence of convex polygons converging to a convex set with smooth boundary in the sense of Hausdorff, we show that the coefficients of order $t$ in the small-time asymptotic expansions of the Dirichlet and the Open heat contents converge to those of the limiting set. While, for a sequence of convex sets with smooth boundary converging to a convex polygon in the sense of Hausdorff, we show that the coefficients of order $t$ do not converge to that of the limiting polygon.
title: Inverse problems and continuity of heat content coefficients

summary: ProPaST v1.0.0 This is the first official release of ProPaST, a graph representation learning framework for spatial transcriptomics data integration and analysis. ProPaST integrates gene expression and spatial information through graph representation learning, combining expression reconstruction, spot-neighborhood contrastive learning, and niche-level prototype contrastive learning to support spatial domain identification and multi-slice integration.
title: QinlinMa/ProPaST: ProPaST v1.0.0

summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models reduce computation through sparse activation, but storing their expert parameters remains a major memory bottleneck. We introduce GS-MoE, a training-free compression framework that addresses redundancy across and within experts through two compression axes: shared-subspace rank and expert intermediate width. Groupwise low-rank representations capture shared structure across experts while retaining expert-specific projections, and Nyström-based neuron compression reduces intermediate width within each expert. For fixed shared subspaces, we derive per-expert reconstruction-error reductions from the reconstruction objective and use them to guide expert grouping. Budgets are allocated hierarchically using a gradient-free layer-importance score to guide the allocation of rank and width budgets across layers, which eigenvalues and leverage then distribute as non-uniform ranks across groups and intermediate widths across experts. Experiments demonstrate the complementary benefits of compression along both axes, particularly at high compression rates on fine-grained MoE models. On DeepSeek-MoE-16B-Base, at a 60% reduction in total model parameters, GS-MoE retains approximately 90% of the uncompressed model's average reasoning performance, compared with 73% for D$^2$-MoE, while achieving 20% lower out-of-domain perplexity. We provide a code implementation at: https://github.com/cbacary/GS-MoE
title: GS-MoE: Training-Free MoE Compression via Groupwise Subspace Sharing and Pruning

summary: Video provides a natural source of supervision: what happens next serves as a learning signal for visual world modeling. Yet masked video pretraining focuses on recovering missing content from surrounding context rather than predicting the future from the past. Autoregressive methods instead predict forward one token at a time, but have yet to match joint-embedding methods in representation quality. This gap motivates us to revisit the granularity and space of future prediction. In this work, we introduce VANE, a self-supervised visual pretraining framework built on next-frame prediction in embedding space. A causal encoder summarizes past observations for a state predictor that infers the representation of the entire next frame, making temporal evolution the primary learning signal. This prediction is carried out in a fixed embedding space provided by a frozen semantic tokenizer, emphasizing scene content and structure. To retain fine-grained spatial detail alongside semantic content, a lightweight auxiliary generative decoder reconstructs future-frame patches conditioned on the predicted representations. To unify visual modeling across images and videos, we construct a local-to-global crop sequence for still images, allowing the same encoder to predict newly revealed regions from earlier crops under the same objective. Experiments show that VANE improves with model and data scaling, achieving SOTA on most anticipation, recognition, and dense perception benchmarks among unified encoders. Especially on EPIC-KITCHENS-100 action anticipation, it surpasses V-JEPA 2.1 by 7.1 points in mean-class recall@5. These results demonstrate that next-frame prediction in embedding space is effective and scalable for visual world modeling.
title: Learning from Next-Frame Prediction: Towards Unified and Scalable Visual World Modeling

summary: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) rely on role-specific prompts and execution models to solve complex tasks collaboratively. However, prompt optimization typically keeps model assignments fixed, leaving differences in role requirements and their associated inference costs outside the search. We present UniMASO, a Unified framework for heterogeneous Multi-Agent System Optimization through the joint adaptation of prompts and model assignments. UniMASO evaluates candidate updates through local, downstream, and global feedback, using cost-aware Pareto search to retain useful quality-cost trade-offs. Topology-aware co-evolution then coordinates these updates according to agent roles and dependencies. Cross-level trajectory memory further supplies historical successes and failures to guide subsequent optimization. Experiments on five benchmarks and five execution topologies show that UniMASO achieves competitive task performance at substantially lower deployment cost than the strongest homogeneous configurations. Under centralized execution, it improves the average score from 69.79 to 70.40 while reducing token-weighted deployment cost by 85.2% relative to DeepSeek-V4-Pro with MASPO. These results support joint prompt-model adaptation as an effective approach to efficient multi-agent collaboration. The code is available at https://github.com/Achilles008/UniMASO_main.
title: Not Every Agent Needs the Strongest Model: Unified Prompt-Model Optimization for Heterogeneous LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems

summary: This collection provides the code, data, and verification evidence supporting the study “Payment Menu Design for Safe Identification and Recoverable Coverage Deployment” by Jiaming Hu and Cuixia Miao. The study examines payment-menu design for providers with unknown local update rules, jointly requiring safe identification, recovery to ordinary operation, and preservation of the informed benchmarks. The collection contains two complementary archives: • S3_EJOR_Code_Data_v1.0.zip: versioned source code, frozen synthetic inputs and modeled coverage instances derived from public SNDlib topologies, original result ledgers, environment specifications, a data dictionary, mappings between manuscript results and source data, and scripts for rebuilding tables and figures and running verification tests. • S3_EJOR_Full_Evidence_v1.0.zip: retained certificates, verification receipts, execution logs, and failure and timeout records, stored with hash-based deduplication and mappings for restoring their original relative paths. Extract both archives into the same parent directory and follow the README in the Code_Data archive. The public-network instances are modeled coverage and payment scenarios, not observations of real network operations. The external PaGE comparison uses a source-mapped adaptation rather than a successfully built native Storm implementation. All eight extended ten-site tasks passed full V1 verification; seven additional independent audits passed and one timed out. Failed, timed-out, and gated runs are retained and distinguished from completed results. Corresponding author: Jiaming Hu (14438120260091@sdmu.edu.cn).
title: Reproducibility materials for Payment Menu Design for Safe Identification and Recoverable Coverage Deployment

summary: Municipal and rural solid waste management is a multi-stage public service that depends on reliable waste data, source segregation, collection coverage, transport logistics, treatment capacity, recycling markets, institutional coordination and citizen participation. This paper develops an Ahilyanagar District-focused assessment framework informed by the integrated solid waste management perspective described by Abarca Guerrero, Maas, and Hogland (2013), but written independently and adapted to the local administrative context. Official district information lists 16 urban local bodies, while the Ahilyanagar Municipal Corporation reports daily waste generation of approximately 140–150 metric tonnes and an approximate present population of 400,000 for the city. Rahata Municipal Council is listed with a 2011 Census population of 22,335 and an area of 22.74 km². These figures provide a limited baseline, not a complete district waste inventory. The paper proposes a mixed-method approach combining official records, ward-level waste audits, household surveys, stakeholder interviews and statistical analysis. It recommends a district data dashboard, four-stream segregation, decentralised processing where feasible, formal integration of waste pickers, and performance monitoring. Since district-wide measured waste quantities and survey results were not available in the sources reviewed, no unsupported district-wide rates or empirical correlations are claimed.
title: ASSESSING SOLID WASTE MANAGEMENT CHALLENGES AND DATA-DRIVEN IMPROVEMENT OPPORTUNITIES IN AHILYANAGAR DISTRICT, MAHARASHTRA, INDIA

summary: University technical festivals combine event discovery, registration, payment collection, venue attendance, certification, feedback, and reporting in one workflow, yet they are commonly handled through disconnected forms, spreadsheets, and payment dashboards. This paper presents the design, implementation, and functional verification of Supernova 2.0, a web-based event management platform deployed for the School of Engineering and Technology, MGM University, for a festival held on 4–5 September 2026 with nine flagship competitions. The system is a lightweight PHP/MySQL monolith that binds registration to server-side Razorpay payment verification, records physical venue attendance against the same participant identity, and gates certificate access on that attendance record. Administrative, organizer, and finance duties are separated through role-based access control, and a spreadsheet import path admits offline attendance records. Security controls include CSRF tokens, password hashing, session regeneration, login throttling, prepared statements, security headers, and HMAC signature verification. Validation is functional and workflow-oriented; no performance benchmark, usability study, or penetration test was performed, and no quantitative results are reported. The contribution is the integration of established mechanisms into a single working workflow in a focused, single-event institutional deployment.
title: An Integrated Event Management System for a University

summary: The Quantum Internet is commonly envisioned as a network that transports quantum states and distributes entanglement as the key resource underpinning distributed quantum applications. This view is necessary but incomplete if quantum phenomena are confined to what the network carries or manages, while network functionalities remain grounded predominantly in classical abstractions. This Perspective advances a broader thesis: quantum phenomena can also participate directly in the realization of network functionalities. We first establish the architectural baseline by introducing entanglement as a stateful network resource whose operational condition is non-locally distributed across remote nodes, evolves through manipulation or consumption, and degrades over time through decoherence. Its evolving state must therefore remain visible to the functionalities acting on it. We then move beyond resource visibility and use two mechanisms as proof points of a broader quantum-native functional design space: entanglement generation during propagation through coherent spatial-path superposition, and operational connectivity induced by shared entanglement that can depart from the physical graph. These examples show that paths, neighbors, or participating nodes may become operationally relevant in ways determined by quantum coherence and shared entanglement, rather than by physical connectivity alone. We identify Quantum Addressing as a transversal abstraction capable of representing such relations while complementing, rather than replacing, classical addressing and signaling. The resulting perspective broadens the Quantum Internet from transporting quantum information and distributing entanglement to exploiting quantum phenomena in network functioning, opening a coupled frontier spanning routing, forwarding, control, and functionality placement.
title: Beyond Quantum Messages: Toward Quantum-Native Network Functioning

summary: Contents Folder Contents data/discovery/ Repository metadata and discovery scores for 500 projects. data/analysis/ The 1,500-record human–LLM dataset, 17,180 additional LLM classifications, classification inputs and counts for 117 repositories. data/extraction_used/ Per-repository exports of the analyzed candidates. data/manual_classify/ Master classification sheet and human–LLM comparison sheets. data/survey/ Category-level and demographic survey aggregates. protocol/ Taxonomy categories, LLM instructions, output schema and workbook prompts. scripts/archive/ Repository discovery, historical SATD extraction and LLM classification scripts. provenance/mining_logs/ Compressed SATD extraction logs. results/computed/ RQ1 and RQ2 counts, repository distributions, false-positive counts and RQ3 aggregates. figures/ AI-CPS taxonomy and practitioner criticality figures. survey/ Practitioner questionnaire. Setup Install Python and Git. Open a terminal in the folder containing requirements.txt , then install the Python dependencies: python -m pip install -r requirements.txt Repository discovery Run the discovery script to generate a repository metadata CSV: python scripts/archive/discover_repositories_original.py --output repos_for_satd.csv --max-repos 500 --include-readme The command exports up to 500 repositories and includes README inspection. Other available settings are listed with: python scripts/archive/discover_repositories_original.py --help For authenticated GitHub requests, set the GITHUB_TOKEN environment variable before running the script. Historical SATD extraction Run the miner on the supplied repository list: python scripts/archive/mine_satd_original.py --input data/discovery/repos_for_satd.csv --output-dir satd_results --repo-cache tmp_repos --log-dir satd_logs --since-year 2022 The script traverses available commits from the specified year, retrieves marker-bearing deleted source lines and their available pre-change context, and writes per-repository CSV files and logs. tmp_repos is the script's temporary clone directory. LLM classification In scripts/archive/llm_classification.py , replace the input, output and sample-count placeholders. For example, to classify the additional input: INPUT_FILE = r"data/analysis/additional_input_17180.csv" OUTPUT_FILE = r"new_additional_llm_results.csv" MAX_SAMPLES = 17180 To use the initial subset instead, set INPUT_FILE to data/analysis/manual_input_1500.csv and MAX_SAMPLES to 1500 . The sample count must be an integer. Set the OPENAI_API_KEY environment variable, then run: python scripts/archive/llm_classification.py The script reads ID , SATD_Keyword , SATD_Comment , Context_Type and Context_Code , and saves broad classifications, AI-CPS categories and proposed category names. Checkpoints are saved beside the output. To resume an interrupted run, use the same input, settings and output path. Results The supplied summaries are in results/computed/ . RQ1 percentages exclude false positives; RQ2 percentages use the AI-CPS-specific total within each analysis. Figures are supplied as PDFs in figures/ .
title: Replication Package of the Paper: "Self-Admitted Technical Debt in AI-Intensive Cyber-Physical Systems: An Empirical Study"

summary: CSE-Sp: Spanish adaptation of the Creative Self-Efficacy Scale Analysis materials and supplemental material This repository contains the analysis materials and the supplemental material for a psychometric validation study of the Spanish adaptation of the Creative Self-Efficacy Scale (CSE-Sp) in a sample of 503 university students. FILES   CSE-Sp_supplemental_material.docx       Supplemental Material S1 to S13 cited in the manuscript (19 tables).   cse_sp_analysis.R       Complete analysis script, organized in the order of the manuscript:       item analysis, outlier screening, random split, exploratory and       confirmatory factor analyses, bifactor indices, estimator sensitivity       (WLSMV), cross-validation, reliability, measurement invariance by sex,       disciplinary area and institution, MIMIC model, sensitivity analysis       excluding participants older than 30, convergent, criterion and       discriminant validity, and the item-level comparison with the original       and Turkish versions.   cse_sp_export_matrices.R       Script used to generate the correlation matrices deposited here.   matrix_halfA_polychoric.csv       Polychoric correlation matrix of the 20 items, half A (n = 253).       Input of the primary exploratory factor analysis.   matrix_halfA_pearson.csv       Product-moment correlation matrix of the 20 items, half A (n = 253).       Input of the replication reported in parallel.   matrix_total_pearson.csv       Product-moment correlation matrix of the 20 items, total sample       (N = 503). SOFTWARE ENVIRONMENT   R version 4.6.0 (2026-04-24 ucrt), platform x86_64-w64-mingw32/x64,   running under Windows 11 x64.   Packages: psych 2.6.5, lavaan 0.6-21, semTools 0.5-8, MVN 6.3,   readxl 1.5.0, mnormt 2.1.2, pbivnorm 0.6.0, quadprog 1.5-8.   Seed used for the stratified random split of the sample and for the   bootstrap confidence intervals: 2026. The split assigns 253 cases to   half A (exploratory analyses) and 250 to half B (confirmatory analyses). WHAT CAN AND CANNOT BE REPRODUCED FROM THESE FILES The deposited correlation matrices reproduce the sampling-adequacy indices (KMO, Bartlett), the exploratory factor analysis on both the polychoric and the product-moment matrix, the factor-retention criteria (parallel analysis, MAP, VSS, eigenvalue ratio), and the internal-consistency coefficients computed on standardized items. They do not reproduce the confirmatory factor analyses, the bifactor indices, the cross-validation, or the measurement-invariance and MIMIC models. These were estimated with robust maximum likelihood (MLR), which requires individual response data in order to compute the robust corrections to the fit statistics and standard errors. The same applies to the validity correlations, which were computed on subsets of participants with varying sample sizes. The analysis script documents every one of these analyses so that they can be reproduced on the individual data. ACCESS TO THE INDIVIDUAL DATA The individual response data are not deposited here. They were collected within an institutional assessment program and their ownership lies with the institution rather than with the research team. Both input files used by the analysis script (cse_sp_full_sample.xlsx and cse_sp_validity_subset.xlsx) are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request. LICENSE CC BY 4.0
title: CSE-Sp: Spanish adaptation of the Creative Self-Efficacy Scale. Analysis materials and supplementary material

summary: Nepal’s Constitution of 2015 protects dignity, personal liberty, peaceful assembly and constitutional remedies. Yet investigations into the 2015 Terai protests and the September 2025 Gen Z uprising expose a persistent gap between rights and the use of state coercion. This paper argues that the gap is best understood through an accountability chain: broad public-order powers, qualified protection for official acts, evidentiary dependence and uncertain institutional implementation. The analysis focuses on sections 35, 37 and 38 of the Police Act, 2012 B.S. (1955 C.E.), sections 6, 6A and 6B of the Local Administration Act, 2028 B.S. (1971 C.E.) and Nepal’s duties under the ICCPR and Convention against Torture. Through doctrinal analysis, a source-critical reconstruction of protest events, peer-reviewed scholarship and carefully delimited comparative jurisprudence, the article separates contemporaneous death counts from later totals, inquiry recommendations from court judgments and state violence from crimes by other actors. It incorporates the 2026 inquiry and National Human Rights Commission findings, one-year anniversary reporting and the October 2026 review of protest-related criminal cases. Its central contribution is a rights-consistent and measurable program for controlling force, preserving evidence, independently investigating deaths and protecting remedies without undermining legitimate public safety.
title: Constitutional Liberty and Protest Policing: A Comparative Perspective on Structural Impunity, Gen Z Dissent and Accountability Reform in Nepal Doctrinal and comparative legal research

summary: Timely state updates are essential for coordination and monitoring in multi-agent systems, such as teams of mobile robots exchanging state information. When agents share a wireless channel, collisions and slow convergence of distributed access schemes can degrade information freshness over finite operating periods. This paper proposes age-threshold frame-based random access (AFRA), a distributed medium access control protocol for minimizing age of information (AoI). Once its age reaches a threshold, an agent starts a local frame with a mandatory transmission and, if unsuccessful, makes one further attempt at a uniformly selected remaining slot. Each attempt carries a freshly generated update. AFRA requires only local state and acknowledgment feedback, with shared slot boundaries but independently timed local frames. We prove almost-sure convergence from any legal initial state to collision-free periodic operation when the frame length $L$ and age threshold $T$ satisfy $L\ge T>N\ge2$, where $N$ is the number of agents. We also derive closed-form expressions for steady-state throughput, average AoI, and average peak AoI. Simulations demonstrate that AFRA combines rapid convergence at small age thresholds with lower window-averaged AoI than the existing age-aware random access schemes evaluated in this study.
title: AFRA: Age-Threshold Frame-Based Random Access for Timely Communication in Multi-Agent Systems

summary: Collective behavior in biological systems emerges through adaptive interactions among units, enabling large populations to coordinate without centralized control. This mechanism raises the question of whether collective behavior in engineered multi-agent systems can likewise be regulated by modifying the interaction law between agents, rather than by directly controlling individual units. To answer this question, we consider large-scale multi-agent systems evolving on a ring and treat the interaction kernel as a time-varying control variable whose evolution regulates the collective dynamics. Using a mean-field formulation, we develop a framework for the analysis and design of kernel-based controllers. We derive explicit conditions for controllability in application-relevant scenarios, and synthesize a state-feedback controller to regulate the kernel dynamics, validated on the microscopic, discrete dynamics. Numerical simulations demonstrate the approach's effectiveness and robustness to unmodeled perturbations. This work constitutes a first step in the design of bio-inspired control strategies for large-scale multi-agent systems by modulation of interactions between agents.
title: Density control of large-scale multi-agent systems via tuning of agent interactions

summary: Disease surveillance increasingly integrates automated data collection, yet predefined sources and procedures require manual adaptation as reporting practices change. We explore agentic artificial intelligence (AI) as an approach to coordinating surveillance data collection across heterogeneous sources. Specifically, we built a multi-agent framework that integrates source discovery, source assessment, evidence structuring, event linking, and validation. Three retrospective applications illustrate its promise. The workflow recovered all 13 individual cases in a hantavirus outbreak, with links to 85 distinct publisher domains compared with 28 in the reference benchmark, reconstructed Canadian measles counts with a final total 0.33% below the national reference and higher cumulative counts on 79.8% of comparable days, and increased the share of days with recent Sierra Leone mpox reports from 28.2% to 65.6% by incorporating attributed media. These demonstrations also reveal limitations in record completeness and accuracy, while prospective gains in timeliness remain untested. We envision agentic AI as a complementary layer of public health data infrastructure, coordinating evidence-linked collection under surveillance goals and standards defined by public health professionals.
title: Toward an Agentic AI Approach to Public Health Data Collection

summary: Pre-built per-gene covariate matrices for TCGA-READ (Rectum adenocarcinoma. Biologically and genomically the same disease as COAD (TCGA's own marker paper pooled them as COADREAD), so every covariate source is COAD's, re-verified 2026-10-03: GTEx maps to the colon tissues (representative Colon_Transverse_Mucosa, the epithelial cell of origin; GTEx has no rectum). No TCGA ATAC-seq for READ (atac: null). Roadmap uses COAD's E075 (colonic mucosa), E106 (sigmoid colon, 6/7 marks -- H3K9ac 404s) and E101/E102 (rectal mucosa, the direct organ match, 7/7 each); all 27 live (EID, mark) pairs checked 2026-10-03; E103 (rectal smooth muscle) rejected as the wrong compartment. ENCODE's adult rectal-mucosa histone experiments (two donors, 50y/61y, Bernstein lab, Roadmap award, 2013) are E101/E102's own sources and are not added, to avoid duplicating them in another assembly; no rectum DNase exists. encode_chromatin is COAD's: adult colonic mucosa DNase and the six colorectal cancer lines HCT116, Caco-2, LoVo, SW480, HT-29 and RKO (native GRCh38, all 19 files re-checked released). Replication timing is COAD's HCT116 16-fraction MAT (GSE137764), a colorectal cancer line, the same disease. Assemblies: Roadmap hg19; RT (MAT), encode_chromatin GRCh38/hg38; expression TCGA-READ (166 tumor and 10 normal RNA-seq files, so the default Tumor+Normal pair).), built with sigmutselcovs : GTEx tissue-matched gene expression, TCGA per-sample gene expression, replication timing (mean replication time and CLR-transformed S-phase fractions), Roadmap Epigenomics histone marks, and TCGA ATAC-seq accessibility, indexed by Ensembl gene ID. Files: cov_matrix_full.parquet — the full matrix (all covariate columns) cov_matrix_pca.parquet — PCA-reduced to 956 components, the smallest number reaching 99% cumulative explained variance (see pca_manifest.json) cov_matrix_columns.csv — a data dictionary: one row per column of the full matrix, with source, description, assembly, and units build_manifest.json , pca_manifest.json — build provenance and PCA parameters Full source citations and methodology: SOURCES.md . Release of 2026-10-26. Every chromatin and ATAC column is one track, summarized as log1p of the mean signal over the gene's CDS span (first to last coding base); replication timing covers chrX. cov_matrix_pca.parquet now reduces the combined matrix : this cohort's own covariates plus the tissue-agnostic GENERIC pool ( GENERIC record ), with the pool's columns for chromatin tracks this cohort already has left out. That is the matrix the sigmutsel covariate model is fitted on; it predicts held-out mutation counts better than the cohort's own matrix alone in the cohorts tested, so the first components of this artifact are the ones a model should use. Versions before 2026-10-26 reduced the own matrix alone. cov_matrix_full.parquet is still the cohort's own matrix; GENERIC's is in its record. pca_manifest.json records which matrix was reduced ( matrix ) and the column counts. To rebuild: sigmutselcovs pca-artifact READ --data-dir DIR --generic-dir GENERIC_DIR .

summary: Pre-built per-gene covariate matrices for TCGA-PRAD (Prostate adenocarcinoma. GTEx maps to Prostate (gtex_prostate). TCGA-PRAD has normal RNA-seq (52 Solid Tissue Normal files), so gexp keeps the default tumor+normal means. TCGA ATAC-seq covered (Corces et al. 2018; the tarball's bigWigs are named PRAD_..., read from its first member). roadmap null: Roadmap's 127-epigenome panel has no prostate epigenome. encode_chromatin: adult prostate gland tissue from one ENTEx donor (ENCDO845WKR, 37y; DNase, H3K27ac, H3K27me3, H3K36me3, H3K4me1, H3K4me3), plus H3K9me3 from a second adult donor (ENCDO451RUA, 54y), the only donor with that mark; ENCODE has no adult prostate H3K9ac. summary: TEMPLATE-DIRECTED MASS FABRICATION OF BIOMEDICAL MICRO/NANOROBOTS AT THE LIMIT is a 770-page, high-density English research monograph on scaling template replication without losing dimensional fidelity, surface integrity, functional consistency or scientific traceability. The book treats the template as a stateful manufacturing ancestor rather than a passive tool. Every cavity and replication cycle is registered so that template wear, release-coating decay, demolding force, replica bias, particle residue, spatial defect clustering and functional outcomes can be linked across the full template life. Its central falsifiable claim asks whether lifetime-aware monitoring can predict rising defect probability before damage spreads. Thirty mathematically distinct research plates cover cavity filling, squeeze flow, material relaxation, cure conversion, shrinkage, residual stress, adhesion, demolding, fracture, Archard wear, coating survival, hidden wear states, geometry transfer, Hausdorff error, spatial point processes, defect ancestry, survival hazards, change points, capability, conservative yield, hierarchical variance and qualified-part cost. Across 82 chapters and 410 single-page studies, the monograph develops replication physics, release mechanics, template wear, spatial defect genealogy, adaptive process control, functional qualification, lifecycle economics and independent transfer. Two hundred Research Gates define blind challenges, strong comparators, evidence packages, hard stops and successor forks. Thirty-three Phoenix Answer Embryos present genuinely different witnesses, challenge artifacts, estimators, controllers, economic falsifiers, release keys and handoff kits. The work is explicitly nonclinical and hypothesis-generating. It does not claim a completed manufacturing campaign, human treatment, autonomous in-body efficacy or regulatory approval. Its release rule is conjunctive: wear, demolding force, geometry, defect clustering, unselected yield, task function and traceability must pass together over the complete template life. Author: Feng Cheng-en (33) x Starli Series: STARLI Research Institute XXXIV / Flagship 09 Edition: Research Working Edition v1.0 / October 2026

summary: A Turing machine carries a computation forward through successive configurations, but continuation beyond infinitely many steps requires a rule assigning the configuration from which the next instruction can proceed. The Quantum Γ-Turing machine considered here retains a finite-dimensional register’s trace-norm limit when it exists, preserving the coherence needed by subsequent operations. Averaging a history that never settles permits another continuation, although registers independent at every finite stage can then acquire correlations through their shared timing. We characterise when an assigned state can replace its history without changing a later joint calculation. For assignments compatible with every fixed quantum operation, the largest composition error equals the mean trace-norm distance from the assigned state, and a partner carrying classical labels can approach that value. Independent composition with every partner holds precisely when temporal variance under the chosen mean vanishes. Requiring this under every shift-invariant mean gives uniform vanishing of average squared fluctuations, a condition that permits sparse excursions despite failure of ordinary convergence. For a programme repeatedly applying one fixed channel, independent composition is instead equivalent to ordinary convergence, with the exact error determined by its surviving nonstationary spectral component. Algebraically specified channels and initial states admit a finite decision procedure and certified bounds, while bounded repetitions of states preserve the stronger averaging condition and transfer its certificates to a simulation. These results connect transfinite continuation to finite verification for specified programmes and provide composition certificates that can be carried through a controlled simulation.
title: Independent Composition and Quantum Limits in Transfinite Γ-Turing Machines

summary: Per distruggere la Rotta dei Chersoneso, venne fatta la Battaglia di Cheronea https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battaglia_di_Cheronea_(87_a.C.) Per distruggere i commerci con Etruschi e Cartaginesi, venne fatta la Battaglia di Alalia https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battaglia_del_Mare_Sardo Per distruggere i rapporti con la Facies Sarda dei Bessi di Perperikon, venne fatta la battaglia del Monte Emo:   La battaglia del Monte Emo (o Haemus ) è storicamente legata a due momenti distinti dell'antichità che videro scontrarsi gli eserciti invasori con le tribù tracie, in particolare i Bessi , e il cui contesto geografico e spirituale è strettamente connesso al celebre sito monumentale di Perperikon , situato nelle montagne dei Rodopi in Bulgaria. [ 1 , 2 ] Ecco come si collegano questi tre elementi:   1. La prima battaglia del Monte Emo (335 a.C.) Prima di lanciare la sua campagna contro i Persiani, Alessandro Magno guidò una spedizione nei Balcani per rendere sicuri i confini settentrionali del suo regno. Sul Monte Emo (l'attuale catena dei Monti Balcani) affrontò i Traci Liberi e altre tribù locali. [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] La tattica dei carri: I Traci si erano posizionati sulla vetta e intendevano far rotolare dei pesanti carri giù dai ripidi pendii per rompere la falange macedone. [ 1 , 2 ] La contromossa di Alessandro: Il re macedone ordinò ai suoi soldati di aprire i ranghi per far passare i carri oppure di sdraiarsi a terra coprendosi con gli scudi intersecati (creando una sorta di testuggine). La tattica funzionò alla perfezione: i carri rimbalzarono sugli scudi senza causare vittime tra i Macedoni. Le truppe di Alessandro caricarono poi la vetta, sbaragliando i difensori. [ 1 , 2 , 3 ]   2. Lo scontro dei Bessi con Roma (72 a.C.) In epoca successiva, il nome della battaglia del Monte Emo si associa alla sottomissione definitiva dei Bessi , una delle tribù tracie più bellicose e fanaticamente dedite al culto religioso. Il proconsole romano Marco Licinio Lucullo affrontò i Bessi proprio nei pressi della catena del Monte Emo, sconfiggendoli duramente in una grande battaglia campale, conquistando il loro centro principale ( Uscudama ) e aprendo la strada alla successiva egemonia romana nella regione. [ 1 , 2 , 3 ]   3. Il legame con Perperikon La tribù dei Bessi era storicamente la custode del famosissimo Santuario e Oracolo di Dioniso , situato proprio sulla maestosa roccia sacra di Perperikon . Questo luogo ha un valore storico eccezionale per due importanti profezie collegate ai protagonisti di queste guerre: [ 1 , 2 ] La profezia di Alessandro Magno: Secondo le fonti antiche, prima di iniziare la sua spedizione in Asia (subito dopo aver pacificato la Tracia), Alessandro visitò l'oracolo di Dioniso a Perperikon. Il vino versato sull'altare creò una fiammata altissima fino al cielo, un segno divino che i sacerdoti interpretarono come il presagio che avrebbe conquistato il mondo intero. [ 1 ] La profezia di Ottaviano Augusto: Anni dopo, anche il padre di Augusto (Gaio Ottavio) ricevette nello stesso santuario dei Bessi la medesima profezia sul futuro dominio globale di suo figlio. [ 1 ] In sintesi, la resistenza dei Traci sul Monte Emo rappresenta lo scontro militare per il controllo dei Balcani, mentre Perperikon costituisce il cuore spirituale, politico e identitario della tribù dei Bessi che contro quegli imperi tentò invano di difendere la propria indipendenza. [ 1 , 2 ]   Attenzione: questo documento è stato appena pensato: si tratta di una bozza iniziale basata sul Paradigma Sardo Corso Atlantideo di Luigi Usai. summary: Deepwave provides wave propagation modules for PyTorch, for applications such as seismic imaging and inversion. It performs forward modelling and backpropagation, so it can simulate wave propagation to generate synthetic data, or invert for the scattering potential (reverse-time migration, RTM, or its least-squares counterpart, LSRTM), other model parameters (full-waveform inversion, FWI), initial wavefields, or source wavelets. It can also be used inside a larger chain of operations, with forward and backpropagation flowing through the whole chain end to end. You can use your own objective functions, or functions that generate the propagator's inputs, and PyTorch's automatic differentiation calculates how to backpropagate through them. New to seismic/wave-equation terminology? The glossary defines the terms (PML, CFL, Born, FWI, and more) used throughout this README and the rest of the documentation. Deepwave requires Python 3.9 or later and PyTorch 2.4 or later. First install PyTorch for your CPU or CUDA device using the instructions on the PyTorch website . Then install Deepwave: pip install deepwave   macOS wheels support Apple Silicon. Intel Mac wheels are no longer provided: PyTorch 2.4 and newer do not publish wheels for that platform. Prebuilt x86 wheels require AVX2. Older CPUs need a source build; see installation troubleshooting . PyTorch is Deepwave's only dependency. The example scripts under docs/ additionally import matplotlib (to draw their figures) and, in some cases, numpy , scipy (smoothing and filter design), torchaudio (applying those filters), torchvision and geomloss , but those are needed only to run the examples, never by Deepwave itself. To install all of them: pip install 'deepwave[examples]'   The documentation contains examples and instructions on how to install and use Deepwave. You might also like to watch a video summary of Deepwave . Not every propagator supports every option (dimensionality, backend, boundary faces, batching, second-order differentiation, callbacks, ...). See the capability matrix (declared in the code and checked by conformance tests) before assuming a combination works. Why Deepwave Computationally efficient. Deepwave's compiled kernels use a hand-derived adjoint for better performance and lower memory requirements than pure PyTorch implementations. See what Deepwave calculates . Second derivatives are supported, not just first. The scalar, acoustic, and elastic propagators can compute Hessian-vector products (derivatives of gradients); see the Hessian example . Born (linearised) modelling. Model scattered waves from perturbations to a background medium for linearised inversion and imaging. See the torch.func example . Deepwave fits into an ordinary PyTorch workflow. Because propagation is a normal PyTorch autograd Function , it works directly with PyTorch optimisers, DistributedDataParallel over shots, torch.func transforms, and any PyTorch loss function or neural-network model of the input parameters. See the capability matrix for exactly what each propagator supports. Deepwave does not try to be a general symbolic PDE solver, a multi-node HPC code, or a non-differentiable simulation toolkit — see Devito , SPECFEM , and k-Wave respectively for those needs. If you are choosing between wave-propagation packages, see the comparison guide . (Note: the DeepWave-KAUST GitHub organisation, home of the SWEEP package, is unrelated to this project.) Features Supports the 1D, 2D, and 3D constant density acoustic / scalar wave equation (regular and Born modelling), variable density acoustic, elastic, viscoacoustic (single-mechanism SLS attenuation), elastic VTI (anisotropic), and pseudo-acoustic VTI ( deepwave.acoustic_vti , the Duveneck et al. 2008 V_S=0 reduction) wave equations Runs on CPUs and appropriate GPUs The gradient of all outputs (final wavefields and receiver data) can be calculated with respect to the model parameters (wavespeed, scattering potential, etc
title: Deepwave

summary: Replication package for the paper "Risk, not sunshine: financing costs drive the price of reliable solar-plus-storage electricity in the Middle East and North Africa" (Younas Khan and Štefan Bojnec). WHAT THIS IS Code, input data, result tables, figures and a supplementary data workbook for an hourly solar-plus-battery cost comparison of 19 Middle East and North African countries (24 sites: the 19 capitals plus five interior desert sites). The study decomposes the cross-country cost gap into cost of capital, regional equipment price and solar yield, and tests the result against finance shocks, 24 weather years, CMIP6 climate change and Monte Carlo uncertainty. The manuscript itself is not part of this deposit. CONTENTS - code/: all analysis scripts (photovoltaic model, hourly dispatch and design search, climate factors, 24-weather-year test, build-out link, decomposition, bootstrap, Monte Carlo, figures, supplementary tables) and run_all.sh, which reproduces everything in about 6 minutes on one core. - data/inputs/: the input data the scripts read (NASA POWER weather, CMIP6 point extracts, IRENA and SIPRI data, demand and footprint indicators). - results/: result tables (CSV) and results.json, which holds every number quoted in the paper. - outputs/Supplementary_Data.xlsx: a workbook with one sheet for each supplementary table (S1–S26). - outputs/figures/: the figures generated by the code (PNG and PDF). - README.md: step-by-step instructions, a map from each figure and table to its script, and the provenance and terms of each input file. HOW TO REUSE Install the packages in requirements.txt (Python 3.13), then run ./run_all.sh. All random draws use fixed seeds, so a rerun with the default 2,000 Monte Carlo draws reproduces results.json. LICENCE AND THIRD-PARTY DATA The code is released under the MIT licence and the derived results and workbook under CC BY 4.0. Input files from NASA POWER, IRENA, SIPRI, Ember and the Copernicus Climate Data Store keep the terms of their providers and must be cited to the original sources (see README.md). KNOWN LIMITS Costs of capital for Algeria, Libya, Palestine, Syria and Yemen and all hydrogen-chain costs are placeholders; hourly load is assumed, not measured; each country is represented by one reference site. These are documented in Supplementary Tables S20–S22. VERSIONS Version 1.1.0 contains the files listed above. Further datasets will be added as new versions of this record or as separate records linked to it.
