summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models are bottlenecked by loading routed-expert weights from memory during interactive decoding at small batch sizes. Because most intermediate channels in a routed expert contribute little to any single token, channel selectors predict which channels matter and read only their weights, typically keeping channels above a threshold calibrated on offline data. We show that channel selection needs no calibration data. First, a calibrated threshold does not fix how much a selector reads, because the number of channels passing it varies across inputs; Prox with thresholds calibrated for an 18% read budget actually reads only 12.9% on average across our benchmarks. Second, top-k keeps each token's k highest-scoring channels and needs no calibration data. At the calibrated budget, a selector's top-k version matches or beats its threshold version on the same score in 40 of 43 comparisons at 13% and 18% budgets, including all 23 on generation tasks. The top-k versions also avoid the repetition-loop collapse that calibrated thresholds cause on Gemma 4. Calibrating a threshold thus provides neither of the two things selectors use it for: a known read budget and a consistent accuracy gain at that budget. We furthermore introduce a reader built entirely from the model's weights, which screens channels with a ternary sketch and recovers the skipped ones with a low-rank map. Across three post-trained MoE models, our reader retains 98.1% of full-model accuracy at 17.8% of routed-expert reads, with Triton kernels running MoE blocks 1.60 to 1.90x faster than optimized vLLM at batch one and up to 2.69x at larger batches on the same three models.
title: Channel Selection for Mixture-of-Experts Decoding Needs No Calibration Data

summary: Vision--Language--Action (VLA) models generate robot actions from visual observations and language instructions, but their understanding of physical dynamics remains limited. Video world models can capture scene dynamics, yet generating future videos introduces high latency into the control loop. We introduce PDRVLA, whose lightweight Physical Dynamics Module extracts physical tokens from vision--language features to condition action generation without online video generation. The module learns through direct prediction of future RGB, depth, and optical-flow features, with auxiliary supervision through a frozen pretrained video world model. Training relies entirely on publicly available data, expanded through human-to-robot synthesis, subtask annotation, and embodied chain-of-thought (ECoT) annotation. Across four simulation benchmarks, PDRVLA achieves success rates of 99.3% on LIBERO, 89.9% on LIBERO-Plus, 93.6% on RoboTwin~2.0, and 81.5% on SimplerEnv. Ablations show improved future prediction with world-model supervision and evaluate how subtask conditioning, future object-pose supervision, and ECoT training affect action success.
title: PDRVLA: A Vision-Language-Action Model with Physical Dynamics Representations

summary: Large language models (LLMs) require substantial memory, motivating low-bit weight quantization for efficient deployment. Existing vector quantization (VQ) methods often improve accuracy by increasing the effective coding dimension, which can complicate independent lookup and local codeword updates. We propose CoS-VQ (Coordinated Shared-Scale Vector Quantization), which preserves low-dimensional codewords while jointly optimizing hard indices and their shared scale across positions. The key challenge is scale-induced coupling: the optimal scale depends on the entire codeword combination and, in turn, changes candidate rankings across positions, so pointwise updates can stall even after scale re-optimization. CoS-VQ collects candidates at multiple probe scales and constructs a tangent separable upper bound for the residual-aware quadratic objective. By reducing candidate comparisons to lower envelopes of lines over positive scales, it identifies finitely many representative intervals for joint index--scale updates without exhaustively enumerating codeword combinations. On Qwen3.8-27B, CoS-VQ outperforms QTIP and LLVQ on the evaluated language modeling, coding, and reasoning benchmarks. Ablations from the same initialization further show larger gains from joint updates than from scale-only refinement, highlighting joint selection as an alternative to increasing codeword dimensionality. The code is available at https://github.com/xzktx003/Cos_VQ.
title: CoS-VQ: Coordinated Shared-Scale Vector Quantization for Large Language Models

summary: Embedding-level scaling expands the capacity of language models through lookup-based memory rather than by increasing model depth, width, or dense computation. Extending this idea to vision-language models (VLMs) is challenging because visual features are continuous, spatially structured, and query-dependent, unlike discrete text tokens that naturally support n-gram lookup. We introduce V-LUMEN, a visual lookup memory for VLMs. V-LUMEN discretizes visual features with a frozen codebook, builds spatially aware memory keys through spatial aggregation-based hashing, and modulates them with text-conditioned relevance signals; all addressing is non-parametric, and the retrieved embeddings are fused into the backbone through a gated residual pathway. On five reasoning-intensive benchmarks, V-LUMEN substantially improves a frozen Qwen3-VL-2B backbone and transfers zero-shot to three benchmarks whose images are disjoint from the training data. At a matched parameter budget, moving part of a LoRA or MoE adapter's capacity into V-LUMEN preserves accuracy on two backbones, indicating that external visual memory is an independent capacity axis rather than a stronger adaptation method. Because lookup cost is constant in table size and incurred only once at prefill, this capacity grows in storage rather than in per-token compute. Code is available at https://github.com/miso-choi/V-Lumen.
title: V-LUMEN: Visual Lookup Memory for Embedding Scaling in Vision-Language Models

summary: Proactive LLM agents anticipate service opportunities from ongoing observations and accumulated history. Existing approaches emphasize recent context or retrieval of related memories, providing limited support for validating recurring behavioral regularities and assessing their applicability to the current event. We propose Proactive Memory (ProactMem), which organizes history into recent events, temporal trajectories, and behavioral regularities. Trajectory facts are checked against source events, and regularities are assessed through historical replay before being matched to current conditions. We also construct ProactiveStream, a longitudinal benchmark covering three application scopes, where agents process isolated event streams chronologically under episode-aware opportunity labels. On ProactiveStream, ProactMem achieves an overall effectiveness (F1) of 52.6%, a 21.4% relative improvement over the strongest of five external baselines. Code is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/ProactMem-5351/.
title: Proactive Memory for Event-Driven LLM Agents

summary: Films introduce characters incrementally as they progress. We study the problem of identifying principal characters and assigning their names directly from the movie itself, without using external cast lists, actor photographs, or pre-built character banks. We introduce the character naming task: given a name mentioned in dialogue and the associated video context, the model must determine which visible character bears that name. This task is challenging because name resolution often depends on cinematic cues such as shot-reverse-shot structure, self-introduction, direct address, third-party reference, gaze, and temporal continuity. We provide a dataset and annotations for evaluating character naming and first character appearances, develop a video-and-dialogue model for the task, and compare it with proprietary multimodal large language models. We further introduce a progressive framework for building a character bank as the film unfolds. Together, these contributions support online, human-like movie understanding in which character identities are inferred from the film itself.
title: As the Story Unfolds: Watching a Film and Identifying Characters as a Human Does

summary: Thomson scattering (TS) is a key diagnostic for inferring plasma parameters from scattered power spectra, but its interpretation depends strongly on assumptions about the underlying velocity distribution functions (VDFs). Conventional analyses typically assume Maxwellian distributions, which can be invalid in high-energy-density and laboratory astrophysics plasmas where collisionless, multi-population dynamics produce non-thermal features. In such cases, Maxwellian models may reproduce observed spectra while yielding inaccurate or misleading plasma parameters. We present a generalized TS analysis framework that represents species-specific VDFs in flexible, physically motivated bases and so reconstructs complex, non-equilibrium distributions. To explore the resulting high-dimensional parameter space, we build the forward model from differentiable operations and optimize the VDF parameters by gradient descent. We apply the method to synthetic TS spectra generated from particle-in-cell simulations of a collisionless shock with interacting hydrogen and carbon populations. Immediately upstream of the shock, where the plasma is most non-thermal, the flexible bases cut the mean normalized ion VDF residual from 38.7% for a Maxwellian model to 20.3% and 20.5%, with correspondingly improved time-resolved plasma parameters. We also introduce a systematic method of uncertainty quantification that reveals degeneracies between ion species, highlighting the importance of both flexible VDF modeling and a statistical mapping of the solution space for this inherently ill-posed inversion problem.
title: Recovering Non-Maxwellian Velocity Distribution Functions from Collective Thomson Scattering Spectra Using Generalized Basis Representations

summary: For each time $t$, the regression function $m_t(x)=E[Y_t\mid X_t=x]$ of an outcome on contemporaneous covariates can be regarded as a field on covariate space. We study how this field evolves when the covariates of individual units move as a diffusion and the outcome attached to each unit changes according to its own dynamics. Under mild regularity we show that $m_t$ satisfies a second-order evolution equation whose diffusion term is $\frac12\mathrm{tr}(Σ\nabla^2 m_t)$, the trace of the Hessian of the regression function weighted by the instantaneous covariance $Σ$ of the covariate increments, whose transport term is the drift of the time-reversed covariate process, and whose source term is the conditional mean rate of change of the outcome. The equation is a regression-theoretic reading of a classical transport law, and it yields a Feynman-Kac representation of $m_t$ along reversed covariate paths. We connect the Hessian appearing in the equation to the Hessian estimated by quadratic regression (under Gaussian design the best quadratic approximation has Hessian $E[\nabla^2 m(X)]$ exactly) and to the leading bias of kernel smoothers. For binary outcomes governed by bistable replicator dynamics with imitation among units with similar covariates, the closed equation is of Nagumo type, its planar travelling fronts are exactly logistic in $(x,t)$, and a single logistic regression of the outcome on covariates and time identifies the ratio of diffusion to reaction and the direction of invasion. We discuss identification under panel versus repeated cross-sectional designs and a two-stage estimation strategy, and we illustrate the results with simulations.
title: Regression Functions as Fields on Covariate Space: Evolution Equations, the Hessian, and Identification

summary: For each time $t$, the regression function $m_t(x)=E[Y_t\mid X_t=x]$ of an outcome on contemporaneous covariates can be regarded as a field on covariate space. We study how this field evolves when the covariates of individual units move as a diffusion and the outcome attached to each unit changes according to its own dynamics. Under mild regularity we show that $m_t$ satisfies a second-order evolution equation whose diffusion term is $\frac12\mathrm{tr}(Σ\nabla^2 m_t)$, the trace of the Hessian of the regression function weighted by the instantaneous covariance $Σ$ of the covariate increments, whose transport term is the drift of the time-reversed covariate process, and whose source term is the conditional mean rate of change of the outcome. The equation is a regression-theoretic reading of a classical transport law, and it yields a Feynman-Kac representation of $m_t$ along reversed covariate paths. We connect the Hessian appearing in the equation to the Hessian estimated by quadratic regression (under Gaussian design the best quadratic approximation has Hessian $E[\nabla^2 m(X)]$ exactly) and to the leading bias of kernel smoothers. For binary outcomes governed by bistable replicator dynamics with imitation among units with similar covariates, the closed equation is of Nagumo type, its planar travelling fronts are exactly logistic in $(x,t)$, and a single logistic regression of the outcome on covariates and time identifies the ratio of diffusion to reaction and the direction of invasion. We discuss identification under panel versus repeated cross-sectional designs and a two-stage estimation strategy, and we illustrate the results with simulations.
title: Regression Functions as Fields on Covariate Space: Evolution Equations, the Hessian, and Identification

summary: We develop a multifidelity black-box variational inference (MF-BBVI) approach for PDE-constrained Bayesian inverse problems in which forward solves are expensive and PDE gradients are unavailable. The method is built on score-function estimators for the evidence lower bound (ELBO), which avoid differentiation through the PDE model but are known to suffer from high variance. To address this high variance, we employ multifidelity approximate control-variate estimators that combine a small number of high-fidelity samples with a larger number of low-fidelity samples to reduce estimator variance and the number of high-fidelity evaluations required for optimization. We further develop a PDE-derivative-free second-order optimization strategy based on both gradient and Hessian score-function estimators. For low-fidelity model generation, we propose an on-the-fly strategy that builds and adaptively updates a reduced-order model (ROM) as the variational distribution evolves throughout the optimization. We investigate strategies for adapting the ROM and estimating the approximate control-variate gains, examining tradeoffs between estimator bias, variance reduction, and computational cost. The resulting approach facilitates derivative-free variational inference for large-scale inverse problems through a reduction in overall computational cost. We demonstrate the method on four numerical examples: a linear benchmark with an exact posterior and three PDE-constrained inverse problems.
title: Multifidelity variational inference for derivative-free PDE-constrained inverse problems

summary: We present a survey of approaches to Bayesian inference with simulator forward models, focusing on settings with prohibitively expensive simulators. In this domain, Bayesian optimization-based methods have emerged as the most promising approach. We unify existing methods into a general framework, enabling consistent reasoning about shared algorithmic structure across the fragmented literature. Within this framework, we identify the primary design choices and perform a systematic empirical comparison of their effects on inference efficiency in terms of required simulation budget. A key result of our study is that inference efficiency is often dominated by the choice of surrogate-model response variable, as it directly governs the complexity of the modeled function. Specifically, we demonstrate that the prevalent scalar log-likelihood is a poor response variable, as it discards crucial information. Based on this insight, we introduce the concept of custom \emph{proxy variables}: transformations of simulator outputs engineered to retain more information and provide smoother response surfaces, substantially improving inference efficiency over standard response variables. We provide actionable guidance and a numerically robust Julia package to facilitate practical adoption of Bayesian optimization for simulator inverse problems.
title: Bayesian Inference of Expensive Simulators: Survey and Comparison of Design Choices

summary: Abstract: This paper investigates the computational mathematics of Fs-subsets within the refined framework of Complete Boolean algebras. Using computable homomorphisms, we establish key mathematical properties such as the Fs-De Morgan laws and structural projections. Finally, we discuss practical applications of those computational paradigms in multicriteria decision-making fuzzy soft topology.
title: Computational Mathematics and Structural Properties of Images of Fs-Subsets under an Fs-set Function

summary: According to the overall findings, young adults experiencing difficulties with emotion regulation (suppressing emotions, being unable to understand what they are feeling) have significantly higher levels of social anxiety and anxiety. It was found that young adults who manage their emotions using ‘Cognitive Restructuring’ (the ability to view situations from a positive or flexible perspective) feel much more at ease in social settings and experience reduced anxiety levels.A strong, negative (inverse) correlation has been found between young adults’ general self-efficacy (belief in oneself/confidence in one’s ability to succeed) and their levels of social anxiety. In other words, the higher a young person’s self-efficacy belief—that ‘I can cope with this situation’—the less they fear being humiliated or excluded (social anxiety) when entering social settings. A direct link has been found between young adults’ levels of social anxiety and their emotion regulation skills. The results of the analysis and research confirm that emotion regulation skills are a key variable in predicting anxiety in social settings.
tags: Social Anxiety, Self-Efficacy, Emotional Regulation, Young Adults, Psychological Resilience.
title: The Relationship Between Levels of Social Anxiety, Self-Efficacy and Emotion Regulation Skills in Young Adults

summary: This software release presents the formally verified mathematical developments of Matthew J. Hall’s Chronos Time-First Reconstruction through version 439 , extending the previously published v410 release. The Chronos Time-First framework investigates time as a foundational element of physical evolution and develops a mathematical reconstruction connecting temporal change, nonlinear field dynamics, spatial geometry, and established gravitational physics. The reconstruction is independent of the previously investigated universal constant χ. The underlying development constructs a short-time continuum solution of a 55-component nonlinear Fourier evolution system using Galerkin approximations. Archived Lean proofs establish gravitational constraint preservation, reconstruction of a four-dimensional Lorentzian coordinate spacetime satisfying the Einstein–scalar field equations, scalar stress-energy conservation, and independently derived geometric Bianchi identities. The formal development also includes one-sided endpoint curvature and field-equation results within the constructed physical interval. The v411–v439 update substantially extends the mathematical treatment of physical change as a clock. The Change readout is constructed from specified spatial expansion observables associated with selected solutions of the original nonlinear evolution system. Its initial behavior is derived from the governing source equations. After normalization, the readout has zero initial value and unit right derivative, establishing a mathematically precise relationship between accumulated change and elapsed evolution time near the initial instant. The newly verified developments establish several additional properties: Near-origin clock calibration: The normalized Change readout divided by elapsed evolution time approaches unity as time approaches zero from the positive direction. Cross-solution agreement: Change clocks associated with different admissible selected solutions exhibit matching first-order behavior near the initial instant. Ordered temporal events: Scale-separated event schedules produce strictly ordered clock readings, including an explicitly constructed infinite event sequence approaching the origin. Discrete temporal reconstruction: Under the specified separation conditions, clock readings uniquely identify events within the permitted event sets. Finite-schedule separation bounds: The formal development establishes positive minimum gaps between distinct scheduled event readings across finite families. Robust event identification: The latest results prove that observations subject to sufficiently bounded errors remain closer to their correct nominal event readings than to competing readings. This establishes unique nearest-event decoding within the formally specified finite schedules. Together, these results provide a verified mathematical pathway from nonlinear geometric evolution to normalized temporal change, cross-solution calibration, ordered event measurements, and robust discrete event identification. The cumulative verification inventory increased from 5,153 audited declarations at v410 to 5,531 at v439 , including 171 newly introduced named public theorem declarations across the intervening source modules. The Lean verification records report successful incremental compilation, kernel and dependency checks, and cumulative axiom audits using Lean 4.34.0-rc2 and pinned Mathlib dependencies. The reported axioms are limited to propext , Classical.choice , and Quot.sound . The release does not claim a new, complete clean-source rebuild of the entire historical project. The results establish mathematical properties under explicitly stated hypotheses. Remaining research obligations include global nonlinear continuation and uniqueness, unrestricted continuous-time clock injectivity, invariant probe selection, practical numerical decoding, experimentally calibrated error bounds, and identification of the early
title: Chronos Time-First: Lean-Verified Einstein-Scalar Evolution and Local Calibration of a Geometric Change Readout

summary: Unrefereed research candidate. When two copies of a system, one hotter and one cooler, relax in the same bath, the Markovian Mpemba effect is a crossing of their distances from equilibrium. This package gives a sufficient test that rules out such crossings at every time: if the dynamics and its time reverse preserve the cone of observables with nondecreasing arithmetic prefix means, cooling Gibbs preparations stay ordered for relative entropy (both orientations), squared Hellinger and Rényi divergences of order 0<α≤2, including for common schedules of noncommuting stages. For complete-graph bosonic population rates with common coupling, the test holds for every spectrum and bath temperature exactly when the spontaneous jump weight is concave; Ohmic baths with large enough cutoff, Drude–Lorentz and sub-Ohmic weights qualify on explicit ranges, super-Ohmic weights do not. A certified super-Ohmic example (J=d 3 ) shows an actual relative-entropy crossing. Limits: an exact five-state cone-preserving example has a brief total-variation reversal, and for every N≥4 there are N-level systems with a slow-mode inversion although no proper induced subsystem shows one. The archive contains the 27-page manuscript (PDF and LaTeX), exact rational and interval certificates, a reproduction runner, semantic negative controls, CI and SHA-256 sums. Assurance: written proofs, exact certificates, internal AI-assisted review only (not peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification); the closest antecedent (Avitan et al. 2026) already excludes the slow-mode effect for Ohmic and sub-Ohmic spectra. Creator: Anonymous. Text and data CC0-1.0; code MIT.
title: Thermal ordering under Markovian relaxation: a finite-time criterion and its limits

summary: Novel view synthesis and 3D reconstruction have advanced rapidly with radiance fields and splatting, yet their memory and computational demands limit their use in resource-constrained settings. We introduce Hexels: novel planar hexagonal surface elements with a first-order spatial color field for efficient 3D scene and 2D image representation. Hexels exploit locally planar regions with smoothly varying appearance using fewer, larger primitives. Their hexagonal support provides an area- and boundary-efficient domain, while the local color field captures appearance variation within each primitive. Across 34 scenes, Hexels improve PSNR over memory-matched 2DGS by 4.53-7.38 dB across datasets while requiring lower training VRAM. We further ablate Hexels by showing that per primitive, Hexels outperform 2DGS by upto 4.74 dB while using lower training VRAM and having 2.31 times faster FPS. Even in unconstrained settings, Hexels offers complementary quality-memory trade-offs. For efficient 3D surface reconstruction, Hexels reduce error by 28.9% compared with memory-matched 2DGS across 15 DTU scans. On 6 Tanks and Temples surface scenes, Hexels achieves the highest mean F1 among compared methods (34.38%, versus 31.72% for 2DGS). We further also show that Hexels, as a general primitive, improves 2D image representation over Image-GS. Hexels push the Pareto frontier on the quality-efficiency trade-off of surface-aligned primitives.
title: Honeycomb-Surfels: Compact Hexagonal Primitives for Efficient Scene Rendering and Reconstruction

The package contains the corrected and versioned AnxietyVRET OWL 2 DL ontology with embedded SWRL rules, the corrected example ABox, deterministic boundary-test scripts and outputs, ten executable SPARQL competency-question queries, computational-benchmark scripts and logs, eight representative HL7 FHIR R5 JSON resources with structural-validation output, the AnxietyVRET-to-FHIR mapping crosswalk, semantic-preservation materials, and provenance-reconstruction scripts and outputs. No independently collected clinical patient dataset is included. See README.md for reproduction instructions.

summary: DIGITAL TWINS OF VOLITION, BIOELECTRICITY AND NANOSENSING ACUPUNCTURE AT THE LIMIT is a 777-page English Research Working Edition developing a falsifiable engineering architecture for synchronizing prospective task labels, authorized noninvasive EEG/EMG records, and the physical state of an isolated needle-emulator on a nonliving phantom. The principal question is whether a frozen digital twin improves independently verified prediction of event time, signal and surrogate-device state under deliberately hidden cross-sensor clock delays. The central candidate relation is x[k+1]=A x[k]+B u[k]+w[k], z[k]=C x[k]+v[k]. This is an established mathematical modeling form, not an original biological law or evidence of private thought decoding. The framework treats timebase skew, cue leakage, repeated EEG-window contamination, model discrepancy, shared calibration covariance and hidden actuator latency as explicit challengers. A strong ordinary baseline includes prospective persistence, linear autoregression, calibrated Kalman models and time/cue-only prediction, evaluated on entirely held-out acquisition episodes and unseen days. Thirty differentiated physical and mathematical plates connect state observability, clock drift, covariance propagation, prediction intervals, source ablation, independent actuator safety and external validation to their respective experiments. Across 82 scientific chapters and 410 separately paginated studies, the book develops signal identity, calibration, synchronization, latent-state recovery, prospective prediction, blind falsification, hardware interlocks and second-site replication. Two hundred detailed Research Gates, printed with prominent deep-navy questions on individual pages, lead future investigators through unknown perturbations, strong countermodels, measurable disconfirmation, hard stops and successor evidence packages. Thirty-three Phoenix Answer Embryos propose scientifically distinguishable instruments and paths for revision. The three STARLI author mother volumes contribute method ancestry on sensing identity, functional requalification and sample-to-signal provenance. Eleven separately identified published method references support classical state estimation, EEG algorithm benchmarking, clock synchronization, leakage prevention, cross-subject validation and digital-twin qualification. Those sources do not constitute experimental evidence for the new architecture. All proposed experiments remain unperformed: the volume does not establish clinical acupuncture, autonomous microneedle treatment, volition-to-actuation efficacy or regulatory authorization. Safe early validation is restricted to consent-scoped archived or noninvasive data, inert bench devices and independently calibrated reference instruments. summary: QIGONG BREATHING AND INTELLIGENT ACUPUNCTURE NEUROFEEDBACK COUPLING AT THE LIMIT is a 777-page English Research Working Edition that constructs a falsifiable, explicitly nonclinical research program joining measured breathing tasks, cardiorespiratory and EEG feedback, and isolated microscale actuator surrogates. The central problem is not whether breathing changes heart-rate variability - that has established ordinary physiological explanations - but whether a proposed feedback architecture adds independently measurable predictive or benchtop-control value after breathing rate, phase, expectancy, ordinary cardiorespiratory dynamics, sensor calibration, stimulus timing and strong conventional controllers have been fairly matched. The primary hypothesis is deliberately narrow. A prospective factorial design separates a preregistered breathing condition from an isolated, non-human phantom-drive condition. Its interaction term, order effects, washout, hierarchical sampling units, pressure-related mechanisms and full-episode denominators are subjected to masked scheduling, matched sham sensory cues, covariance-aware uncertainty and independent laboratory reconstruction. Any apparent signal explained by paced breathing or cue entrainment is treated as a legitimate negative result. A bench interaction is not evidence of physiological effects from actual acupuncture in a person. Thirty mathematically differentiated research plates address factorial contrasts, hierarchical estimands, respiratory sinus arrhythmia, ECG event genealogy, pressure-respiration transfer, spectral coherence, lag and phase, multiple comparisons, uncertainty covariance, causal identification, feedback latency, safe-state projection, isolated charge and thermal constraints, abstention and provenance. Across 82 chapters and 410 separately paginated scientific investigations, the book examines operational breathing definitions, reference instruments, EEG and ECG artifacts, blinded feedback protocols, mechanical and electrical phantoms, strong ordinary competitors, statistics, safety vetoes and reproducible handoff. Two hundred full-page Research Gates place their complete falsifiable research question in large deep-navy type, followed by an independently measurable outcome, adverse experiment, conventional physical rival and stopping rule. Thirty-three Phoenix Answer Embryos propose distinct successor objects ranging from calibration bridges and sham credibility tests to independent hardware vetoes, covariance sentinels, multisite reference capsules and protected null-result archives. An accompanying Excel index links formulas, chapters, Gates, candidate objects, citations and explicit evidence limitations. This work reports no executed integrated experiments, in-human needling, electrical stimulation, clinical efficacy, diagnosis or regulatory authorization. Its three STARLI mother-volume DOIs establish author research-method ancestry. Thirteen separately identified external research and metrology DOIs support established measurement, breathing physiology, neurofeedback reporting, uncertainty and statistical methodology, not the novel combined hypothesis. The 777-page layout, formula-clearance checks and 200 Gate color checks were automated; recurring editorial phrasing remains and full independent scientific peer review has not taken place. The primary hypothesis is deliberately narrow. A prospective factorial design separates a preregistered breathing condition from an isolated, non-human phantom-drive condition. Its interaction term, order effects, washout, hierarchical sampling units, pressure-related mechanisms and full-episode denominators are subjected to masked scheduling, matched sham sensory cues, covariance-aware uncertainty and independent laboratory reconstruction. Any apparent signal explained by paced breathing or cue entrainment is treated as a legitimate negative result. A bench interaction is not evidence of physiological effects from actual acupuncture in a person. Thirty mathematically differentiated research plates address factorial contrasts, hierarchical estimands, respiratory sinus arrhythmia, ECG event genealogy, pressure-respiration transfer, spectral coherence, lag and phase, multiple comparisons, uncertainty covariance, causal identification, feedback latency, safe-state projection, isolated charge and thermal constraints, abstention and provenance. Across 82 chapters and 410 separately paginated scientific investigations, the book examines operational breathing definitions, reference instruments, EEG and ECG artifacts, blinded feedback protocols, mechanical and electrical phantoms, strong ordinary competitors, statistics, safety vetoes and reproducible handoff. Two hundred full-page Research Gates place their complete falsifiable research question in large deep-navy type, followed by an independently measurable outcome, adverse experiment, conventional physical rival and stopping rule. Thirty-three Phoenix Answer Embryos propose distinct successor objects ranging from calibration bridges and sham credibility tests to independent hardware vetoes, covariance sentinels, multisite reference capsules and protected null-result archives. An accompanying Excel index links formulas, chapters, Gates, candidate objects, citations and explicit evidence limitations. This work reports no executed integrated experiments, in-human needling, electrical stimulation, clinical efficacy, diagnosis or regulatory authorization. Its three STARLI mother-volume DOIs establish author research-method ancestry. Thirteen separately identified external research and metrology DOIs support established measurement, breathing physiology, neurofeedback reporting, uncertainty and statistical methodology, not the novel combined hypothesis. The 777-page layout, formula-clearance checks and 200 Gate color checks were automated; recurring editorial phrasing remains and full independent scientific peer review has not taken place. summary: BIOELECTRIC FEEDBACK AND PERSONALIZED INTELLIGENT ACUPUNCTURE CONTROL AT THE LIMIT is a 777-page prospective nonclinical research monograph on the boundary between measured bioelectric variability, personalized feedback algorithms, and genuinely verified safe closed-loop operation on inert phantoms and isolated bench hardware. Its primary question is whether a controller calibrated on limited reference data retains a meaningful improvement for entirely unseen simulated individuals while meeting hard, independently witnessed limits. The governing design separates physiological sensing, identification of individual model parameters, selection of feedback commands, and observed physical outcomes. The inherited objective is corrected to a unit-consistent normalized tracking loss and separately measured bench-output burden; no mathematical optimum can compensate a failed hardware veto, force cap, thermal boundary, or missing permission record. A synthetic dummy-output budget is explicitly not a clinical stimulation dose or therapeutic recommendation. Thirty differentiated mathematical plates explore covariance-aware metrology, personal and hierarchical system identification, robust model predictive control, posterior coverage, safe-set feasibility, population shift, abstention, actuator latency, thermal loading, physical isolation, state-space reachability, distributional tail risk and independent requalification. Each plate states construction assumptions, native units, blind tests, stop conditions and a crosswalk to relevant chapters and successor gates. Eighty-two chapters, each with five separately paginated studies, develop electrode and reference calibration, timebase reliability, individual parameter uncertainty, adversarial new-person transfer, fair PID and classical MPC comparisons, closed-loop constraints, sham feedback, safety engineering and handoff to an unrelated laboratory. Two hundred full-page Research Gates are designed as distinctly falsifiable future entry points, including blind reconstruction, strong conventional rivals and external adversarial continuation. Thirty-three Phoenix Answer Embryos propose different metrology tools, decision records, baseline devices or smaller successor theories that can survive disproof of the larger control claim. The three author mother-volume version DOIs are M1 10.5281/zenodo.23480803, M2 10.5281/zenodo.23486020 and M3 10.5281/zenodo.23318840. Separately identified published external DOI studies on neural decoding, population generalization, system identification, control and neurostimulation provide context only: none demonstrates this F47 integrated apparatus. This is a Research Working Edition, not an executed laboratory study, clinical trial, review approval or evidence of therapeutic benefit. Future human stimulation, puncture, clinical research and patient-facing equipment require their own independent regulatory and ethics program. title: BIOELECTRIC FEEDBACK AND PERSONALIZED INTELLIGENT ACUPUNCTURE CONTROL AT THE LIMIT is a 777-page prospective nonclinical research monograph on the boundary between measured bioelectric variability, personalized feedback algorithms, and genuinely verified safe closed-loop operation on inert phantoms and isolated bench hardware. Its primary question is whether a controller calibrated on limited reference data retains a meaningful improvement for entirely unseen simulated individuals while meeting hard, independently witnessed limits. summary: At the start of 1984 Britain still had a large deep coal industry; by the end of 1994 almost all of it had gone, and the last deep mine closed in 2015. Do the towns that grew up around the pits still look different from other towns, and does it matter when their pit closed? I compile a list of 196 deep mines working at the start of 1984 from the Northern Mine Research Society's tables of National Coal Board collieries and Wikipedia's colliery lists, with closure years and locations from OpenStreetMap, Wikidata and OS Open Names. 167 (85%) closed by the end of 1994, with a peak of 32 in 1985. Linking the pits to the ONS built-up areas of 2022, I find 209 pit towns of 2,000 to 100,000 people in England and Wales. Compared with towns of the same size in the same region that had no pit, in Census 2021 they have 2.0 percentage points more adults long-term sick or disabled (a comparison-town median of 2.9%), 3.2 points more adults inactive for reasons other than retirement or study, 6.5 points more in routine or semi-routine work, 8.0 points fewer in managerial or professional work and about £5,900 a year lower mean household income, but the same share in work. Towns with older collieries show about half the gap. Among pit towns, the year the last pit closed makes no clear difference. Because the coalfields differed from other places long before 1984 and no earlier baseline is used, these are associations, not effects of the closures. Interactive version: https://tristan-hotham.github.io/pit-closures/ . Data and code: https://github.com/Tristan-Hotham/pit-closures . Blog post: https://blog.tristanhotham.com/2026/10/28/pit-closures/ .

summary: This record provides the research data and supporting documentation for the revised systematic review “Tactile and Physical Interaction Problems in In-Vehicle Infotainment Systems: A Systematic Literature Review”. The current corpus comprises 342 eligible reports assessed using 34 operational codes across seven categories, yielding 11,628 report–code decisions: 3,635 positive, 7,677 negative and 316 unresolved. The materials are organised into eight editable Word volumes, each with a linked table of contents: Methods and Figures: supplementary sections S1–S12, review methods, operational codebook, PRISMA crosswalk, Figures 1–2 and a source-to-volume index. Corpus and Eligibility: the complete bibliography, bibliographic provenance, retrieval records and eligibility decisions. Characterisation and Appraisal: report characteristics and MMAT domain-level appraisals. Coding Evidence: all 11,628 coding decisions, source-page locators and supporting rationales. Synthesis and Decision Changes: synthesis matrices, coverage and overlap bounds, sensitivity analyses, historical-to-current decision comparisons and Figures 3–5. Historical Citation Screening: historical citation metadata and title-and-abstract screening decisions. Historical Full-Text Eligibility: historical reviewer assessments, eligibility decisions and consensus records. Historical Coding and Reproducibility: historical calibration, independent coding, adjudication and reliability records, together with package documentation and verification-script texts. The current 342-report evidence base is distinguished from the earlier 228-report archive. Historical-to-current linkage covers 5,916 decision pairs for 174 retained reports. Historical independent ratings and consensus decisions remain separate from the authors’ joint source verification conducted from 13 to 23 October 2026. Tables are presented as editable Word content. Repeated wording is retained through linked value keys, and verification scripts are reproduced as editable text in Volume 8. Five updated figures are embedded in the relevant volumes. Copyrighted primary publications and extended verbatim source quotations are not redistributed. Bibliographic identifiers, source-page locators and paraphrased rationales support traceability. Computational consistency checks do not, by themselves, establish scientific validity.

summary: Fine-grained visual perception remains a bottleneck during post-training of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), as perceptual errors can constrain gains from reasoning-focused optimization. Although image-caption pre-training improves perception, its influence can weaken as subsequent stages change data mixtures and objectives. Continuing caption supervision during post-training is challenging because subjective, information-dense descriptions complicate verifiable reward design. We present PerceptRL, which strengthens perception at two complementary levels. Perception RL uses a multi-agent pipeline to extract verified errors from dense image captions and convert the corresponding visual facts into QA pairs with fixed answer labels and rule-based rewards. Chain QA links correlated errors, while multiple-choice QA combines unrelated errors. A specialized route targets high-error domains with tailored verification, and a domain-agnostic general route covers errors beyond these domains. Perception Agentic RL addresses fine-grained and dense cases unresolved by single-turn Perception RL through multi-turn inspection with visual tools. We observe coordinate drift even in models trained to use tools, where incorrect crops or annotations distort evidence and propagate errors. Coordinate Injection corrects spatial operations in cold-start trajectories, while a grounding-aware process reward supervises intermediate spatial fidelity alongside final-answer correctness. Training proceeds through shared cold-start SFT, single-turn Perception RL, and multi-turn Perception Agentic RL. Across seven benchmarks under a shared tool-use protocol, PerceptRL achieves 71.6% average accuracy, surpassing the base model with the same tools and the strongest evaluated frontier VLM by 15.7 and 5.2 percentage points, respectively.
title: PerceptRL: Making Visual Perception Rewardable in MLLMs from Answers to Interactions

summary: AI agents no longer act alone: they cooperate, coordinate and compete within and between groups, increasingly alongside humans who are in, on or out of ``the loop''. Whether such mixed groups can govern themselves is an open question about machine behaviour and human-computer interaction that needs a testbed for hybrid institutions. We present Megabike, a multi-agent simulator and serious game with interdependent arenas for common-pool resource management, cooperative survival and constitutional choice. Riders sharing a megabike must agree their arrangements for steering, pedalling and distributing resources, and their political regime, while negotiating with rival bikes and avoiding an existential threat. Every rule is enforced by the simulator, every action is logged, and any seat can be taken by a human or a machine, so governance can be studied under well-defined metrics. We demonstrate Megabike with forty sessions in which language-model riders with cooperative, lazy, subversive or opposing dispositions chose regimes, elected leaders and expelled one another. The results show that different combinations of agent archetypes could produce unexpected and counterproductive outcomes. We conclude with extensions for systematic experiments mixing human and computational agents.
title: A Serious-Game Testbed for Self-Governing Human-Machine Institutions

summary: Construction safety management still struggles to produce daily safety bulletins (DSBs), structured daily communications that identify site-specific hazards, convey safety protocols, and set preventive measures for workers. Manual DSB creation takes 2-3 hours daily and yields inconsistent quality, with 25% of crews never conducting pretask planning (Olson et al., 2016), diverting safety personnel from field supervision. This study proposes the Lightweight Multi-Agent DSB System (LM-DSB), which integrates retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) with a locally deployable Large Language Model (LLM) to automate DSB generation on consumer-grade personal computers. LM-DSB coordinates specialized planner, researcher, and writer agents in a hierarchical architecture, enhanced by domain-specific fine-tuning on construction safety documentation and RAG grounding in 37 health, safety, and environment (HSE) documents. A two-phase validation assessed feasibility. Phase 1 comparative evaluation showed the multi-agent RAG system (Llama 3-8B) outperformed all alternative configurations, with strong lexical alignment and coherence (TF-IDF: 0.70, BLEU: 0.39, ROUGE-1: 0.66) and near-complete document generation (length ratio: 1.01 vs. 0.39 for single-agent RAG). Phase 2 expert evaluation (N=40) confirmed practical acceptability (mean scores 3.50-4.20 on a 5-point scale), particularly in regulatory compliance (4.20) and factual accuracy (4.10). The findings show that architectural design enables lightweight models to handle safety-critical documentation on consumer-grade hardware, advancing technology democratization in construction safety management. Limitations include knowledge base scope, language constraints, and lack of field deployment validation; future work should address multimodal integration and workflow adoption.

summary: Electric vehicle (EV) charging stations integrating photovoltaic (PV) generation, battery storage, and bidirectional grid exchange must coordinate access to limited chargers with energy supply while considering both energy cost and carbon emissions. This paper proposes a solver-free greedy heuristic (SFGH) for dynamic vehicle scheduling (VS) and a twin delayed deep deterministic policy gradient (TD3) controller for carbon-aware energy dispatch (ED). SFGH assigns EVs according to reductions in service delays, and TD3 controls battery operation to balance energy costs and carbon emissions while meeting the resulting charging demand. The model allows both PV and battery exports, accounting for export revenue and carbon credits. Simulations on year-long case studies show that SFGH--TD3 achieves the lowest accumulated service delay, energy cost, and carbon emissions among the evaluated heuristic and multi-agent deep reinforcement learning (DRL) configurations.
title: Electric Vehicle Scheduling and Carbon-Aware Energy Dispatch for Charging Stations

summary: Evaluating natural language explanations in recommender systems is essential for fostering user trust, transparency, and engagement. However, existing evaluation approaches like human evaluations, while accurate, are resource-intensive and impractical at the scale required by modern recommendation platforms. Also, automated methods using single-agent LLMs suffer from prompt sensitivity and inconsistent outputs. To address these challenges, we propose MAREval, a structured multi-agent framework for evaluating recommendation explanations using large language models. MAREval orchestrates (i) a planner agent that uses a novel Chain of Debate (CoD) prompting strategy to coordinate agent roles and enforce logically consistent evaluation plans; (ii) a moderator agent that regulates discussions by mitigating prompt drift; and (iii) an arbitrator agent that aggregates outputs from multiple evaluation rounds and (iv) a Monte Carlo sampling method, improving robustness and alignment with human judgment. We conduct comprehensive evaluations on both public (TopicalChat) and proprietary recommendation datasets, demonstrating that MAREval outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. Comprehensive experiments on a public benchmark and a proprietary e-commerce dataset show that MAREval improves alignment with human judgments over strong singleand multi-agent baselines. Stability analyses indicate substantially lower variability across repeated trials. In a large human-annotation gate, MAREval meets production quality thresholds where prior evaluators fall short, and online A/B testing demonstrates statistically significant improvements in engagement and revenue metrics. These results establish MAREval as a scalable and reliable solution for human-aligned evaluation of recommendation explanations in real-world systems
title: MAREval: A Multi-Agent Framework for Evaluating Natural Language Recommendation Explanations

summary: Independently developed autonomous agents, such as autonomous vehicles, must guarantee joint compatibility, such as safety and task-completion requirements, when they operate in a shared environment. Existing methods require a centrally designed specification, or interaction mechanism before any agent is deployed. However, such centralized design is unrealistic when agent designs are confidential to their developers, and it is not flexible enough to accommodate future agent designs. We study a bi-level structure in which a regulator coordinates developers by publishing seed agents, and each developer independently tests its agent to ensure that it is compatible with every seed-compatible agent, a property we call future-proofness. Under this structure, joint compatibility is guaranteed for any agents that are designed and tested independently, without any coordination with each other. In this work, we first formulate compatibility for general multi-agent systems and show why it is not trivially implied by seed-compatibility. We then characterize the future-proof agents as the closure of the seed and show that this closure is monotone in the seed. Finally, we study a class of executable tests that involve interaction with the seed alone, and we ask to what extent such tests can distinguish the future-proof agents.
title: Compatibility and future-proof testing for multi-agent systems

summary: Language-model agents increasingly coordinate in large groups, and current agent protocols focus on delivering messages. For these agents, however, the scarce resource is not delivery but reading: every message costs tokens, and the context is finite. Current infrastructure works by push: the sender decides when a message enters the recipient's context, so the recipient reads in arrival order and drops the oldest messages once its context is full. We study the alternative, pull, in which messages wait in an inbox outside the context and the recipient's own rules decide what it reads and keeps. We argue that the inbox is a coordination primitive: each agent sets its rules privately, and those rules decide whether other agents' requests reach it. In simulated societies of up to 16,000 agents, with every decision an LLM judgment, we report three findings. First, push fails as an agent takes part in more coordination at once: an agent leading 20 negotiations with a full memory proposes options already rejected 97% of the time, because it has dropped the oldest replies. Second, an inbox is necessary under heavy, noisy traffic. Where first come, first read misses every request, an inbox that first reads messages carrying a refundable deposit still finds about 60% of the agents a request needs, at every size from 1,000 to 16,000. On a real email network, losses compound: when half the agents adopt such an inbox, forwarded search recovers only 5% of full adoption, against 42% for one-hop search. Third, an inbox comprises four decisions (what to read, what to keep, what a sender pays, and what a reply may say), and the best rule for each depends on the traffic and the agent's role. Multi-agent coordination under load requires an inbox layer designed for the traffic each agent receives.
title: The Inbox as a Coordination Primitive for LLM Agent Societies

summary: TRUSTWORTHY MANUFACTURING AND DIGITAL QUALITY PASSPORTS FOR BIOMEDICAL MICRO/NANOROBOTS AT THE LIMIT Manufacturing Evidence x Digital Traceability x Quality Release This 770-page Research Working Edition develops a falsification-oriented, nonclinical architecture for proving whether every biomedical micro/nanorobot product or batch can be linked to sufficient material, tool, model, process, test and failure evidence for an independent team to reconstruct its release rationale. It distinguishes record completeness from product qualification and treats physical identity, typed provenance, signature status, version compatibility, raw functional evidence, uncertainty, recall and retirement as separate scientific objects. The monograph contains 30 mathematical research plates, 82 chapters, 410 single-page investigations, 200 differentiated Research Gates and 33 genuinely distinguishable Phoenix Answer Embryos. The minimum demonstrator conceals three critical evidence gaps inside a signed passport and tests whether an independent audit refuses release without original-author assistance. A critical missing ancestor, ambiguous product identity, unverifiable signature, incompatible model evidence or unreplayable release decision is a hard veto. This is a prospective scientific architecture, not an executed clinical or regulatory study. It does not claim in-body safety, therapeutic efficacy, regulatory approval or clinical benefit. DOI-linked publications support component methods and boundaries; they do not validate the integrated F25 system. Technical profile: 770 pages; approximately 166,832 English words; 30 formula families; 82 chapters; 410 single-page studies; 200 Research Gates; 33 Phoenix Answer Embryos; 22 DOI records; navigable bookmarks; sixfold QA. summary: This release provides R code, processed data, analysis outputs, and documentation supporting an exploratory investigation of a candidate circRNA–miRNA–mRNA network associated with triple-negative breast cancer recurrence. The package includes differential expression analyses, paired expression comparisons, probe aggregation sensitivity analyses, multiple-testing assessments, descriptive ROC analysis, and archived network and functional annotation results. Input provenance, software session information, and instructions for running the R script are provided. The analyses draw on publicly available GEO datasets GSE154255, GSE38167, GSE101123, GSE182471, and GSE43502. The proposed network represents a computational hypothesis requiring independent clinical and experimental validation. Patient-level survival analysis and direct circRNA–miRNA binding validation are outside the reproducible scope of this package.

summary: Version 1.2 (28 October 2026) adds a notice on the arithmetic precision of the split‑Gibbs runs (NOTICE_v1.2.md), with the check behind it (TF32_CHECK.md, tf32_check_files.zip). DP1’s split‑Gibbs runs used reduced‑precision (TF32) matrix products, which a later like‑for‑like check found shift that sampler’s estimates, while its predictions ran in full float32. The split‑Gibbs null result therefore has a further candidate explanation that DP1 cannot separate. DPS is unaffected. No file of earlier versions has changed. A pre-specified pilot testing whether a blindness-risk score computed before any target data are seen ranks the realised blindness (undetected and uncovered error) of diffusion-prior inference on real X-ray CT objects (2DeteCT) under simulated restricted access. Study DP-A: weak attenuation (F = 32,000), 240 errors × 20 bases. Study DP-B: bounded-reach control, 120 errors × 20 bases. Two samplers: split-Gibbs plug-and-play (primary) and diffusion posterior sampling (secondary). It follows the learned (VAE) pilot, arXiv:2610.28155 (reproducibility package doi:10.5281/zenodo.23392686). The analysis plan, decision rules and fixed result sentences were approved by the author, and predictions and calibration were committed by SHA-256 hash, before any trial. The plan was not lodged with an external registry, so the study is described as pre-specified; the files named PREREG_… are that plan (their names, and the word "pre-registered" inside the hashed plan and the dated log, are kept unchanged so that the recorded hashes still match). Version 1.1 (26 October 2026) adds a post-hoc check of the linear response used by the blindness-risk score, specified in a dated plan and approved before any computation (response_check_plan_v1.md, response_check.py, response_check_results.json, RESPONSE_CHECK.md). Under the plan’s pre-specified reading, the response was not adequate for either sampler in either study, so the null result for the learned score does not separate the learned prior from this approximation. The pre-specified results of version 1.0 are unchanged. README.md and freeze_log.txt are updated accordingly.
title: BLINDSET diffusion-prior blind-set pilot: analysis plan, code, frozen predictions, trial records and results

summary: This is the second annual account of BR implementation and biosecurity under the D4.1 Biosecurity Measures Plan. It updates the ante-operam position reported in D4.3 and focuses on the physical construction pathway, the materials and equipment used, and the controls that limited the risk of transferring non-indigenous species (NIS), pathogens or associated organisms during BLR deployment. Permitting and design: the EIA process concluded positively in July 2025, and the executive project was adopted by the Municipality of Ravenna on 26 August 2025. Construction materials: netting and geotextile were new, while limestone was sourced from a quarry. The physical structure was therefore not assembled from previously used marine materials. BLR design: the executive design uses 5.00 x 2.00 x 0.30/0.60 m modular wire-mesh mattresses filled with 100/200 mm limestone, arranged in macro-blocks over an approximately 100 x 48 m footprint (4,800 m²). Local logistics: mattresses were assembled in the Port of Ravenna, approximately 7 nautical miles from the receiving site. The barge used for deployment operated only on local Emilia-Romagna coastal works and was not used at other sites during the LIFE NatuReef work period. Diving operations: support divers worked only at the project site or in its immediate vicinity during the period; equipment was washed between different jobs. NIS baseline: Jassa slatteryi, Paranthura japonica, Ruditapes philippinarum and Callinectes sapidus were already documented in the area before BLR deployment and remain the appropriate baseline for post-construction interpretation.

summary: Abstract A dimensionless closure relation associated with the five-constant system {e_c, m_e, h, c, G} predicts the frequency ν_zp = 0.0605390 Hz. The same scale has the equivalent laboratory representations τ_zp ≈ 16.5183 s, ν_zp = 0.06053898(67) Hz, ℓ_zp ≈ 10.9614 cm. The present paper formulates a metrological test of this prediction. An admissible determination must identify one of these quantities through an independently observed physical phenomenon rather than calculate it from the closure relation or from an algebraically equivalent expression. In particular, the predicted value must not enter the apparatus, calibration chain, or analysis through G or through any quantity whose numerical value has itself been fixed from the closure. The target follows from α_eG · hν_zp/(m_ec²) = 1, with α_eG = e_c/(m_e√G), which links the electron–gravitational dimensionless sector to the electron Compton frequency. The dimensional origin of the three-member structure {α, α_eG, η_j}, with η_j = hν_j/(m_ec²), is developed in a companion paper, where the closure is proposed as a physical conjecture. An independent realization would provide a direct experimental test of the proposed closure and, within the framework, an alternative route to the gravitational constant, G = [e_chν_zp/(m_e²c²)]². The problem is therefore reduced to a specific metrological question with defined numerical targets, independence criteria, uncertainty propagation, and falsification conditions.
title: Metrological Test of a Predicted Closure Scale at 0.0605390 Hz: Frequency, Period, Velocity, and Length Realizations

summary: Longitudinal baseline studies are rare in temperate agroforestry research, with the vast majority being space-for-time substitution studies. The current temperate agroforestry evidence base is misaligned with greenhouse gas accounting approaches employed by the IPCC and with MRV approaches employed in carbon markets.
title: Towards Improving the Evidence Base for Temperate Agroforestry as a Natural Climate Solution

summary: Lake-Zurich-Bacterial-Integrated-Time-Series (LZ-BITS) Genome architecture predicts proteome allocation in natural bacterial communities Cyrill Hofer¹, Lucas Serra Moncadas¹, Jakob Pernthaler¹, Adrian-Stefan Andrei¹* ¹ Limnological Station, Department of Plant and Microbial Biology, University of Zurich, Kilchberg 8802, Switzerland *Corresponding author: stefan.andrei@limnol.uzh.ch Overview This Zenodo record contains the archived data and analysis resources associated with the study "Genome architecture predicts proteome allocation in natural bacterial communities". The project integrates metagenomic, metaproteomic, flow-cytometric, and environmental time-series data from Lake Zurich, Switzerland, to investigate how genome architecture constrains and predicts proteome investment patterns in natural bacterial communities. Primary raw Lake Zurich metagenomic and metaproteomic data are deposited in ENA and PRIDE, respectively. This archive contains the processed and integrated datasets, analysis workflows, supporting data, Lake Zurich flow-cytometry data, and independent MockD6300 benchmarking datasets. Archive organization Data.zip — Data processing, prepared data, and supporting raw data Contains data-type-specific processing workflows, processed and curated data, intermediate files, and selected raw supporting datasets. Depending on the analysis, files from Data/ are either used directly or incorporated into integrated datasets. The archive additionally contains: Lake Zurich flow-cytometry raw data ( .fcs and CytExpert .xit ) MockD6300 Illumina and Nanopore raw sequencing data MockD6300 raw and corrected draft genome assemblies and assembly benchmarking MockD6300 raw proteomics data ( .mzML ) and associated processing and benchmarking data Datasets.zip — Integrated datasets Contains curated and integrated datasets generated by combining information across data types. These analysis-ready tables are used in downstream comparative and statistical analyses. DataAnalysis_SpringBloom2021.zip — Analysis workflows Contains the workflows used to generate the main and supplementary results of the study, including analysis scripts, statistical analyses, intermediate analysis objects, figure-generation workflows, and figure outputs. Depending on the analysis, inputs originate from Data/ , Datasets/ , or both. Lake Zurich flow cytometry Raw flow-cytometry data are located under: Data/Lake_Data/Raw_Data/Flowcytometry_Data/ Measurements were acquired using a CytoFLEX S flow cytometer (Beckman Coulter) and analyzed using CytExpert v2.4.0.28. 01_Epilimnion_SB2021/ and 01_Epilimnion_SB2021.xit contain the high-resolution integrated epilimnetic measurements corresponding to the same integrated samples as the 37 samples represented in the LZ-BITS dataset. The ZS_YYMMDD directories contain complementary approximately biweekly depth-resolved measurements from the Lake Zurich long-term sampling point at 0, 2.5, 5, 7.5, 10, 12.5, 15, 20, and 40 m depth. A dedicated README.txt accompanies these files. MockD6300 benchmarking data A ZymoBIOMICS Microbial Community Standard D6300 (MockD6300) was used as an independent benchmark for the metagenomic assembly and metaproteomic workflows. To keep the primary public ENA and PRIDE repositories restricted to environmental Lake Zurich LZ-BITS samples, the MockD6300 benchmarking data are provided through this Zenodo archive. Genomic data are located under: Data/Mock_Data/Genomic/ and include paired-end Illumina raw reads, Nanopore raw reads, alternative raw and corrected draft assemblies, and assembly workflow comparisons. Proteomic data are located under: Data/Mock_Data/Proteomic/ and include raw .mzML files, protein-database preparation, DIA-NN outputs, peptide and protein tables, quality-control analyses, and benchmarking workflows. Data repositories Raw Lake Zurich metagenomic sequencing: ENA – European Nucleotide Archive Accession: PRJEB95916 Raw Lake Zurich
title: Lake-Zurich-Bacterial-Integrated-Time-Series-LZ-BITS

summary: Supplementary material for the TGDK article "What the Oracle Knew". It contains the answer-generation and judging harness, the retrieval scorer, the benchmark fixtures and slices whose licences allow redistribution (LC-QuAD 2.0 CC BY 4.0, MetaQA CC BY 3.0, BRINK-family MIT; ComplexWebQuestions as identifiers only), and the frozen outputs of every condition, with md5 checksums. Every retrieval and generated-answer table of the article can be recomputed from these files without the Knowledge Navigator code; README.md gives the commands. The Knowledge Navigator code needed to re-run retrieval is deposited separately with restricted access. Version 1.3: adds the rebuilt MetaQA slice metaqa-kn-v1 (DECISIONS D14): the same 300 questions, with the relation path read from the official MetaQA question types instead of being inferred from the answers, and the full MetaQA knowledge base as A-Box. Includes the slice, the MetaQA files it is built from (question types, test questions, KB; CC BY 3.0) and its builder; the C_metaqa_v1 captures, revision summaries, generations and judgements for the six conditions and both generators (outputs/rev2, with MANIFEST.json and DIAGNOSTICS.md); and paper-side scripts (rev2_stats, agreement_v1, answer_bounds, metaqa_audit_sensitivity, diagnostics_to_json) checked by run_all.sh. In the article MetaQA v1 replaces v0 in Tables 3 to 8 and Figures 2 and 3; v0 is discussed only in Section 5.3 and stays in the archive for comparison. Every version 1.2 file and result is unchanged except the documentation (README, DATASETS, LICENSE-DATA, EXCLUDED, code/paper README), the harness (C_metaqa_v1 support; every earlier output reproduces byte for byte), run_all.sh (now 21 checks, Python 3.12 or later) and the md5 lists. Version 1.2: adds the linker-restricted baseline (Graph BFS restricted to the relations the production relation linker returned, DECISIONS D11) and the MetaQA vector-retrieval cell (D12), both at Knowledge Navigator commit 3e850458, with their captures, revision summaries, generations and judgements, the harness that recomputes them (KN_PAPER_REVISION=1) and three paper-side scripts (ci_rev1, linker_breakdown, answer_sensitivity) checked by run_all.sh. Used in Tables 3, 4, 6, 7 and 8 and Sections 6.4, 6.5 and 7.1 of the article. The frozen version 1.1 results are unchanged. Correction: byte-identical reproduction needs Python 3.12 or later (version 1.1 stated 3.10+); run_all.sh now checks it. Version 1.1: adds code/paper (the statistics the article reports outside the two summary files, with frozen expected outputs and run_all.sh); keeps, for the ComplexWebQuestions runs, the per-case relation-linker error flag (no dataset text) so that Table 5 can count timeouts; removes a stray __pycache__ present in 1.0. Tables and frozen outputs are unchanged.

Version 1.1: adds code/paper (the statistics the article reports outside the two summary files, with frozen expected outputs and run_all.sh); keeps, for the ComplexWebQuestions runs, the per-case relation-linker error flag (no dataset text) so that Table 5 can count timeouts; removes a stray __pycache__ present in 1.0. Tables and frozen outputs are unchanged.
title: Supplementary material for "What the Oracle Knew": relation linking and generated answers in the Knowledge Navigator benchmark

summary: Supplementary material for the TGDK article "What the Oracle Knew". It contains the answer-generation and judging harness, the retrieval scorer, the benchmark fixtures and slices whose licences allow redistribution (LC-QuAD 2.0 CC BY 4.0, MetaQA CC BY 3.0, BRINK-family MIT; ComplexWebQuestions as identifiers only), and the frozen outputs of every condition, with md5 checksums. Every retrieval and generated-answer table of the article can be recomputed from these files without the Knowledge Navigator code; README.md gives the commands. The Knowledge Navigator code needed to re-run retrieval is deposited separately with restricted access. Version 1.3: adds the rebuilt MetaQA slice metaqa-kn-v1 (DECISIONS D14): the same 300 questions, with the relation path read from the official MetaQA question types instead of being inferred from the answers, and the full MetaQA knowledge base as A-Box. Includes the slice, the MetaQA files it is built from (question types, test questions, KB; CC BY 3.0) and its builder; the C_metaqa_v1 captures, revision summaries, generations and judgements for the six conditions and both generators (outputs/rev2, with MANIFEST.json and DIAGNOSTICS.md); and paper-side scripts (rev2_stats, agreement_v1, answer_bounds, metaqa_audit_sensitivity, diagnostics_to_json) checked by run_all.sh. In the article MetaQA v1 replaces v0 in Tables 3 to 8 and Figures 2 and 3; v0 is discussed only in Section 5.3 and stays in the archive for comparison.
