summary: The shift from Industry 4.0 to Industry 5.0 marks a profound paradigm evolution in strategic human resource management (HRM), transitioning from pure technological automation to human-centric socio-technical synergy, sustainability, and organizational resilience. This critical review synthesizes peer-reviewed literature published between 2021 and 2026 to evaluate the influence of digital HR transformation—encompassing artificial intelligence, predictive people analytics, cloud-based HRIS, and collaborative robotics (cobots)—on multi-dimensional employee engagement (vigor, dedication, and absorption). Guided by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA 2020) framework, 16 benchmark empirical and conceptual studies were systematically selected and categorized. The synthesis reveals that while digital HR transformation significantly drives operational efficiency, its direct impact on employee engagement is mediated by digital fluency, perceived organizational support, and psychological safety. Furthermore, algorithmic transparency and responsible data governance serve as critical moderators that mitigate techno-stress, privacy anxieties, and algorithmic burnout. The paper delivers an integrative socio-technical framework for Industry 5.0, offering strategic guidance for organizational leaders seeking to align cutting-edge HR technologies with human well-being and sustainable performance.
tags: Artificial Intelligence in HR; Digital HR Transformation; Employee Engagement; Human-Centricity; Industry 5.0.
title: A CRITICAL REVIEW ON DIGITAL HR TRANSFORMATION AND EMPLOYEE ENGAGEMENT IN THE ERA OF INDUSTRY 5.0

summary: In an increasingly competitive global labor market, organizations face unprecedented challenges in attracting and retaining early-career talent. This critical review synthesizes empirical and theoretical literature published between 2021 and 2026 to examine the influence of employer branding on Millennial and Generation Z talent attraction. Grounded in Signaling Theory, Social Identity Theory, and Person-Organization Fit Theory, this study analyzes 16 benchmark empirical articles identified through PRISMA 2020 systematic review protocols. Findings reveal that while Millennials prioritize career advancement, competitive compensation, and work-life integration, Generation Z candidates place significant emphasis on Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) authenticity, diversity and inclusion, mental health support, and transparent digital communication. Furthermore, the integration of social media employer branding and AI-personalized candidate experiences significantly enhances job application intentions, mediated by perceived organizational prestige and psychological contract trust. The review concludes with a multi-level strategic framework to assist HR practitioners in optimizing omnichannel employer branding value propositions.
tags: Candidate Experience; Employer Branding; Employee Value Proposition (EVP); Generation Z; Millennial Talent; Talent Attraction.
title: EMPLOYER BRANDING AND ITS INFLUENCE ON MILLENNIAL AND GENERATION Z TALENT ATTRACTION: A CRITICAL REVIEW

summary: Writing the Related Work section is a challenging task for inexperienced researchers, requiring significant time, effort, and skill. This study aims to ease this burden by introducing an ICT-based framework that automates the generation of cohesive and well-structured Related Work sections. We propose SciRelate, a novel framework that combines abstractive multidocument summarization and automated keyword-based subsection heading extraction. SciRelate comprises three main modules: (1) document clustering using Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA), (2) related Work generation via a fine-tuned Bidirectional and Autoregressive Transformer (BART) model, and (3) Topic keyword extraction using TopicFusion-MP, a hybrid method that integrates LDA, TextRank, and MPNET embeddings. Experiments were conducted using the NudtRwG dataset, and BART was evaluated using 10-fold cross-validation. LDA clustering effectively identified subsection headings aligned with ground truth structures. The BART model achieved high ROUGE scores: 81.53 (ROUGE-1), 76.19 (ROUGE-2), and 79.03 (ROUGE-L). TopicFusion-MP outperformed six baseline keyword extraction methods in four scenarios, reaching a top similarity score of 0.6398. This study presents a comprehensive, automated pipeline for generating Related Work sections, integrating clustering, summarization, and keyword extraction in a unified framework. SciRelate highlights the potential of ICT tools to support scientific writing, particularly for new researchers.
title: SciRelate: A Framework for Related Work Generation with TopicFusion-MP for Subsection Heading Extraction

This study aims to ease this burden by introducing an ICT-based framework that automates the generation of cohesive and well-structured Related Work sections. We propose SciRelate, a novel framework that combines abstractive multidocument summarization and automated keyword-based subsection heading extraction. SciRelate comprises three main modules: (1) document clustering using Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA), (2) related Work generation via a fine-tuned Bidirectional and Autoregressive Transformer (BART) model, and (3) Topic keyword extraction using TopicFusion-MP, a hybrid method that integrates LDA, TextRank, and MPNET embeddings. Experiments were conducted using the NudtRwG dataset, and BART was evaluated using 10-fold cross-validation. LDA clustering effectively identified subsection headings aligned with ground truth structures. The BART model achieved high ROUGE scores: 81.53 (ROUGE-1), 76.19 (ROUGE-2), and 79.03 (ROUGE-L). TopicFusion-MP outperformed six baseline keyword extraction methods in four scenarios, reaching a top similarity score of 0.6398. This study presents a comprehensive, automated pipeline for generating Related Work sections, integrating clustering, summarization, and keyword extraction in a unified framework. SciRelate highlights the potential of ICT tools to support scientific writing, particularly for new researchers.

summary: Transformer-based architectures have revolutionized Question Answering (QA), yet navigating the trade-off between architectural complexity, computational efficiency, and robust generalization remains a critical challenge. This study presents a rigorous, side-by-side evaluation of four distinct Transformer models—ALBERT, RoBERTa, DeBERTa, and XLNet—on the SQuAD v2.0 benchmark, which demands both precise span extraction and calibration to abstain from unanswerable queries. By employing identical preprocessing pipelines and hyperparameter schedules, we isolate the impact of specific architectural innovations, including dynamic masking, disentangled attention, and permutation language modeling. Experimental results establish RoBERTa as the performance leader (85.90% EM, 88.69% F1), validating the efficacy of robust optimization strategies. Notably, DeBERTa followed closely (85.41% EM, 88.54% F1) but achieved superior performance on unanswerable questions (88.24%), suggesting that its disentangled attention mechanism offers enhanced verification capabilities against distractor entities. XLNet demonstrated competitive potential (78.30% EM) via its autoregressive formulation, while ALBERT confirmed its status as the efficiency benchmark, delivering respectable accuracy (80.70% EM) with a fraction of the parameter footprint. Qualitative error analysis reveals that while lighter models are prone to "hallucinating" answers, advanced architectures primarily fail due to subtle reasoning errors rather than entity mismatch. These findings provide a definitive decision framework for practitioners: prioritizing RoBERTa and DeBERTa for maximum reliability in complex domains, and leveraging ALBERT for scalable, resource-constrained deployments.
title: Comparative Analysis of Transformer-Based Models for Question Answering on SQuAD v2.0

summary: Objective pain assessment is challenging due to the inherently subjective and multidimensional nature of pain, compounded by intersubject variability and noise in naturalistic settings. These factors limit the development of reliable digital biomarkers for clinical decision support and remote monitoring. In this work, we propose a hybrid deep learning architecture that performs early fusion of single channel EEG band power streams with peripheral biosignals recorded by a wristband (electrodermal activity, photoplethysmography/BVP, triaxial accelerometry, and skin temperature). The model uses residual 1D CNN encoders to learn EEG representations and a multilayer perceptron to encode wearable features; the two embeddings are fused in a unified layer to produce predictions for four classes under a strict subject independent evaluation protocol. On PhysioPain, the proposed approach achieves 86.98% accuracy and 87.46% weighted F1, surpassing widely used machine learning baselines, while maintaining an average inference latency of 0.1495 ms per sample for real time operation. In addition to widely used machine learning baselines, we benchmark contemporary deep 1D CNN baselines for a fair comparison: the proposed model improves over 1D DenseNet by 4.49 percentage points in accuracy and 4.70 percentage points in weighted F1, and over 1D ResNet by 7.90 percentage points in accuracy and 7.93 percentage points in weighted F1. To our knowledge, this is the first study to perform subject independent multiclass classification of natural pain phenotypes with explicit handling of class imbalance by early fusion of MindWave EEG with Empatica E4 signals, representing a step toward generalizable and clinically useful digital biomarkers of pain.
title: Multimodal EEG–Wearable Integration for Generalizable Pain Classification

summary: World models can achieve strong control performance without faithfully capturing the dynamics of their environment, limiting their potential for mechanistic interpretability and scientific discovery. Here, we introduce world2vec to learn mechanistic world models without reward information directly from observations and actions. World2vec learns latent dynamics that faithfully reproduce the true system over long prediction horizons, with at least one order of magnitude fewer parameters than DreamerV3, TD-MPC2 and LeWM. This enables state of the art performance in controlling continuous environments from pixels and accurate system identification across a benchmark of 71 attractors, demonstrating how world models are amenable to scientific discovery.
title: world2vec: Mechanistic world models through latent dynamics learning

summary: AI has made remarkable progress in mathematics, solving challenging problems with machine-checkable proofs in Lean, yet typically relying on predefined mathematical definitions and formal specifications. This raises a natural question: can it reason rigorously about an unknown world? We introduce the Algebraic World Model (AWM), a framework that turns interaction with unfamiliar environments into explicit mathematical models supporting formal reasoning. AWM explores the environment and develops executable Python hypotheses, continually testing and revising them against observations. It then structures these hypotheses into typed objects and shared rules, simplifies their structure through category-theory-guided transformations, and formalizes the resulting model in Lean 4 to prove reachability and impossibility. AWM can formally prove that a goal is unreachable, even beyond explored trajectories. On two impossible game levels, it constructs closed, kernel-checked Lean proofs excluding every legal winning sequence in all six runs, while Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra, equipped with coding tools, produce none in twelve baseline runs. Four of AWM's six initial bounds are correct, compared with one for Opus 5.5 and none for GPT-6 Astra; given only feedback that a cheaper win exists, AWM revises its rules and constructs new proofs, reaching six of six correct bounds. Moreover, AWM produces interpretable mathematical models whose rules can be inspected and tested step by step. Across all 25 public ARC-AGI-3 games, these models enable Lean to replay the winning trajectories of all 183 levels and generalize beyond observed play, predicting unseen transitions and detecting changes in game mechanics. With Claude Opus 5, AWM clears all levels with a score of 99.9, while its certified winning trajectories use only 43% of the human baseline's actions.

summary: We introduce Continuous-Action World Models (CoAWM), a framework for learning cross-embodiment spatiotemporal dynamics priors that support robot action generation across embodiments and execution frequencies. At its core is a shared latent function space that captures the spatial and temporal structure of robot actions. We learn this space through two stages. First, function pretraining brings trajectories from different embodiments and sampling frequencies into a common representation, learning shared dynamics priors through action reconstruction and consistency across temporal sampling views. By accommodating heterogeneous robot trajectories, this stage broadens the range of data sources available for pretraining and facilitates scaling to larger and more diverse datasets. Second, we connect the pretrained function space to a world-model backbone, enabling observations, language instructions, and the current robot state to condition the prediction of a latent action function. A single decoder takes any query time and returns the corresponding end-effector action. By separating shared dynamics priors from task-conditioned action selection and temporal sampling, our approach provides a unified foundation for transferring robot experience across embodiments and control frequencies.

summary: Modern LLMs strain device memory through large model weights and attention states, particularly in resource-constrained scenarios. Existing systems separately provision memory for model weights and attention states, imposing fixed fixed boundaries that cannot adapt to the changing memory demands of workloads. Under heavy workloads, insufficient state capacity limits request concurrency and reduces throughput; under light workloads, idle memory in one region cannot be reallocated to another, wasting device memory. Meanwhile, modern LLM architectures introduce heterogeneous tensors with diverse layouts and lifetimes, further complicating memory management. These problems motivate unified memory management for heterogeneous tensors. However, a shared pool alone does not make memory directly reusable across tensors with different allocation granularities and execution layouts. This paper presents Rimuru, a modern LLM serving system that unifies memory management through elastic expert offloading. Rimuru establishes a shared page pool to enables elastic memory sharing across heterogeneous tensors. To accommodate different allocation granularities, Rimuru introduces memory views that allow each tensor type to interpret the shared memory space using its own page size and page table. Furthermore, Rimuru combines huge-page alignment with a multi-level page allocator that splits and merges pages, enabling cross-type capacity reuse. A page-table-aware fused MoE kernel directly accesses non-contiguous expert weights, avoiding copy overhead. Building on these mechanisms, Rimuru employs a workload-aware adjuster that dynamically reallocates pages across tensor types according to runtime demands. Implemented on top of vLLM, Rimuru remains compatible with modern LLMs. Evaluations show that Rimuru achieves up to 19.03x baseline throughput and reduces TTFT by 98.1% on average.
title: Rimuru: Unified Memory Management for Modern LLM Serving via Elastic Expert Offloading

summary: Automatic operator design (AOD) has increasingly adopted large language models (LLMs) to generate problem-specific search and variation operators for multi-objective combinatorial optimization (MOCO). Yet most methods evolve the operators while leaving the process that discovers them fixed. This limits adaptation as new Pareto trade-offs and operator interactions change where and how the search should proceed. We introduce HEMO, which makes the AOD harness itself a self-evolving optimization target. HEMO maintains a persistent harness state and updates one module at a time, revising the logic that determines which experience to retrieve, which operators to improve, which parents to select, and how to formulate the orchestration of search steps. Downstream solution quality and runtime guide these updates, while a discounted UCB scheduler directs adaptation toward promising modules as their utility changes. A persistent memory filesystem preserves candidate outcomes and diagnostic feedback across harness states, enabling successive states to build on accumulated optimization experience. Experiments across eight MOCO tasks and two structurally distinct evolutionary backbones demonstrate strong performance against conventional evolutionary, neural, and LLM-based AOD baselines, together with effective transfer to related tasks. HEMO extends automatic operator design beyond evolving individual operators to improving the search process that discovers them.
title: HEMO: Harness Self-Evolution for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Optimization

summary: Automatic operator design (AOD) has increasingly adopted large language models (LLMs) to generate problem-specific search and variation operators for multi-objective combinatorial optimization (MOCO). Yet most methods evolve the operators while leaving the process that discovers them fixed. This limits adaptation as new Pareto trade-offs and operator interactions change where and how the search should proceed. We introduce HEMO, which makes the AOD harness itself a self-evolving optimization target. HEMO maintains a persistent harness state and updates one module at a time, revising the logic that determines which experience to retrieve, which operators to improve, which parents to select, and how to formulate the orchestration of search steps. Downstream solution quality and runtime guide these updates, while a discounted UCB scheduler directs adaptation toward promising modules as their utility changes. A persistent memory filesystem preserves candidate outcomes and diagnostic feedback across harness states, enabling successive states to build on accumulated optimization experience. Experiments across eight MOCO tasks and two structurally distinct evolutionary backbones demonstrate strong performance against conventional evolutionary, neural, and LLM-based AOD baselines, together with effective transfer to related tasks. summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) rely on Multi-Head Attention (MHA) for sequence modeling, but scaling to long contexts is constrained by the quadratic cost of attention, motivating sub-quadratic recurrent alternatives. This paper formalizes a Dynamic Wave recurrent layer, based on input-dependent exponential damping and cosine phase modulation, and evaluates three 10.94M-parameter configurations (Pure Transformer, Pure Wave, and Hybrid Wave-Attention) on TinyStories under perplexity, latency, throughput and peak VRAM profiling up to 4096 tokens. The Hybrid configuration reaches the best perplexity, 5.95 on the full held-out split against 6.93 for the Transformer and 7.26 for Pure Wave. The efficiency picture, however, is governed by implementation rather than by architecture. Against an unfused attention baseline, Pure Wave uses 78.7% less peak VRAM at a 4096-token context (1404.3 MB vs. 6601.6 MB); against a fused scaled-dot-product attention kernel the same comparison yields no advantage at all (1404.3 MB vs. 1403.6 MB), and in training mode Pure Wave is 8.3% more expensive than the Transformer. Likewise, hoisting elementwise terms out of the recurrence loop speeds the layer up 2.53-fold with no custom kernel, reducing its latency gap to attention from 2.48-fold to 1.12-fold. A hybrid stack is found to inherit the cost of its more expensive mixer rather than the advantage of its cheaper one, its peak VRAM matching the Pure Transformer to within 0.1%. A closed-form memory model reproduces these measurements and predicts the context length beyond which attention overtakes the vocabulary projection. The findings indicate that reported efficiency gains for recurrent attention replacements must be stated relative to a named attention backend and a named implementation, and that hybridization is best justified on quality grounds.

summary: Long-horizon consistency is essential for video world models, yet it becomes difficult to maintain once observed content falls outside the context window. Existing memory mechanisms either retrieve history as implicit context, which remains constrained by context capacity and entangles static and dynamic information or consolidate history into explicit global representations, which struggle to model evolving dynamics and accumulate geometric errors. To overcome these limitations, we introduce \textbf{GROME}, a novel factorized memory framework that augments video world models for long-horizon coherence across both static scenes and dynamic entities. GROME operates via three synergistic components: 1)~\emph{Static-Dynamic Factorization} decouples historical evidence into static and dynamic components, preserving static scene geometry and dynamic entity states separately; 2)~\emph{Local Memory Retrieval} selects spatially aligned static history to eliminate geometric drift alongside the latest dynamic entity states to ensure temporal continuity; 3)~\emph{Training-Free Memory Injection} seamlessly grounds the factorized memory into video world models via their native conditioning pathways. Experiments on long-horizon revisit scenarios demonstrate that GROME substantially enhances scene persistence and dynamic entity fidelity over existing methods, all while preserving the visual quality and controllability of the frozen backbone without additional training. Beyond self-rollouts, GROME readily accommodates external observations as plug-and-play memory, unlocking flexible and controllable video continuation and scene exploration.
title: GROME: GROunding Factorized MEmory into Video World Models

summary: Long-horizon dialogue agents require effective memory systems to recall facts, events, and relationships from interaction histories. In this work, we propose a hybrid-memory architecture comprising episodic memories and structured relational memories and a consolidation mechanism which preserves efficiency. We conduct an empirical study across two benchmarks: LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S. Our experiments demonstrate that the two memory types are consistently complementary, combining both outperform state-of-the-art memory frameworks and achieves 90.2% accuracy on LoCoMo and 85.5% on LongMemEval-S.

In this work, we propose a hybrid-memory architecture comprising episodic memories and structured relational memories and a consolidation mechanism which preserves efficiency. We conduct an empirical study across two benchmarks: LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S. Our experiments demonstrate that the two memory types are consistently complementary, combining both outperform state-of-the-art memory frameworks and achieves 90.2% accuracy on LoCoMo and 85.5% on LongMemEval-S.

summary: Multi-agent LLM systems increasingly rely on persistent memory and inter-agent communication. These capabilities create privacy risks that extend beyond individual interactions: a release appropriate in isolation may become inappropriate when combined with information previously disclosed to a recipient or propagated to downstream agents along the planned workflow. Existing Contextual Integrity (CI) mechanisms for agentic systems typically rely on local judgments that assess each disclosure in isolation, with or without regard to the recipient's history, but do not account for how information propagates downstream. However, compliance at the current boundary does not guarantee appropriateness across the workflow. We introduce Task-Graph Contextual Integrity (TG-CI), to our knowledge the first task-graph-native formalization of Contextual Integrity for multi-agent systems. TG-CI represents a workflow as a Multi-Agent Task Graph (MATG) and extends CI from atomic transfers to stateful, graph-level information flows by jointly considering an item's intended propagation scope and recipients' evolving disclosure states. We operationalize TG-CI through propagation-scoped authorization under two complementary policies: Full-Scope, which requires admissibility across the complete downstream scope, and Auto-Region, which confines each item to its maximal admissible region using lightweight frontier gates. We further introduce MAPLE-Bench, a benchmark of 144 cases across four scenarios that jointly vary MATG topology, disclosure history, compromised-agent placement, and item-level privacy policies. In our primary experimental configuration, TG-CI reduces the mean unauthorized disclosure count by 85.8-94.1% relative to the Local-History CI baseline, while retaining 93.6-96.1% of the baseline's task accuracy, with the two enforcement policies providing complementary privacy--cost--utility trade-offs.
title: Judging Before Propagation: Task-Graph Contextual Integrity for Multi-Agent Privacy

summary: Next point-of-interest (POI) recommendation aims to predict a user's next destination from spatio-temporal check-in data, and serves as the foundation for many location-based services. Recent advances incorporate large language models (LLMs) into this task by textualizing user trajectories to exploit their semantic reasoning ability. However, directly generating POI identifiers with such models is unreliable: POIs are sparse, localized, and long-tailed entities with weak natural-language semantics, which creates a semantic-to-entity gap between high-level mobility intent and concrete POI prediction. To bridge this gap, we propose ANCHOR, a category-anchored framework for semantic-to-entity grounding in next POI recommendation. Specifically, ANCHOR first estimates category-level mobility intent in a compact and stable semantic space, rather than predicting concrete POI entities directly. The inferred intent is then grounded into a candidate set by integrating three complementary sources of mobility evidence: category anchors, historical visit memory, and user preferences. Finally, a history-aware reranker selects the target POI by matching each candidate with the user's historical mobility patterns and current context. Experiments on three real-world check-in datasets show that ANCHOR consistently outperforms representative traditional, structure-enhanced, and LLM-based baselines on the reported metrics. Further analyses validate the effectiveness of semantic-to-entity grounding and show favorable trade-offs among candidate coverage, ranking quality, and inference efficiency.

summary: Gravitational observations can leave material properties undetermined in two different ways: distinct states can have the same total source, and distinct spacetime histories can have the same retained observations. We organize these inverse problems in general relativity through a property-level identifiability criterion, with applications to stars and black hole candidates. Two ideal massless gases illustrate equal-source ambiguity: their temperatures differ by a factor of $(8/29)^{1/4}$ and their entropies differ while their stress-energy tensors agree. A separate causal-fluid example starts with identical sources and geometric data but different constitutive responses; the two models' curvature histories separate at linear order in proper time and their scale factors at cubic order. For black hole candidates, the relevant distinction is between stationary exterior parameters, perturbing fluxes and constituent history. The framework provides a test for whether retained data identify a material property, separating instantaneous source equality, history-wide source equality and observational projection.
title: Curvature Blindness: Material Inference in Stars and Black Hole Candidates

summary: Weight-normalized (WN) training is emerging as a compelling alternative to conventional weight decay (WD), with recent studies reporting substantial pretraining loss gains. We show that these gains are driven primarily by the induced effective learning rate (ELR) trajectory rather than by normalization alone. Matching ELR trajectories largely collapses the training loss dynamics of WN and WD. Schedule design should therefore target ELR rather than the nominal learning rate (LR) alone. Building on this principle, we propose AIR (Affine Inverse-square-Root decay), which combines a theoretically derived $1/\sqrt{t}$ decay with an affine adjustment to satisfy prescribed peak and terminal LRs over a finite training horizon. We further identify late-stage ELR scheduling as a key source of its gains, because a shared late schedule attenuates the effect of earlier LR choices. Experiments on 128 B-token Mixture-of-Experts pretraining demonstrate that AIR outperforms cosine and other candidate schedules in training loss, downstream performance, and hyperparameter robustness, reducing terminal training loss by approximately 0.01 relative to cosine at matched cumulative LR. Applying the same ELR trajectory to WD reproduces the corresponding training dynamics, showing that the benefits extend beyond fixed-norm training and establishing ELR as the principled scheduling object.
title: Your LR Schedule May Not Be Principled: Effective Learning Rate Scheduling in Weight-Normalized Training

summary: Recommender systems face a tension between broadening exposure to diverse viewpoints and avoiding interactions that reinforce extreme positions. This tension is especially consequential in already polarized populations. Here we investigate whether recommendation strategies can reverse polarization rather than merely slow its development. Building on the Attraction--Repulsion Model of opinion dynamics, we introduce two complementary design principles: Tolerance-aware recommendation, which seeks to learn each individual's tolerance for disagreement and reduces exposure to viewpoints beyond that tolerance, and adaptive diversification, which broadens exposure for agents with more extreme opinions while retaining stronger personalization for moderates. Agent-based experiments show that highly personalized recommendations intensify polarization under polarized initial conditions. Tolerance awareness alone primarily slows polarization, whereas combining it with adaptive diversification can reduce polarization below its initial level and, under suitable conditions, restore consensus. Additional experiments incorporating persistent extreme influencers and a spiral-of-silence mechanism show that the combined strategy can mitigate polarization under social pressure and selective participation. To examine whether these findings extend beyond predefined opinion-update rules, we repeat the experiments on a simulated social platform populated by 100 LLM-driven agents prompted to move toward opinions similar to their own and away from those that differ substantially. Across three runs, the combined strategy is again the only recommendation policy tested that reverses polarization in every run. These findings distinguish polarization prevention from reversal and identify tolerance-aware, adaptive exposure as a promising recommendation design principle for reconnecting divided populations.

summary: We present posterior-landscape, a Python framework to identify and characterize morphological features in two-dimensional probability densities. The framework combines concepts from topological data analysis, statistical density-ridge estimation, and scale-space image analysis. It extracts localized concentrations, valleys, ridges, and changes of slope; for Bayesian reconstructions, it propagates uncertainty in feature recovery, geometry, and correspondence across posteriors. The framework also connects two-dimensional structures to features in one-dimensional marginals, and quantifies their correlation with other inferred parameters. We validate the method on controlled densities, and demonstrate its use on gravitational-wave population reconstructions, where it provides a systematic way to identify and interpret population features and assess which ones carry information relevant for cosmology. The resulting catalogues also offer a common morphological representation for future comparisons between predictions and population reconstructions.
title: posterior-landscape: morphological feature finding in two-dimensional probability densities

summary: Artificial intelligence (AI)-based channel state information (CSI) feedback reduces overhead in frequency division duplexing (FDD) massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems, yet its reconstructed CSI depends on the integrity of pilot acquisition. This paper identifies and evaluates the attack path of adversarial pilot injection against this feedback. A transmitted disturbance can damage the user-side estimation before encoding; correctly delivered quantized bits can still represent a contaminated channel estimate. We model this path through attacker propagation, linear minimum mean square error estimation, compression, quantization, and decoding under a total transmit-energy constraint. An adversarial perturbation generator (APG) implements the attack using channel statistics without current legitimate CSI or instantaneous attacker-channel observations at deployment. At a Rician attacker-channel factor of 10~dB and a transmit perturbation-to-signal ratio of $-4$~dB, APG produces a normalized mean-square error (NMSE) of 0.84~dB in base-station CSI reconstruction, compared with $-10.31$~dB for Gaussian interference. Estimator-targeted and reconstruction-targeted attacks yield different error orderings, and reconstruction damage also degrades beamforming. As a countermeasure, alternating adversarial training (AAT) adapts the feedback encoder and decoder to contaminated pilots. With condition-matched training and APGs reoptimized for the final receiver, AAT reduces NMSE by 2.40--3.79~dB across six representative channel--power conditions. The results demonstrate the importance of protecting pilot acquisition alongside quantized feedback delivery.

summary: We have developed an array of up to 20 organic glass scintillator detectors, each consisting of a $3~\mathrm{cm}\times3~\mathrm{cm}\times3~\mathrm{cm}$ scintillator cube coupled to a photomultiplier tube. Sensitive to neutrons from a few hundred keV to several tens of MeV, the array was designed for use with recoil separators in inverse-kinematics measurements of astrophysical $(α,n)$ and $(p,n)$ reactions. It provides a prompt start signal for identifying recoil-neutron coincidences from the recoil time of flight. We characterize eight detectors used in an inverse-kinematics measurement of $^{22}\mathrm{Ne}(α,n)^{25}\mathrm{Mg}$, using source and in-beam data. From the widths of $γ$-ray Compton-edge peaks at 311, 341, 477, and 1062 keVee, we find an energy resolution described by $\mathrm{FWHM}(E)/E=\sqrt{A^2/E+B^2/E^2+C^2}$, with $A=0.00(7)$, $B=0.0618(54)$, and $C=0.135(5)$. The time-difference spectrum of nearest-neighbor $γ$-$γ$ coincidences from a $^{22}\mathrm{Na}$ source (250--600 keVee) gives a FWHM coincidence timing resolution of $910(40)$ ps, corresponding to a single-detector resolution of $640(30)$ ps. Mixed neutron-$γ$ fields from the in-beam reaction and a $^{241}\mathrm{AmBe}$ source show pulse-shape discrimination with an $n$-$γ$ figure of merit $>1$ down to about 100 keVee. Below 100 keVee, the total neutron yield can still be extracted using two-Gaussian fits to energy-gated pulse-shape discrimination spectra. Monte Carlo simulations of the present $^{22}\mathrm{Ne}(α,n)^{25}\mathrm{Mg}$ measurement give a neutron singles detection efficiency of $1.56(45)%$, with uncertainty dominated by systematic effects in the simulation inputs.
title: {DEMAND}: {A}n organic glass scintillator array for direct measurements of $(α,n)$ and $(p,n)$ reactions in inverse kinematics

summary: We consider three-dimensional imaging of compactly supported anisotropic electric media from fixed-frequency polarimetric Maxwell far-field data. Maxwell transversality creates an obstruction absent from scalar Born inversion: each measurement determines only a projected action of the tensor-valued Fourier transform. We first resolve this obstruction by a finite-dimensional polarimetric inversion. For a general complex $3\times3$ contrast, three incidence--observation configurations are necessary, and we give an explicit three-configuration design that is sufficient at every nonzero interior Fourier point. Its Gram determinant yields quantitative conditioning information and exhibits the loss of recoverability at the boundary of the accessible Fourier ball. After tensor demixing, the inverse problem reduces componentwise to restricted Fourier inversion on the unit ball, which we regularize by spectral cutoff in three-dimensional ball generalized prolate spheroidal wave functions. For discrete acquisition, a combined reconstruction error estimate separates the effects of measurement noise, polarimetric amplification, off-grid Fourier mismatch, quadrature error, Born modeling error, and spectral truncation. Numerical tests examine polarimetric conditioning and use analytically generated Born data to compare three- and six-configuration recovery and assess off-grid sensitivity. Reconstructions from full-Maxwell volume-integral data assess the effects of noise, wavenumber, and basis choice, as well as the recovery of different tensor components.

summary: Quantum key distribution (QKD) offers information-theoretic security, but device imperfections introduce implementation vulnerabilities. Experimental evidence of the security consequences of transmitter vulnerabilities in continuous-variable QKD (CV-QKD) remains limited. Here, we experimentally investigate a reversible photorefractive attack in a local-local-oscillator CV-QKD system. Moderate blue-light illumination reduces the modulation variance of a lithium-niobate IQ modulator to a stable value without appreciably increasing estimated excess noise. The variance recovers after illumination is removed. We elucidate the underlying physical mechanisms and develop an attack that exploits recovery to compromise modulation calibration. Receiver measurements confirm that the resulting calibration mismatch leads to overestimated channel transmittance and underestimated excess noise. Key rate calculations based on measured parameters yield a positive estimated rate when the correctly calibrated rate is nonpositive. Recovery can also make the preceding manipulation harder to identify through later inspection. This work provides the first system-level experimental evidence that a reversible photorefractive response can be exploited to compromise modulation calibration in CV-QKD. These findings highlight reversible changes in quantum transmitters as a practical security concern, motivating security analyses and protection strategies that account for both optical perturbations and subsequent recovery.

summary: Low-bit quantization enables efficient deployment of large language models by reducing memory footprint and computational cost. Achieving high accuracy at low precision requires selecting quantization ranges, linear transformations, and weight rounding decisions. Existing approaches typically optimize these components independently using local reconstruction objectives, which fail to account for the varying impact of quantization errors on downstream predictions. Direct optimization of task-level metrics would provide a more faithful objective, but is challenging due to the discontinuous nature of quantization operations and the high computational cost of evaluating their downstream effects. In this work, we derive a Hessian-guided approximation of the output change induced by joint weight and activation quantization. Based on a tractable Fisher approximation, we formulate a unified post-training quantization framework that enables the joint optimization of quantization ranges, linear transformations, and weight rounding under a common output-sensitivity objective. The resulting method remains practical for modern large language models and consistently outperforms state-of-the-art transformation and rounding methods across both channel-wise and block-wise quantization settings.
title: A Unified Hessian-Guided Framework for Post-Training Quantization

summary: As Large Language Model (LLM) agents increasingly participate in persistent social environments, understanding their long-term social interaction capabilities becomes increasingly important. While existing research has advanced long-term memory and conversational context retrieval, less attention has been paid to whether agents can autonomously re-engage with previously inactive conversations. In particular, remembering a past interaction does not necessarily mean that an agent can identify when to revisit it, decide to return, or reconstruct the context needed for a coherent continuation. To investigate this gap, we introduce agent social re-entry as a multi- dimensional evaluation problem, distinguishing three complementary capabilities: Finding, Returning, and Reconstructing. We develop a shared-snapshot evaluation framework that measures these dimensions independently, allowing us to examine how conversational resurfacing and persistent memory relate to different aspects of social re-entry. summary: Training language models whose parameters and optimizer state exceed a single node's memory requires sharding these tensors across devices. Under tensor parallelism (TP) or fully sharded data parallelism (FSDP), matrix-aware optimizers such as Muon introduce communication to perform global matrix operations across shards. We propose Dobb (Distributed Optimizer with Block-diagonal Eigenbases), a matrix-aware optimizer designed to compute updates locally within parameter shards. Dobb approximates the input-activation second moment with diagonal blocks and tracks a complete basis within each block. It projects momentum into these bases, applies sign normalization to the coefficients, and reconstructs the update. When each block lies within one shard under TP or FSDP, Dobb applies its matrix update locally, requiring no communication beyond data-parallel synchronization of the activation second moments. We benchmark Dobb against Dion, a distributed matrix-aware optimizer designed to retain the benefits of orthonormalized updates while reducing communication. On GPT-2 XL (1.56B parameters), Dobb with 16 blocks reaches a validation loss of 2.476, compared with 2.511 for Dion at rank fraction 1/16. Under FSDP on 32 H100 GPUs, Dobb reduces the amortized optimizer-call time from 124.1 ms for Dion to 9.2 ms.
title: Dobb: Shard-Local Preconditioning in Block-Diagonal Eigenbases

summary: A memory can be outdated for present-day reasoning yet indispensable for reconstructing the past. Relevance-based retrieval overlooks this tension: semantic relevance, evidence-grounded validity, and query-specific eligibility are distinct. We propose CALM, a conflict-aware lifecycle memory governance framework that decouples persistent memory preservation from query-time admission. CALM converts heterogeneous records into evidence-grounded memory cells, updates validity and lifecycle states using support, conflict, and dependency signals, and admits query-appropriate evidence through training-free or learned gating informed by temporal applicability. Across LongMemEval-S and LoCoMo with Qwen and GPT backbones, CALM outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving the best overall accuracy. Compared with simple filtering and reranking, query-conditioned admission further improves evidence selection. Conflict-blocking and robustness analyses show CALM suppresses erroneous retrieved memories while retaining useful evidence. Historical-reconstruction experiments demonstrate that preserving superseded records supports accurate earlier-state reasoning without compromising current-state answers.
title: CALM: Conflict-Aware Lifecycle Memory Governance for Long-Horizon Language Agents

summary: Weight-only, lossy quantization substantially reduces the storage and memory requirements for serving large language models (LLMs), but the growing key-value (KV) cache remains a bottleneck for long-context inference on personal devices. We present Group-Adaptive Additive Codec (GAAC), a lossless KV compression and serving system that exploits exponent redundancy to reduce storage and accelerate attention without introducing KV approximation. GAAC encodes BF16 exponents using calibrated per-channel base-plus-offset codes over contiguous ranges. GAAC adapts code widths across small groups while preserving KV values bit-for-bit. A fused attention kernel reconstructs KV tiles on the fly, avoiding full-cache decompression. Block-wise compression and fixed-capacity slots support incremental cache updates and paged serving. Across five tested models, GAAC achieves 1.405-1.407$\times$ lossless BF16 KV compression. We also study compression performance on low-precision tensors FP8 E4M3 caches ( 1.09-1.14$\times$) and E5M2 caches (1.25-1.30$\times$). On NVIDIA DGX Spark, GAAC accelerates decode attention at a 64K-token context by 1.19-1.27$\times$ and end-to-end W4A16 decode steps by 1.04-1.15$\times$. In serving, it reduces resident KV memory by approximately 26% and increases aggregate throughput by 13-29% under comparable KV-memory budgets. On Apple M4, GAAC achieves 1.02-1.25$\times$ attention speedups, demonstrating portability beyond NVIDIA GPUs.
title: GAAC: Lossless KV Compression for Bandwidth-Efficient LLM Inference on Personal Devices

summary: Stationary learning admits an ideal-gas description under restrictive noise assumptions. In neural networks whose gradient noise departs from these assumptions, however, an entropy-scaling relation resembling a Maxwell relation remains approximately valid. We ask which thermodynamic-looking relations follow from scale symmetry rather than equilibrium, and how departures from the ideal-gas description can be quantified, for discrete stochastic gradient dynamics with memory. An exact rescaling of trajectories explains the entropy relation without assuming thermal equilibrium. Within a local harmonic approximation, self-adjusting weight norms yield a spectral equation of state whose virial coefficients are set by moments of the curvature spectrum, and coupled parameter groups can sustain stationary probability currents. Our central result beyond this approximation is an exact curvature-transport identity. Together with a finite-step loss balance, it decomposes corrections to the harmonic fluctuation relation into measurable curvature changes, finite-step remainders, gradient-memory correlations and finite-window drift terms. A related displacement-weighted curvature change provides a diagnostic of the arrow of time; its mean and second moment give a lower bound on the relative entropy between forward and reversed state pairs. We also calculate the activation-boundary contribution to curvature for rectified teacher-student networks with Gaussian inputs. Tests in sphere models, teacher-student networks and convolutional networks on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 support the transport description and identify limits of the harmonic and cubic-remainder approximations. These results separate symmetry-based relations from equilibrium assumptions and provide quantitative diagnostics of nonideal fluctuations in learning dynamics.
title: Finite-step statistical mechanics of scale-invariant learning: spectral equations of state and curvature transport

summary: Full-order surrogates for high-dimensional nonlinear flows are often unnecessary when applications require only selected degrees of freedom. We propose reduced-order models that bypass full-state reconstruction by deploying graph neural networks (GNNs) directly on coarse meshes. Applied to parameterized 2D/3D confined cylinder flows and an unevenly heated cavity over Reynolds/Rayleigh-number ranges, the models generalize to unseen conditions and accurately predict sparse probe locations and integrated quantities. Coarse-mesh GNNs match or outperform finer-mesh surrogates while reducing training time and memory, even for 3D chaotic dynamics. A dynamics-informed adaptive sampling strategy guided by frequency-spectrum variations reduces maximum errors by an order of magnitude versus uniform sampling at negligible cost. Coarse-mesh training also makes noise-augmented multi-step unrolling practical, improving long-horizon autoregressive predictions. The approach outperforms parametric DMD, sparse MLPs, U-Nets, and Fourier neural operators at lower cost, and enables system identification and state estimation from sparse observations. These results show that coarse-mesh representations, adaptive sampling, and noise-augmented unrolled training form an efficient framework for reduced-order modeling of parameterized unsteady flows without solver-resolution reconstruction.
title: Predicting Sparse Observables in Parameterized Unsteady Flows Using Coarse-Mesh Graph Neural Networks

summary: Metis is a bet that better data, better training methods and new architectures can buy what a bigger parameter count cannot, at a fraction of the cost. Metis-1.6 is its latest step: two language models built from scratch by a single researcher, Praxis (2.94B parameters, 0.46B active per pass) and Logos (10.23B parameters, 1.18B active per pass). Both run a hybrid Mamba-2 and attention mixture-of-experts stack twice for every token, so each token gets a second look. Each was trained on 1.02T tokens in total: 804.76B of pretraining, 18B of context extension to 131,072 tokens, and 200B of supervised fine-tuning. Metis-1.6 was never meant to challenge frontier models, and across 40 post-trained benchmarks it mostly does not: Logos averages 52.93, seventh of 17 models in its comparison set and within a point of Qwen3-4B. But it gets there on roughly a twelfth of the median training data of the comparators that disclose it, and with fewer active parameters per token than any model that beats it, which puts it on the Pareto frontier for both. In mathematics it ranks second of 30 models, with 67.50% on AIME 2025 and 63.64% on HMMT February 2026. It is weak at code, instruction following and long context. The rest of the report is the part I found most valuable: what went wrong. The optimizer I configured never ran, and attention trained with AdamW for all of pretraining. A 1.77B-parameter n-gram memory learned to switch itself off. Five fine-tuning choices cost capability. And a length reward under group-mean normalization punished correct solutions for being long once a group's pass rate passed 2/3, a sign inversion I prove and fix with a one-line clamp. I close with the 10B-token ablations behind MoRE (Mixture of Recursive Experts), the looped architecture of Metis-1.7.

Metis-1.6 was never meant to challenge frontier models, and across 40 post-trained benchmarks it mostly does not: Logos averages 52.93, seventh of 17 models in its comparison set and within a point of Qwen3-4B. But it gets there on roughly a twelfth of the median training data of the comparators that disclose it, and with fewer active parameters per token than any model that beats it, which puts it on the Pareto frontier for both. In mathematics it ranks second of 30 models, with 67.50% on AIME 2025 and 63.64% on HMMT February 2026. It is weak at code, instruction following and long context. The rest of the report is the part I found most valuable: what went wrong. The optimizer I configured never ran, and attention trained with AdamW for all of pretraining. A 1.77B-parameter n-gram memory learned to switch itself off. Five fine-tuning choices cost capability. And a length reward under group-mean normalization punished correct solutions for being long once a group's pass rate passed 2/3, a sign inversion I prove and fix with a one-line clamp. I close with the 10B-token ablations behind MoRE (Mixture of Recursive Experts), the looped architecture of Metis-1.7.

summary: Large language models can often identify useful semantic structure in formal artifacts, but their outputs cannot be trusted as proofs or solver decisions. We study whether LLMs can instead guide formal reasoning systems through a narrow, solver-verifiable interface. We instantiate this idea in quantified array SMT solving, where modern instantiation-based techniques can fail when key ground terms and equalities are hidden by auxiliary variables, axiom guards, and nested array terms. We observe that many instances are largely driven by a small set of focal ground terms or constraints, similar to the backdoor sets in SAT solving. Building on this, we present LinguaArray, a framework where an LLM proposes a small Semantic Focus Set (ground terms/constraints), while a conventional SMT solver remains the sole proof engine and certifies all results. LinguaArray uses these LLM-suggested, solver-validated finite sets to significantly enhance solver capability, solving additional satisfiable and unsatisfiable instances that the backend alone fails to solve. It interacts within a finite time and then falls back to the backend solver to mitigate potential regressions. Evaluation on 1015 SMT-LIB instances across five logics under 1200s timeout (including LLM latency) shows that LinguaArray solves up to 69.1% of instances and increases solved-instance counts by 105%--397% over the corresponding backends.
title: Verifiable LLM-Guided Focal SMT Solving for Quantified Arrays

summary: TRUSTWORTHY MANUFACTURING AND DIGITAL QUALITY PASSPORTS FOR BIOMEDICAL MICRO/NANOROBOTS AT THE LIMIT Manufacturing Evidence x Digital Traceability x Quality Release This 770-page Research Working Edition develops a falsification-oriented, nonclinical architecture for proving whether every biomedical micro/nanorobot product or batch can be linked to sufficient material, tool, model, process, test and failure evidence for an independent team to reconstruct its release rationale. It distinguishes record completeness from product qualification and treats physical identity, typed provenance, signature status, version compatibility, raw functional evidence, uncertainty, recall and retirement as separate scientific objects. The monograph contains 30 mathematical research plates, 82 chapters, 410 single-page investigations, 200 differentiated Research Gates and 33 genuinely distinguishable Phoenix Answer Embryos. The minimum demonstrator conceals three critical evidence gaps inside a signed passport and tests whether an independent audit refuses release without original-author assistance. A critical missing ancestor, ambiguous product identity, unverifiable signature, incompatible model evidence or unreplayable release decision is a hard veto. This is a prospective scientific architecture, not an executed clinical or regulatory study. It does not claim in-body safety, therapeutic efficacy, regulatory approval or clinical benefit. DOI-linked publications support component methods and boundaries; they do not validate the integrated F25 system. Technical profile: 770 pages; approximately 166,832 English words; 30 formula families; 82 chapters; 410 single-page studies; 200 Research Gates; 33 Phoenix Answer Embryos; 22 DOI records; navigable bookmarks; sixfold QA. summary: This release provides R code, processed data, analysis outputs, and documentation supporting an exploratory investigation of a candidate circRNA–miRNA–mRNA network associated with triple-negative breast cancer recurrence. The package includes differential expression analyses, paired expression comparisons, probe aggregation sensitivity analyses, multiple-testing assessments, descriptive ROC analysis, and archived network and functional annotation results. Input provenance, software session information, and instructions for running the R script are provided. The analyses draw on publicly available GEO datasets GSE154255, GSE38167, GSE101123, GSE182471, and GSE43502. The proposed network represents a computational hypothesis requiring independent clinical and experimental validation. Patient-level survival analysis and direct circRNA–miRNA binding validation are outside the reproducible scope of this package.

summary: Version 1.2 (28 October 2026) adds a notice on the arithmetic precision of the split‑Gibbs runs (NOTICE_v1.2.md), with the check behind it (TF32_CHECK.md, tf32_check_files.zip). A pre-specified pilot testing whether a blindness-risk score computed before any target data are seen ranks the realised blindness (undetected and uncovered error) of diffusion-prior inference on real X-ray CT objects (2DeteCT) under simulated restricted access. Study DP-A: weak attenuation (F = 32,000), 240 errors × 20 bases. Study DP-B: bounded-reach control, 120 errors × 20 bases. Two samplers: split-Gibbs plug-and-play (primary) and diffusion posterior sampling (secondary). It follows the learned (VAE) pilot, arXiv:2610.28155 (reproducibility package doi:10.5281/zenodo.23392686). The analysis plan, decision rules and fixed result sentences were approved by the author, and predictions and calibration were committed by SHA-256 hash, before any trial. The plan was not lodged with an external registry, so the study is described as pre-specified; the files named PREREG_… are that plan (their names, and the word "pre-registered" inside the hashed plan and the dated log, are kept unchanged so that the recorded hashes still match). Version 1.1 (26 October 2026) adds a post-hoc check of the linear response used by the blindness-risk score, specified in a dated plan and approved before any computation (response_check_plan_v1.md, response_check.py, response_check_results.json, RESPONSE_CHECK.md). summary: VIDEPE ( V isualization & I ntegration of D ata for E pilepsy P resurgical E valuation) is an open-source web application for reviewing EEG and neuroimaging data (MRI, PET, SPECT) side by side, developed at the Epilepsy and Brain Networks Lab, University of Geneva. It runs entirely in the browser: no installation, and no data is uploaded. Try it at https://videpe.github.io/videpe/ VIDEPE is in active development ( pre-1.0 ); features and interfaces may still change. This work was funded by: the CIBM Center for Biomedical Imaging a grant from the Private Foundation of the Geneva University Hospitals (HUG) the Pépite Award from the Innovation Center of the Geneva University Hospitals (HUG) the Swiss National Science Foundation (Ambizione grant 209120), supporting Dr. Nicolas Roehri What's new in v0.21.0 EDF/EDF+ support : EEG recordings in .edf can now be opened, as long as they are continuous and all channels share one sampling rate. Segmentation detection : segmentation and atlas volumes (BIDS _dseg , or names with e.g. atlas , seg , parc , label ) are detected as their own type and get a categorical colormap; white matter masks stay gray. CT detection : CT volumes are recognised and get a dedicated CT colormap; MRI volumes are now labelled ANAT, following BIDS. ESI method on the settings card : the inverse solution method is shown as a subtype on the ESI settings card. Updated demo : the demo now uses an eLORETA inverse solution, an atlas and an updated EEG recording. Full changelog : https://github.com/VIDEPE/videpe/compare/v0.20.0...v0.21.0

summary: First CRAN release. Install with install.packages("glyospalettes") . 208 palettes from Onell Design's Glyos line and 18 Glyos-compatible partner lines, with ggplot2 scales, palette search by plotting use case, colour picking and combining, and designer credit lines for figure captions. Browse every palette at https://bmaitner.github.io/glyospalettes/articles/browse.html. What's new in 0.3.0 Fifteen new palettes from releases since the first sampling pass: the Paleolords Wave 1 figures (Dan Suarez's new Glyos-compatible line, listed under his company "Swamp City Collectibles" with the paleo_ prefix), plus new Battle Tribes, Mighty Maniax, Warlords of Wor, A/V Robot and Cappy Space figures. 208 palettes in total. New glyos_credit() writes a figure-caption or acknowledgments sentence naming the colorways used and the companies that designed them, and follows picks and combines back to their source palettes. citation("glyospalettes") now returns a reference for the package itself. New glyos_pick() pools the colors of one or more palettes (or of a whole company or product line), drops those with poor WCAG contrast against a light, dark or grayscale background, and returns the n colors whose closest pair is farthest apart in CIE Lab, optionally judged under simulated color-vision deficiency. New glyos_combine() takes one color from each of a set of palettes, so a product line becomes a categorical palette with one color per figure; distinct = TRUE spreads the choices out for legibility. Both return named vectors (color by source palette) and print with their provenance; picks draw their swatches on the background they were chosen for. These mirror tf_pick() and tf_team_palette() in the sibling transformerpalettes package.

summary: This version (v1.4) extends the reproducibility package for “Before the weights: a validated admission gate for data-derived decision inputs, demonstrated on aggregate inward FDI” (Results in Engineering, manuscript RINENG-D-26-21905). It adds the records of a prospective, prespecified, synthetic-only benchmark comparing the frozen admission gate (G) with two simpler calibrated admission rules: a Ridge-only rule (A) and a single-split rule (B). The principal finding is unfavourable to the gate. At the smaller planted effect (δ = 0.005), G admitted 27 of 50 cases, A admitted 26 of 50, and B admitted 49 of 50. None of the three rules admitted any of 50 synthetic null or 40 persistence-matched null candidates at their calibrated operating points. The prespecified outcome labels were “No statistically resolved difference” for A and “Evidence favouring the comparator” for B. The comparison is conditional on the tested synthetic designs. It does not establish equal population-level false-admission rates, demonstrate downstream decision improvements, or test genuinely environment-dependent planted effects. The deposit contains the benchmark protocol, implementation, calibration records, seed registry, 190-cell execution return, reduction report, execution history, and independent verification records. Certain operational records have been anonymised to protect identifying information. The included anonymisation map links the public files to their original hash-bound verification records. The public reproduction procedure independently reproduces the scientific reduction, with its documented protocol-hash substitution. The previously published v1.3 record remains unchanged. Consult README.md inside the archive for the reproduction instructions, scientific limitations, and relationship between the public derivative and the verified originals.
title: Before the Weights: Reproducibility package for a validated admission gate for data-derived inputs to mineral-resource decision support

summary: PhenoRewire is a Python command-line tool for detecting network rewiring in metabolomics data. It builds one metabolite co-variation network per biological state, classifies every pair of metabolites as shared, specific to one state or reversed in sign, and tests whether the difference between the two networks exceeds what an arbitrary split of the same samples produces. It identifies metabolites whose correlation neighbourhood reorganised between two states, including those whose abundance did not change and which a differential-abundance analysis cannot report. This release carries the ground-truth benchmarks behind its claims, against DiffCorr and DGCA, with their result tables.
title: PhenoRewire: phenotype-aware metabolomics network rewiring

summary: Raw surface EMG (13 shoulder and elbow muscles) and isometric force/torque recordings (6 channels), sampled at 1 kHz, from three chronic stroke survivors who performed a virtual reaching task in immersive virtual reality with their most affected arm. The virtual cursor was driven either by the measured isometric force (force control) or by the force estimated from EMG (myoelectric control). In myoelectric control, a patient-tailored assistive-adaptive algorithm projected the participant's muscle pattern towards a healthy reference pattern, with an assistance level progressively reduced across blocks. For each participant the dataset contains one session of 9 to 16 blocks (376 trials in total): a maximum voluntary contraction block, force-control baseline blocks and myoelectric-control blocks at different assistance levels. Each trial file contains the raw EMG, forces and torques, the force driving the cursor, the task state, the trial events and the trial metadata (target direction, block, assistance level). A configuration file per participant describes the channels, the sensor calibration and the block settings. The data are pseudonymised. The files are MATLAB v7 MAT-files that can be read in MATLAB and in Python (scipy.io.loadmat). See README.md for the full description of the files and variables. These data support: Nocilli M., d'Avella A., Berger D.J. (2025). A novel approach to promote upper-limb motor recovery in stroke survivors using assistive myoelectric control and adaptive visual feedback in virtual reality. Front. Bioeng. Biotechnol. 13:1628679. https://doi.org/10.3389/fbioe.2025.1628679  Funding: Italian Ministry of Health, European Union - NextGenerationEU - NRRP M6C2 - Investment 2.1, project PNRR-POC-2022-12375705, CUP J83C22002060007.
title: Raw EMG and isometric force data from a pilot study of assistive myoelectric control with adaptive visual feedback in virtual reality in chronic stroke survivors

summary: Description This repository provides supporting data products, analysis code, and reproducibility materials for an independent evaluation of the original satellite-derived modified temperature–humidity index (MTHI) proposed by Feng et al. (2020), using ground-observed air-based temperature–humidity index (THI) as the reference quantity. The study examines two distinct measurement tasks: (1) numerical estimation of air-based THI under frozen cross-network calibration, and (2) within-date spatial ranking of observed air-based THI across urban monitoring stations. The development dataset comprises 849 matched station-date observations from 109 stations across 18 dates in Leuven, Belgium (2021–2022). The independent external evaluation uses 249 matched observations from 19 urban stations across 20 dates in Novi Sad, Serbia (2016–2017). The predefined spatial-ranking analysis includes 197 observations across 13 qualifying dates. The numerical evaluation considers four predictor configurations: LST alone, the original Feng MTHI, LST and NDMI, and LST, NDMI and land surface emissivity. Model selection and calibration were performed using the Leuven development data, with the resulting configurations frozen before external evaluation. The repository supports verification of the reported numerical comparisons, spatial-ranking analyses, uncertainty assessments, and associated sensitivity analyses. The accompanying README documents the included files, their provenance, processing procedures, and reproducibility instructions. Any restrictions on redistribution of third-party observational or satellite data are documented separately. This archive does not constitute a validation of physiological heat stress, thermal perception, or human heat-health risk.
title: Reproducibility Data and Code for Evaluating Satellite-Derived MTHI Against Urban Air-Based THI

The development dataset comprises 849 matched station-date observations from 109 stations across 18 dates in Leuven, Belgium (2021–2022). The independent external evaluation uses 249 matched observations from 19 urban stations across 20 dates in Novi Sad, Serbia (2016–2017). The predefined spatial-ranking analysis includes 197 observations across 13 qualifying dates. The numerical evaluation considers four predictor configurations: LST alone, the original Feng MTHI, LST and NDMI, and LST, NDMI and land surface emissivity. Model selection and calibration were performed using the Leuven development data, with the resulting configurations frozen before external evaluation. The repository supports verification of the reported numerical comparisons, spatial-ranking analyses, uncertainty assessments, and associated sensitivity analyses. The accompanying README documents the included files, their provenance, processing procedures, and reproducibility instructions. Any restrictions on redistribution of third-party observational or satellite data are documented separately. This archive does not constitute a validation of physiological heat stress, thermal perception, or human heat-health risk.
title: Reproducibility Data and Code for Evaluating Satellite-Derived MTHI Against Urban Air-Based THI

summary: Failures of deployed clinical artificial intelligence (AI) systems have often originated in how their training data were generated. Whether the programs that train the health AI workforce teach practitioners to examine data provenance is unknown. We conducted a cross-sectional analysis of the publicly advertised curricula of health AI education programs at U.S. universities, identified through a structured multisource web search between April and July 2026. Two investigators coded coverage of data provenance (structural, dataset limitations, or data management only), ethics, and sustainability; collaborative structure; technical prerequisites; and the disciplinary background and gender of named instructors. The primary outcome was provenance coverage at the structural or dataset-limitations level. Of 43 candidate entries, 36 programs at 25 institutional units in 21 universities were included. Ethics was covered by 29 programs (80.6%; 95% confidence interval [CI], 65.0 to 90.2), data provenance by 8 (22.2%; 95% CI, 11.7 to 38.1), and structural provenance by 6 (16.7%; 95% CI, 7.9 to 31.9). None of the seven master's degree programs met the primary outcome, and no program addressed sustainability. Eighteen programs included team-based work, but only 5 assembled teams across clinical and technical backgrounds. Of 92 named instructors, 76.1% came from computational disciplines and 3.3% from the social sciences or humanities; among the 51 whose gender could be determined, 66.7% were men. U.S. health AI education programs widely taught ethics but rarely taught how clinical data are produced. None addressed the environmental cost of computation, and most instructors came from computational disciplines.
title: Data Provenance and Ethics in the Curricula of U.S. Health AI Education Programs

summary: This paper sets out what a sustained federal research and investment agenda would need to include to close that gap--not within a single budget cycle, but over the decade such an undertaking will realistically require. It identifies where the gap is most pronounced today: in the methods needed to verify and certify components of uncertain origin, in the foundational hardware research that has long been underfunded relative to software, in the physical infrastructure researchers need to test systems at scale, and in the workforce required to build and sustain all of it. Robotics should not be treated merely as a downstream beneficiary of a broader artificial intelligence investment strategy. It constitutes its own supply chain, with its own points of failure, and merits its own sustained federal commitment.
title: Securing the Robotics Supply Chain

summary: Offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning remains challenging in stochastic long-horizon settings, where compounding value estimation errors hinder reliable goal reaching. While prior methods have sought to address this challenge through various approaches, a key challenge remains path mirage, where agents overcommit to spuriously successful trajectories in offline datasets induced by stochasticity, often leading to failure on difficult tasks. To address this issue, we propose Branch-aware Graph Planning (BGP), which captures stochastic branching structures by identifying high-variability points as graph nodes and designing goal-conditioned edges with segmented learning to avoid unreliable branches and reduce unnecessary stochasticity along paths. As a result, BGP enables reliable goal reaching even in highly stochastic long-horizon environments, and experiments on diverse OGBench tasks show that it substantially outperforms prior state-of-the-art offline goal-conditioned RL methods. Our implementation is available at https://umlic.github.io/papers/BGP/.
title: Escaping Path Mirages in Offline Goal-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning

summary: Military installation energy readiness depends on having sufficient resources to sustain mission-critical loads throughout a prolonged utility outage. This paper develops a method to help operators manage energy resources during normal grid-connected operation while preserving islanded readiness. A robust viability kernel identifies combinations of battery energy, fuel, and load-shifting capability sufficient to sustain critical load under uncertain demand and photovoltaic generation. A probability bound translates stochastic generator start failures and recovery into a deterministic generator count selected to meet a specified availability requirement at islanding. Case studies for a fourteen-day islanding requirement at 0.999 islanding-entry availability show that advance warning of an outage can be used to prepare resources to meet a higher readiness requirement before islanding begins. The case studies further demonstrate that economic-only operation and the evaluated fixed battery reserve policy can fail to sustain critical load for the required duration, whereas enforcing the resource-dependent requirement preserves readiness at a modest increase in modeled grid-connected operating cost. These results demonstrate how active resource management can preserve long-duration energy readiness. The framework also helps commanders understand how readiness changes with operating conditions, even when the available resources remain the same.
title: Readiness-Constrained Pre-Islanding Dispatch for Military Microgrids

summary: The way software gets built is changing dramatically. AI agents now create pull requests, select dependencies, refactor codebases, interpret test failures, and execute infrastructure changes across the entire Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC). AI agents are autonomous team members, but unlike human engineers, they are ephemeral - their reasoning, decisions, and tool calls vanish the moment the session ends. Modern Security incidents involving intent mismatch or injection are becoming increasingly common - forcing us to address AI Agents as an insider threat. No widely adopted standard yet enables agentic provenance and governance and its obvious that you can't hold an ephemeral process accountable. The git log was designed for human commits. It shows what changed. It does not show what an AI agent did, which model it used, which tools it called, or whether anyone was accountable for the outcome. Every governance framework, every audit trail, every compliance control in the SDLC was built around one assumption: a human made the decision. That assumption no longer holds. This shift introduces 3 main procedural problems (not addressing scale) - Supply-chain vector - The agentic coder is software, so it is a supply-chain security risk. Policy guardrails - How to ensure the agentic coder is compliant with the policies of the organization. Task-alignment - How to align the agentic coder on its tasks and goals. We introduce Agentic Process Evidence (APE), a signed, tamper-evident, machine-readable attestation of agentic processes, linking the sessions to their outcome (process-aware logging). APE enables Policy-as-Code control over the agentic processes, allowing for human in the loop only when it's needed. We support the in-toto style attestation framework, and the protocol is aligned with the relevant regulations
title: Agentic process evidence

summary: A ring is right pure semisimple if every right module is a direct sum of finitely generated modules, and the pure semisimplicity conjecture asserts that every such ring is of finite representation type. In this article, a division ring extension $H\subseteq T$ is constructed such that the bimodule ${}_HT_T$ has right dimension sequence $(1,2,2,2,\dots)$ and $T$ is infinite-dimensional as a left $H$-space. The division ring $T$ is the union of the fraction division rings of the nearest-neighbour quantum Laurent algebras with parameter $1/2$, and $H$ is the image of $T$ under a compatible family of conjugations. The extension is controlled by right bases of every length and by two-sided flags of adjacent division subrings, which identify all iterated right duals up to explicit twists. It follows that the triangular ring $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}H&T\\0&T\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ is right pure semisimple but neither left pure semisimple nor of finite representation type, so that the pure semisimplicity conjecture fails.
title: A counterexample to the pure semisimplicity conjecture

summary: World action models (WAMs) increasingly couple internal visual or world representations with action generation, making their world-to-action pathways a critical yet poorly understood source of robustness. We investigate when perturbations to these internal representations actually become behaviorally consequential, and uncover a pronounced mismatch between representation perturbability and closed-loop vulnerability: attack effectiveness varies sharply across visual K/V routes, while larger representation displacement does not reliably imply stronger control failure. Our analysis attributes this mismatch to the action-conditioned readout, where keys determine where action queries read and values determine what content they receive. This motivates an action-facing view of vulnerability, in which the effect of a perturbation depends on how it is routed into action generation rather than on representation-space magnitude alone. We instantiate this view with Tail-AV, a short-probe signal for identifying vulnerable routes, and operationalize it in PASA-KV, which selects action-facing K/V targets before training a fresh task-shared attack. Experiments across multiple WAM systems and a physical robot validate readout-informed target selection, demonstrate strong closed-loop attacks, and reveal substantial system-level differences in resistance.
title: PASA-KV: Attacking Action-Facing Visual Routes in World Action Models
